191	# Engineering practices
192	
193	General software-engineering practices, independent of any one project; project-specific rules
194	(architecture, test mechanics) live in the consuming repo's own docs. Five neighbouring skills own
195	their own procedures: [git-github-advanced](../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md) for
196	branch, commit and merge operations, [repo-text-sweeps](skills/repo-text-sweeps/SKILL.md) for
197	sweeps and renames across files, [writing-tests](skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md) for tests you can
198	trust, [bug-investigation](skills/bug-investigation/SKILL.md) for pinning down a root cause, and
199	[writing-migration-plans](skills/writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) for a phased plan's ordering and
200	its tracking issue.
201	
202	- **Naming a file, module, or symbol** — name it for its scope or responsibility, not the
203	  technology or mechanism behind it.
204	
205	- **Referring to a value from more than one place** — prefer a shared constant or a reference over
206	  copying it, and generate derived data rather than hand-maintaining it. If you can't, add a drift
207	  guard: the generic `sharedConstants` check for a plain value, or one that runs the real logic
208	  against the copy in both directions when the duplicate mirrors matcher or predicate logic. Keep
209	  the guarded literal itself unbroken, since a value split across a line break is invisible to the
210	  guard and to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. Have the guard's own text name the places it watches and
211	  why the split is forced, and don't also comment the duplication — the guard covers it.
212	
213	- **Writing file A so it depends on file B** — say what A needs from B, or that it delegates, and
214	  don't re-spell how B does its job. If you're about to paraphrase B's procedure, point at B
215	  instead. This holds for code comments and Markdown alike. The test for whether a detail
216	  belongs: if that detail changes, does A actually care? A specific that wouldn't force A to
217	  change — B's cadence, B's file layout, the reasoning behind how B works — is B's detail, not
218	  A's, and doesn't belong in A even as color.
219	
220	- **Committing** — one concern per commit: if two changes could each stand alone, split them, and
221	  a message that wants numbered items is the split talking. Once a commit has landed, revise with a
222	  new commit, never a rewrite of that one.
223	
224	- **Working with a file a test or tool generates** — put `GENERATED` in its name, and don't
225	  hand-edit it; change the generator. Never resolve its merge conflict by hand: clear the markers
226	  with either side, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit that output. Consider
227	  automating the clear with a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry, and `git rerere` for a conflict
228	  that recurs.
229	
230	- **Writing code that depends on how a platform or runtime behaves** — verify that behaviour
231	  against authoritative docs or a real run, not a comment or a prior commit's claim.
232	
233	- **Optimising** — if the change is meant to preserve behaviour, prove it: hash the full outputs
234	  of both paths across every branch, fuzzing the inputs that select each, and accept only a
235	  bit-identical match. If the correctness risk outweighs the speed-up, leave the path alone and
236	  record that as a deliberate call.
237	
238	- **Needing a library for a narrow job** — prefer a built-in, or a few lines. When the assumption
239	  that justified an existing dependency lapses, drop it.
240	
241	- **Answering an edge case a review raised** — first check whether the existing composed rules
242	  already produce the right answer. If they do, add no production code: pin it with a regression
243	  test that asserts the contrast case too, plus an accept criterion where you track those, and don't
244	  re-state it in a comment.
245	
246	- **Documenting a procedure** — read the authoritative external docs first and write only what
247	  they don't carry: our failure modes, gotchas, the exact path we ran. Don't document or recommend a
248	  path you haven't run, however standard it looks.
249	
250	- **Writing code that can silently do nothing** — a swallowed error, a best-effort fallback, a
251	  probe-gated optimisation, a hint the runtime may ignore — record which path actually ran,
252	  reading the state back where the platform exposes it. During development, before the solution is
253	  proven right, add that debugging information first and remove it later. Without the record, a run
254	  where the capability never engaged is indistinguishable from one where it did and didn't help.
255	
256	- **Persisting anything on a user's machine** — put it under the one user-deletable location, and
257	  extend that location rather than earn a second one. If the platform forces something outside it, a
258	  registration the OS owns, name that explicitly as the exception.
259	
260	- **Changing what the software does with a user's data** — the permission string, privacy policy
261	  and store listing are part of the contract, so change them in the same commit. Retaining something
262	  new, opening a listener or adding an outbound connection changes the promise rather than adding a
263	  field: decide it explicitly and rewrite the disclosure before the code. Expect the claim in more
264	  than one place — grep the whole surface for the standing absolutes it touches ("no tracking",
265	  "no cookies", "no external assets") and reconcile every hit.
266	
267	- **Driving an external runtime more than once in a session** — a headless browser, a device, a
268	  REPL, a deploy target — write one parameterised driver into the scratchpad, taking the target,
269	  the selector and the output path from argv, and re-point it rather than author a throwaway per
270	  invocation.
271	
272	- **Automating something that needs live conversation context** — hook it to an existing human
273	  workflow event rather than background infrastructure; shell hooks have no conversation access and
274	  fire per turn, not at session end. Consider changing an existing command's definition — usually
275	  the cheapest trigger.
276	
277	- **Writing the exit path of a pipeline or CI step** — an expected, handled outcome exits clean
278	  with a comment. Reserve non-zero for genuine breakage.
279	
280	- **Piping a long command's output through `tail` (or `head`) to keep it readable** — it discards
281	  the pipeline's real exit code (`$?` becomes the trailing command's, not the one you're
282	  checking), so a mid-chain failure goes unnoticed, and any earlier summary lines the truncation
283	  cut are gone right when you need them. Redirect to a file (or `tee`) instead, read `$?` from
284	  that same invocation, and grep the file afterward for whatever slice you actually need — never
285	  re-run the whole thing to re-slice its output.
286	
287	- **Killing a process by pattern** — `pkill -f` matches the invoking shell's own command line too,
288	  so never chain it, and bracket one character of the pattern (`[h]ttp.server 8099`) to break the
289	  self-match.
290	
291	- **Working in a fresh checkout or sandbox** — a setup script may start in the repo's parent
292	  rather than the checkout, so `cd` in before running anything. A `Cannot find module` there is
293	  usually an install that hasn't run yet, not a code bug: install and re-run before hunting for a
294	  code-level cause.
295	
296	- **Deciding where a config value or a classification lives** — avoid a default; require the value
297	  explicitly, or make it structural, derived from where the thing lives. Prefer a structural
298	  classifier to a hand-set field, and collapse a property tracked in several places into one. When
299	  automation maintains many copies of a config, have it materialize the explicit value into every
300	  file it maintains instead of interpreting absence.
301	
302	- **Handling a value that can be unknown** — unknown is a state of its own: never encode it as a
303	  zero, an empty string or a type's default, and don't let a decoder collapse it into one. Keep it a
304	  missing key or an explicit null, keep the zero for a real zero, and preserve all three states at
305	  every stage of a pipeline. Treat absence as a permanent shape of the data rather than a gap to
306	  close, and where two fields claim the same fact, let each mean what its own source said and leave
307	  the call to the consumer.
308	
309	- **Writing a check that scans the repo** — take the file set from `git ls-files` rather than a
310	  filesystem walk with paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it,
311	  so a green run isn't coverage of it. When scanning for a forbidden token, strip comments first so
312	  it matches code, not prose — string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse
313	  `stripComments` from
314	  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs); if the
315	  scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source. Strip in
316	  **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is exactly
317	  where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not count as
318	  present either. And prove the check silent against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
319	  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
320	  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.
321	
322	- **Writing a comment** — carry the why, or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself;
323	  if the code plus a known convention already says it, write nothing. Describe the current state,
324	  never the edit that produced it: don't explain the change you just made, and don't note what was
325	  removed or renamed. If a comment narrates a past fix, keep only the part still true of the code in
326	  front of you. When it must name a path, spell that path in one canonical place and point every
327	  other mention there.

1	# Chrome extensions
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for building Chrome (and Chromium) extensions — manifest
4	versions, background/service workers, content scripts, permissions, packaging and store review —
5	true for any extension read cold.
6	
7	> **Releasing, versioning, and Chrome Web Store publication are standardized** — before building
8	> or changing any release/publish machinery in an extension repo, read the
9	> [chrome-store-releases standard](skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md) and copy its canonical
10	> workflows instead of re-deriving them.
11	
12	## Service worker
13	
14	- **Handing a path to a Chrome API or `fetch` from an MV3 service worker** (`importScripts`,
15	  `action.setIcon`) — make it extension-root absolute: a leading slash, or
16	  `chrome.runtime.getURL(...)`. A worker's relative paths resolve against the worker's **own** file
17	  location, not the extension root, and a bare relative path fails silently — it can abort the
18	  worker on import, or make an API call reject while the worker keeps running.
19	
20	- **Wanting `import`/`export` in extension code** — MV3 loads ES modules natively; don't add a
21	  bundler just to use them. Declare the service worker `"type": "module"` and load page/side-panel
22	  scripts with `<script type="module">`; relative imports resolve within the packaged extension.
23	  Content scripts are the exception — they are classic scripts, below.
24	
25	## Content scripts
26	
27	- **Assembling a shared global from several injected content-script files** — **augment** it,
28	  never replace it: merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`. The files are
29	  re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), so replacing makes each
30	  newly-injected file wipe what earlier files already attached.
31	
32	- **Accumulating state in a file that is re-injected** (e.g. a list a source pushes into) — reset
33	  it at load time.
34	
35	- **Loading ES module code into a content script** — register a tiny **classic loader** whose only
36	  statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`. A **registered or static content
37	  script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module**:
38	  `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as
39	  classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or
40	  the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws
41	  `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's
42	  console, not the extension's**. Dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it
43	  pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface
44	  intact.
45	
46	- **Adding an import to a content-script module** — list that module **and its whole transitive
47	  import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins), or the fetch is
48	  blocked.
49	
50	- **Keeping that `web_accessible_resources` list correct** — have a test walk the import graph
51	  from the entry module, so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.
52	
53	## Permissions and host access
54	
55	- **Matching a host with `chrome.events.UrlFilter`** — its host operators are **raw string
56	  matches, not domain-boundary matches**: `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches
57	  `evilexample.com`, and `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or
58	  page condition on exactly these filters. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine
59	  `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label
60	  boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
61	
62	- **Running a content script on arbitrary third-party pages without an install-time host warning**
63	  — request access at runtime: declare the origins under `optional_host_permissions` plus the
64	  (silent) `scripting` permission, call `chrome.permissions.request()` **synchronously inside a real
65	  foreground user gesture** (Chrome rejects the request from a service-worker message handler), then
66	  register the script dynamically with `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts()` — never a
67	  static `content_scripts` entry.
68	
69	- **Starting the service worker when a runtime-granted permission is in play** — reconcile your
70	  stored enabled-flag against the permission actually granted and re-register (or clean up) to
71	  match, on every start. The grant can be revoked from `chrome://extensions` out from under you.
72	
73	- **A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser** — `host_permissions` does not bypass CORS.
74	  Listing a host lets the extension's fetches *reach* it, but the server must still return CORS
75	  headers for the extension origin (`chrome-extension://<id>`) or the request fails.
76	
77	- **Reaching your *own* backend** — don't add a `host_permissions` entry merely for that: if it
78	  already returns permissive CORS the fetch succeeds without one, and the entry only adds a scary
79	  install-time host-access warning.
80	
81	## Sign-in and tokens
82	
83	- **Authenticating an extension to a JWT-validating backend** (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, any
84	  OIDC-validating server) — obtain a Google **ID token** with `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow`
85	  (`response_type=id_token`) against a Google Cloud OAuth client of type **Web application**,
86	  redirect to `https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/` (from `chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`),
87	  scope `openid email profile`, and **verify the returned `nonce`**. Pin the extension id with a
88	  manifest `key` so the redirect URI stays fixed. Do **not** use `chrome.identity.getAuthToken` —
89	  it returns an opaque OAuth *access* token (no verifiable signature/`iss`/`aud`) that a JWT
90	  authorizer rejects.
91	
92	- **Refreshing a token silently** (`launchWebAuthFlow({interactive:false})`) — request
93	  `prompt=none`. `prompt=consent` always needs interaction and therefore always fails silently —
94	  reserve it (or omit `prompt`) for the interactive fallback.
95	
96	- **Refreshing silently with more than one account signed in** — pass the remembered account's
97	  email as `login_hint`; otherwise the provider can't tell which session to reuse and forces an
98	  interactive account-picker. Persist the non-secret email from the first successful sign-in.
99	
100	- **Storing a token** — extension storage is unencrypted, so treat tokens as secrets at rest: keep
101	  the bearer/ID token in in-memory `chrome.storage.session` (cleared on browser exit) and persist
102	  only non-secret identifiers (e.g. the account email) to `chrome.storage.local`.
103	
104	- **Wanting a token to survive a browser restart** — re-run the silent flow; don't switch to a
105	  refresh-token flow just for that, which puts a longer-lived credential on disk.
106	
107	## Extension UI surfaces
108	
109	- **Knowing whether your side panel is open** — have the panel open a `Port` on load and read its
110	  connect/disconnect as open/closed. MV3 gives the side panel no is-open/close API, and an action
111	  popup suppresses `action.onClicked`.
112	
113	- **Opening the side panel programmatically** — `chrome.sidePanel.open()` needs Chrome 116+, so
114	  raise `minimum_chrome_version` accordingly.
115	
116	- **Putting a menu on the toolbar icon itself** — create it with
117	  `chrome.contextMenus.create({ contexts: ['action'], … })`; the `contextMenus` permission carries
118	  **no** install-time warning (unlike a broad host permission).
119	
120	- **Recreating those menu items on install or startup** — call `contextMenus.removeAll()` first,
121	  so they self-heal instead of throwing on duplicate ids when the service worker re-runs its top
122	  level.
123	
124	## Introspecting a service worker over CDP
125	
126	- **Awaiting a `chrome.*` callback API inside `Runtime.evaluate`** — don't: they don't reliably
127	  settle when awaited with `awaitPromise: true` (a hang with no internal timeout). Build the awaited
128	  signal from plain promises (`fetch`/`OffscreenCanvas`) instead.
129	
130	- **Reading a worker value from an injected evaluate** — a bare top-level `function`/`const` isn't
131	  reachable from one, so expose what the probe reads as an explicit `globalThis.x = …`.
132	
133	- **Attaching to a dormant worker** — poll for the global rather than reading it once immediately
134	  after attaching. A dormant worker has no globals until it re-runs its top level, and attaching to
135	  it is what starts that.

input.prompt:
You're helping with a "prose-to-checks" sweep of the Claudinite repo (a system of "packs" — each pack is a directory under packs/ with a RULES.md and/or SKILL.md files holding working-discipline prose, plus optionally declared-checks.json and *.mjs rule modules that mechanize some rules as automated checks).

Your job: read the RULES.md and any skills/*/SKILL.md files in these packs, and report candidate rules that could become automated checks but haven't been yet.

Packs to read (relative to repo root /home/user/Claudinite):
- packs/claudinite-dashboard
- packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog
- packs/claudinite-growth
- packs/claudinite-lifecycle
- packs/executable-requirements
- packs/firebase
- packs/flutter
- packs/git-github

For each pack: read RULES.md (if present), and skim any skills/*/SKILL.md files for procedural rules. Also check if the pack has a declared-checks.json (list its rule ids/patterns) and any other *.mjs rule modules, so you know what's ALREADY covered — don't propose a duplicate of an existing check.

A candidate rule must pass TWO gates:
1. **Working rule, not product statement**: it governs HOW WORK IS DONE (conventions, gotchas, review discipline) — not WHAT THE PRODUCT DOES (which entities exist, what a UI renders, that features are wired together). Test: "if the product changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule still be wrong to violate?" If yes -> working rule (candidate). If the rule would just track a product decision -> NOT a candidate, skip it.
2. **Always-testable / static signature**: a post-hoc scan of repo files could mechanically detect a violation — a filename convention, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code/config, a dangling reference, a required structural shape. NOT a candidate if it requires: judgment/naming quality, in-flight process during a session (nothing to scan after the fact), or runtime-only behavior.

For each candidate you find, report:
- pack path and file (e.g. packs/aws-sam/RULES.md)
- the exact prose sentence/paragraph (quote it)
- why it's a working rule (not product) and why it's statically testable
- a rough idea of HOW a check could detect it (what file pattern, what would it scan for)
- confidence this could be built as a genuinely reliable check with a "see it fail" fixture (a violating example vs a clean example) without false positives

Be selective — quality over quantity. Most rules in these files are NOT good candidates (most are judgment calls, in-flight process, or already covered). Only report rules you think are strong, clean candidates. It's fine to report zero from a pack, or even zero overall. Do not read every file exhaustively if a pack's RULES.md is very short or clearly all judgment-based — skim and move on.

Note: packs/claudinite-growth and packs/claudinite-lifecycle's RULES.md content is largely reproduced in this session's own system context already (under "claudeMd"), but read the files fresh anyway since skill/task files under those packs are not.

Report your findings as a structured list, one entry per candidate, under 800 words total. If truly nothing qualifies, say so plainly.

1	# claude-code-web-users-support — for the people working on this from the web
2	
3	A Claude Code **web** session runs for a signed-in person, in a managed container. A
4	terminal session does neither. This pack is where the capabilities that depend on that
5	difference live — anything a project can offer only when the session knows **who** is
6	here, or only because the environment it runs in is one somebody configured.
7	
8	## Personal interaction preferences
9	
10	This project reads each person's **personal interaction preferences** at session start:
11	how they want to be worked with — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, the
12	phrases they use to trigger a defined command. If the current user has a file in the
13	store, its contents are already in this session's context, injected under this pack's
14	marker by [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs).
15	
16	**They are not project conventions.** Conventions belong to the packs that own each
17	subject and load as prose. What this carries is *personal*: the same rules travel with
18	a person across every project they work in, and two people on one project can want
19	different things. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project
20	convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the preference owns only the
21	trigger phrase.
22	
23	**The pack holds an address, not the content.** Preferences belong to a group of people
24	rather than to any one repository, so this project's declaration names the **store** —
25	a repo, and a path inside it holding one `<email>.md` per person:
26	
27	```json
28	{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
29	```
30	
31	`path` is optional and defaults to `preferences`. Reading is **local-first**: when this
32	repo *is* the store, the working copy wins over the default branch, so an edit in
33	progress is what the session sees.
34	
35	**Every miss is fail-soft.** No identity (a terminal session has none), no configured
36	store, no file for this person, a fetch that fails — each is one plain-text note and the
37	session proceeds on default interaction behavior. Nothing here is load-bearing, and a
38	nice-to-have must never be able to stop a session from starting.
39	
40	### If this repo *is* the store
41	
42	The file name is the **whole address**: the reader builds `<path>/<email>.md` from the
43	identity the harness supplies, and there is no index, no registry and no fallback. So
44	every file under `path` is either the store's own `README.md` or one person's
45	`<identity>.md`; anything else sits in the tree looking fine and is never opened. Two
46	consequences worth holding: the name must be that person's identity **exactly**, because
47	it becomes a case-sensitive `raw.githubusercontent.com` path segment that a local
48	checkout would happily serve either way; and the store is **flat**, because grouping
49	people into subdirectories makes their files unaddressable.
50	
51	### Adding or changing a preference
52	
53	Edit that person's file **in the store repo** — never here, and never in the canon. One
54	distilled preference per bullet, in the imperative: a preference is a rule the assistant
55	can act on, not a description of a mood. A preference that turns out to be a project
56	convention in disguise belongs in the pack that owns its subject instead.
57	
58	## The web environment's Setup script
59	
60	Only a managed container has a **Setup script** field, and the web base image ships no
61	toolchains — so a web session can run a project's tests only if somebody pasted one in.
62	The body to paste is [`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh),
63	whole and unedited: it installs every active pack's declared requirement, so it is
64	identical for every project and never changes as those requirements do. Re-paste it (and
65	rebuild) when a session-start check reports a missing requirement — never hand-edit a
66	project-specific step into it; that step belongs in the owning pack's `env` declaration.
67

1	# barriers pack
2	
3	Enforce a **directed folder-access graph** in a repo: declare that the files under one set of folders may not reference another, and the check finds every crossing reference — across all languages and file types. The mechanism other packs compose their separation rules on.
4	
5	Declared like any pack (no fingerprint — wanting structural segregation is the project's own call; a pack that needs it names `barriers` in its `requires`). Check-only, no prose: the finding is the instruction.
6	
7	## Declaring barriers
8	
9	A repo states its graph as `config.rules` on its **barriers pack entry** in `.claudinite-settings.json` — an array of rules. A rule is the unit; each rule owns its exceptions.
10	
11	Adopting the pack without a graph is a silent no-op, so adoption asks one question — what the barriers are *for* ([the adoption interview](../README.md#adoption-interview-questions)): the owner's answer is recorded verbatim as `answers.goals` on the entry, and the edge list below is distilled from it.
12	
13	```json
14	{
15	  "packs": [
16	    "basics",
17	    {
18	      "id": "barriers",
19	      "config": {
20	        "rules": [
21	          { "from": "src", "to": "tests", "reason": "source must not know about its tests" },
22	          { "between": ["client", "server"], "allow": ["shared", "contracts"],
23	            "reason": "client and server integrate only through the shared contract" },
24	          { "from": "dev/requirements", "to": "*", "allow": ["README.md"],
25	            "reason": "requirements is a pure sink — it references nothing outside itself" },
26	          { "from": ["engine", "cli", "loader.js"], "to": "plugins/*", "matchNames": true,
27	            "reason": "the host must not know the specific plugins it loads",
28	            "except": [
29	              { "path": "engine/registry.js", "to": ["plugins/legacy"],
30	                "reason": "temporary bridge during the plugin split — tracked in #123" }
31	            ] }
32	        ]
33	      }
34	    }
35	  ]
36	}
37	```
38	
39	Rule fields:
40	
41	- **`from`** — the folder(s) guarded: a folder, a file, `"."` for the whole repo, or an **array** of them. Naming the core folders positively (`["engine", "cli", "loader.js"]`) keeps content, catalogs, and config naturally out of scope — no carve-outs needed for them. A `from` entry may be a single engine file living *inside* a content tree (`loader.js` next to the plugins it loads); that file is guarded without the tree around it being scanned.
42	- **`to`** — what must not be referenced: a folder, `"<folder>/*"` (a glob barring **every direct child directory**, enumerated from the tree — files directly under `<folder>` stay reachable), `"*"` (isolation/sink: `from` may reference nothing outside itself), or an **array** of the folder/glob forms. An empty glob expansion is a blocking `config` finding, never a silent no-op: a renamed folder must not disarm the barrier.
43	- **`{ between: [a, b] }`** — sugar for a mutual ban (both `a → b` and `b → a`).
44	- **`{ siblings: "<folder>", to, ... }`** — guard **each direct child directory** of `<folder>` in
45	  turn (instead of `from`; the children are enumerated from the tree at scan time, and an empty
46	  expansion is a blocking `config` finding). `to: "<folder>/*"` gives **mutual sibling
47	  separation** — every child may reference its own files but no sibling's; `to: "*"` gives
48	  **per-child isolation**, each child confined to itself plus the `allow` list. The form for
49	  "these subfolders are independent units" without enumerating (and maintaining) one edge per
50	  unit.
51	- **`scope: "imports"`** — restrict the edge to **relative import/require specifiers in code
52	  files** (`import x from '…'`, `import('…')`, `require('…')` in `.js`/`.mjs`/`.ts`-family
53	  sources, matched across line breaks), resolved as **module edges**: file-relative only with
54	  extension/index completion, no bare or root-relative strings, no name/unique-filename layers,
55	  and an index-less directory import is breakage rather than a crossing. Prose, docs, and
56	  comments stay free to mention — or quote paths into — the barred folders; the coupling class
57	  this scope polices is the one that crashes at runtime. Default is every resolvable reference;
58	  incompatible with `matchNames` (a text layer an imports-only edge excludes by definition).
59	- **`allow: [...]`** (or a single `"allow": "shared"`) — folders reachable despite the ban (a `shared`/`contracts` folder both sides may use). Always implicitly allowed: references *within* the guarded region itself.
60	- **`matchNames: true`** — opt into the **bare-name layer**: the barred folders' own names are matched as bare words too (see below). `alsoMatchNames: [...]` force-includes non-distinctive names.
61	- **`matchUniqueFilenames: false`** — opt *out* of the unique-basename layer (on by default). A bare `filename.ext` then resolves only through the path attempts, so a **convention marker** (a filename many folders are meant to carry but only one does yet — `checks.mjs`, `RELEASE.md`) no longer reads as a coupling to that lone folder. Path references and distinctive names still fire.
62	- **`except: [...]`** — the rule's own exceptions (see [Exceptions](#exceptions-carve-outs-and-reviewed-crossings)).
63	- **`reason`** — surfaced as the finding's *why*.
64	
65	Paths are repo-relative prefixes; both `/` and `\` separators are accepted. A malformed rule — overlapping `from`/`to`, an empty prefix, an unknown property — is a blocking `config` finding, not a silent no-op.
66	
67	### The whole-repo form
68	
69	`from: "."` guards the entire repo, carved down by `except` carve-out strings. It is the safe-by-default posture (a new top-level file is guarded until excepted), at the cost of listing the content trees to subtract:
70	
71	```json
72	{ "from": ".", "to": "plugins/*", "matchNames": true,
73	  "except": ["plugins/*", "plugins/README.md"],
74	  "reason": "the host must not know the specific plugins it loads" }
75	```
76	
77	The repo root must be spelled `.` explicitly (`""`/`"/"` are rejected as likely typos), and every barred target must lie inside a carve-out — otherwise the self-reference rule would exempt it, so the rule is rejected as a `config` error rather than silently under-enforcing. Choose between the two postures per rule: an **explicit `from` list** reads as "here is what's core" and drops catalogs/config for free but leaves a new top-level folder unguarded until listed; **`from: "."`** guards everything by default but needs the content trees carved out.
78	
79	## How detection works — the tree is the oracle
80	
81	The unit of detection is *a reference that resolves to a real tracked path inside the barred folder*. That single rule is what makes it language-agnostic and precise:
82	
83	1. **Candidate extraction** — on every line of every guarded file (comments and Markdown included): quoted strings (import specifiers, `require()`, `@import`, config values, JSON) **and** unquoted path-ish tokens. Test files (`*.test.mjs`) are never scanned — a test references what it tests, so a core test naming content is expected, not a coupling.
84	2. **Resolution against the repo tree** — a candidate resolves via, in order: file-relative (`../server/db.js`, `..\server\db.js`), repo-root-relative (`server/db.js`), Python-style *absolute* dotted module (`import server.pkg.mod` → `server/pkg/mod.py`), then the unique-basename layer. Slash paths get extension/index completion (`../server/db` → `server/db.ts`, `../server` → `server/index.ts`, `../server/theme` → `server/_theme.scss`). The dotted-module attempt completes with **Python extensions only** (`.py`/`__init__.py`) — dotted notation is a Python/JVM module convention, so a JS `receiver.method()` call is never mistaken for a `receiver/method.js` module reference. A **bare `filename.ext`** resolves only when exactly one tracked file carries that basename — unique → no collision → no false positive.
85	3. **Verdict** — a candidate that resolves to a path under `to` (and not into the guarded region itself or an `allow` folder) is a crossing. A word that merely *looks like* a folder name — `"the API server is remote"`, a `https://server/...` URL, a `store.dispatch()` call — resolves to nothing and never fires.
86	
87	**The bare-name layer** (opt-in, `matchNames: true`): a barred folder's own *name* is matched as a bare word — in prose, a backtick cite, a string literal — and resolves to that folder. This catches identifier-level coupling (a hardcoded folder name that no path ever spells out), so it is restricted to **distinctive** names, ones containing `-` or `_`, which ordinary prose never produces; a plain-word name (`server`, `basics`) is matched only when the edge force-includes it via `alsoMatchNames`. A name inside a longer token (`tidy-repo-seed.mjs`) or a URL path never fires. An `alsoMatchNames` entry naming no barred folder is a blocking `config` finding.
88	
89	**In scope for v1:** imports and path strings that resolve into the barred folder, plus unique `filename.ext` mentions — anywhere, comments and docs included — plus opted-in bare names. Vendored/generated files are excluded automatically (the runner drops them from `ctx.files`).
90	
91	### Known limitations
92	
93	The engine is **best-effort for imports and precise (no false positives) by design** — it would rather miss an exotic reference form than block on a guess. It does *not* resolve, and so does not catch, these crossings (a follow-up may add them; each needs real per-language handling):
94	
95	- **Plain-word folder names** in prose (`"see the server module"`). Distinctive names are the `matchNames: true` layer's job; single ordinary words are only matched when force-included via `alsoMatchNames`, because English can't be told apart from an identifier.
96	- **Class/function symbol references** (a `from`-file *using* a symbol *defined* in `to`). Needs per-language symbol extraction and resolution.
97	- **Python *relative* imports** (`from ..server import x`) and **`from x import y`** name imports. Only the absolute dotted form (`import server.x`) resolves today.
98	- **Alias imports** (`@/server/db`, `~/server/db`, tsconfig/webpack `paths`). The engine has no project alias map.
99	- **Rust `::` paths** (`use crate::server::db;`).
100	- **Case-only differences** on case-insensitive filesystems (`../Server/db.js`). Matching is case-sensitive — the same behavior a Linux CI runtime has.
101	
102	One precision caveat cuts the other way: the unique-basename layer can resolve a **convention marker name** (a `RULES.md`-like filename every sibling is *meant* to carry) while only one folder happens to carry it yet. Such a hit is a false coupling — set **`matchUniqueFilenames: false`** on the rule to turn the layer off (path references and distinctive names still fire), or, if you want to keep the layer for other files, accept the one crossing with an exception whose reason says so.
103	
104	## Exceptions: carve-outs and reviewed crossings
105	
106	A rule's `except` array holds two kinds of entry, and a rule owns both — there is no separate top-level accept list.
107	
108	**Carve-out strings** subtract files from the guarded region — they are not scanned, *and* references to them stop counting as self-references (the mechanism that makes `from: "."` coherent). Entries are folders/files, `"<folder>/*"` child-directory globs, or `"*.suffix"` name patterns:
109	
110	```json
111	"except": ["plugins/*", "plugins/README.md", "*.generated.js"]
112	```
113	
114	**Reviewed exceptions** `{ path, to?, reason }` excuse a deliberate crossing, reviewed once like any code:
115	
116	```json
117	"except": [
118	  { "path": "engine/registry.js", "to": ["plugins/legacy"],
119	    "reason": "temporary bridge during the plugin split — tracked in #123" },
120	  { "path": "docs/inventory.md",
121	    "reason": "historical ledger — it enumerates the plugins it catalogs by name" }
122	]
123	```
124	
125	- **`path`** — one file, or a subtree with a trailing `/`.
126	- **`to`** — the barred folder(s) this file may reference. **With `to`**, the exception is *pinned*: a crossing from that file to a *different* barred folder still fails, so no new coupling slips into an already-reviewed file. **Without `to`**, it excuses every crossing from that file — a whole-file exemption for a genuinely enumerative file (a ledger), carrying a reason a bare carve-out string can't.
127	- **`reason`** — required. It is what makes the crossing reviewable.
128	
129	On a whole-repo sweep with a clean config, an exception that matched **nothing** is itself a blocking finding: the coupling it excused is gone, so the entry (or the unused `to` item) gets pruned instead of rotting. Shrinking a rule's reviewed exceptions to none is the definition of "the graph holds."
130	
131	(The runner's generic top-level `accept` — `{ "rule": "barrier", "path": "...", "reason": "..." }` — still works too, retiring *every* barrier finding in a file. Prefer a rule's own `except`: it is pinned per target and staleness-audited, where the generic accept is a silent whole-file waiver.)
132	
133	## Composing a barrier from another pack
134	
135	A pack ships a *fixed* barrier — no project config needed — by **declaring** this pack and **contributing** the barrier as data on its manifest, never by importing this pack's code (`pack-independence`): name `barriers` in the pack's `requires` and carry the barrier under `contributes`:
136	
137	```js
138	// packs/<somepack>/pack.mjs
139	export default {
140	  id: 'somepack',
141	  requires: ['barriers'],
142	  contributes: {
143	    barriers: [{
144	      id: 'requirements-isolation',
145	      edges: [{ from: 'dev/requirements', to: '*', reason: 'requirements is a pure sink' }],
146	    }],
147	  },
148	};
149	```
150	
151	Each contribution becomes a **first-class rule under its own id** — per-rule overrides (`rules: { "requirements-isolation": "off" }`) and acceptances address it directly, and `description`/`why`/`doc`/`severity`/`crossingRemedy`/`crossingExcuse` ride the contribution. The two `crossing*` fields own the halves of a crossing finding's `fix`: `crossingRemedy` replaces the default "route shared code through …" opener where relocating the dependency isn't the way out (a one-sided isolation edge has no shared folder to route through), and `crossingExcuse` names the excusal lever that actually works for a pack-shipped edge. Write the remedy into one of these, not into `description` — a rendered finding carries `what`/`why`/`fix`/`doc` and never the rule's description. `gateDir` is the one declarative gate: the rule stays inert until that directory exists in the repo under test (how the baseline's consumer-isolation wall stays quiet pre-flip). The runner hands this pack the active-pack list (`contributedRules` on its manifest, the generic core seam), and [contributed.mjs](contributed.mjs) builds the rules — an undeclared pack contributes nothing, exactly as its own rules would not run. A consumer's local pack contributes the same way. A helper a pack needs beside a barrier (path containment, say) lives in the engine lib (`engine/checks/helpers/path-containment.mjs`), never in this pack's modules.
152	
153	## The check
154	
155	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
156	|---|---|---|---|
157	| `barrier` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
158

input.prompt:
You're helping with a "prose-to-checks" sweep of the Claudinite repo (a system of "packs" — each pack is a directory under packs/ with a RULES.md and/or SKILL.md files holding working-discipline prose, plus optionally declared-checks.json and *.mjs rule modules that mechanize some rules as automated checks).

Your job: read the RULES.md and any skills/*/SKILL.md files in these packs, and report candidate rules that could become automated checks but haven't been yet.

Packs to read (relative to repo root /home/user/Claudinite):
- packs/google-identity
- packs/headless-browser
- packs/html
- packs/ios
- packs/jwt
- packs/leaflet
- packs/macos
- packs/node
- packs/play-store-release
- packs/product-wiki

For each pack: read RULES.md (if present), and skim any skills/*/SKILL.md files for procedural rules. Also check if the pack has a declared-checks.json (list its rule ids/patterns) and any other *.mjs rule modules, so you know what's ALREADY covered — don't propose a duplicate of an existing check.

A candidate rule must pass TWO gates:
1. **Working rule, not product statement**: it governs HOW WORK IS DONE (conventions, gotchas, review discipline) — not WHAT THE PRODUCT DOES (which entities exist, what a UI renders, that features are wired together). Test: "if the product changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule still be wrong to violate?" If yes -> working rule (candidate). If the rule would just track a product decision -> NOT a candidate, skip it.
2. **Always-testable / static signature**: a post-hoc scan of repo files could mechanically detect a violation — a filename convention, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code/config, a dangling reference, a required structural shape. NOT a candidate if it requires: judgment/naming quality, in-flight process during a session (nothing to scan after the fact), or runtime-only behavior.

For each candidate you find, report:
- pack path and file (e.g. packs/aws-sam/RULES.md)
- the exact prose sentence/paragraph (quote it)
- why it's a working rule (not product) and why it's statically testable
- a rough idea of HOW a check could detect it (what file pattern, what would it scan for)
- confidence this could be built as a genuinely reliable check with a "see it fail" fixture (a violating example vs a clean example) without false positives

Be selective — quality over quantity. Most rules in these files are NOT good candidates (most are judgment calls, in-flight process, or already covered). Only report rules you think are strong, clean candidates. It's fine to report zero from a pack, or even zero overall. Do not read every file exhaustively if a pack's RULES.md is very short or clearly all judgment-based — skim and move on.

Report your findings as a structured list, one entry per candidate, under 800 words total. If truly nothing qualifies, say so plainly.

- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.

Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

1	# claudinite-fleet-sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker
2	
3	Declaring this pack marks a repo as the **fleet enforcer**: the one repo that covers and maintains
4	every repo under an owner. What the pack *is* — its six sweeps, their schedule, their reports, the
5	config schema — is [README.md](README.md). This file is what a session **here** has to get right.
6	
7	## Configuring the fleet
8	
9	- **Keeping a repo out of the fleet** — add its full `owner/name` to `exclude` on this pack's
10	  config entry. Nothing else opts a repo out: an archived or forked repo is reported as out of scope
11	  but still walked, and a repo that simply never adopted is `uncovered`, which is a finding rather
12	  than a choice. If a repo should not be measured, say so in `exclude` and the reports stop asking
13	  about it.
14	
15	- **Adding or changing a `packSeeds` entry** — get it right *before* the sweep next runs. The
16	  sweep seeds and never overrides, so a wrong seed reaches each member exactly once and then sticks;
17	  correcting it here un-writes nothing, and undoing it is a change in every member's repo. Land the
18	  entry and its own declaration together, then read the next run's report rather than assuming.
19	
20	- **Declaring a pack this fleet also seeds** — write the same config in both places, spelling
21	  every default out on both sides rather than leaving one implicit. `seeds-agree` compares them
22	  literally, because nothing in this pack may know what one pack's absent key means. A pack the
23	  fleet standardizes on but this repo does not itself run has nothing to agree with, and is fine.
24	
25	## Acting on what a sweep reports
26	
27	- **Acting on an `add-packs` work-list issue** — the work is a declaration and a reviewed PR **in
28	  the named member**, never here. A session in this repo is scoped to this repo, so if every item
29	  names another repo there is nothing here to do: say the scope is the blocker rather than writing
30	  to the issues, which are the only thing within reach and are not the work.
31	
32	- **Acting on a scanned pack suggestion** — it is a recommendation, never a verdict.
33	  A fingerprint is a way to *suspect* a pack is wanted; whether to declare it is the member's call,
34	  and closing the issue `not planned` is a standing answer the scan honours rather than re-opening.
35	  A **forced** addition is the other thing entirely — a decision already made — so adopt what
36	  its issue says instead of re-judging whether it was wanted.
37	
38	- **Reading `unknown` in a report** — it means the sweep could not look, not that it looked and
39	  found nothing. Never convert one into a verdict: a repo whose declaration could not be read is
40	  neither covered nor uncovered, an undecided fingerprint is not a non-match, and a member the
41	  pack-seed sweep could not reach is not converged. Fix the access and re-run.
42	
43	- **Judging whether a member is behind** — compare `engineVersion` and `packVersions` against
44	  canon, never the age of its stamped `ref`. The update flows deliberately never rewrite `ref` or
45	  `updated`, so the stamp is provenance — which commit first vendored the mount — and stays
46	  frozen on a member that is perfectly current. Its age measures nothing, and measuring it
47	  calls the whole fleet behind on one arbitrary day.
48	
49	- **Answering why the fleet did not move** — read the member's own artifacts first: its
50	  declaration, its stamp, the runs on its head sha. This repo dispatches; each member converges
51	  itself, with its own token and its own delivery policy. Propose a settings change as a conclusion,
52	  never as the diagnosis.
53	
54	## Running the manual levers
55	
56	- **Pushing canon to the whole fleet now** — create the work item, from a checkout of this repo:
57	
58	  ```
59	  node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/create-work-item.mjs claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline
60	  ```
61	
62	  Add `--context "REPOS=owner/a owner/b"` to narrow it (space-separated: a Context line splits on
63	  commas), `--context "DRY_RUN=true"` to see the list without dispatching, or
64	  `--context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"` to reach members that stopped their own scheduler on purpose.
65	  Both knobs are read from the item's Context and nowhere else — an item created without them runs
66	  unscoped and live. It queues one
67	  run per member and does not wait; each member reports its own outcome in its own repo. A member
68	  with nothing to do converges to a cheap no-op, so over-using it is wasteful rather than unsafe.
69	
70	- **Adding a pack across the fleet** — create a `fleet-add-missing-packs` item with
71	  `--context "ADD_PACKS=…"` rather than editing anything. No pack is named anywhere in this pack's
72	  code: every id comes from config or from the item's own Context, which is what keeps the
73	  enforcer from becoming a second place packs are known.
74	
75	## Credentials
76	
77	- **Granting or repairing `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`** — a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's
78	  repositories, granted exactly what [`fleet-token.mjs`](fleet-token.mjs)'s table names — the only
79	  place the permissions are written, because a per-sweep subset is always a defensible answer and
80	  never the right one. Grant it whole: the token is granted once, for the pack.
81	
82	- **A sweep reporting `403` or `no-permission`** — the grant is short a permission, which the
83	  error names. It is a grant to fix once, so widen the token rather than re-running: no sweep
84	  retries, because a work list nobody will act on is not a green outcome.
85

1	# claudinite-growth — authoring Claudinite content here
2	
3	Rules for the content a repo authors for itself: the lessons its capture runs write into its local
4	packs, and the tasks that do the writing. A member's own Claudinite *status* — the mount,
5	the declaration, adoption, the update — is claudinite-lifecycle's.
6	
7	- **Changing a local pack automatically** — adding or removing a prose rule, creating a
8	  check, correcting or deleting a rule a probe disproved — add a row to that pack's own
9	  `VERSIONS.md`, in the same commit as the change. That file is the growth lifecycle's whole
10	  record; no growth task keeps a standing tracker issue, and a run that changed nothing writes no
11	  row.
12	
13	- **Wanting a job to run in Actions** — make it a task with a `code_work` command rather than
14	  authoring a workflow; the vendored workflows already own the trigger, the concurrency, the
15	  secrets and the failure reporting. Work with no cadence is a task too, on
16	  `frequency: 'manual'`, woken by whatever knows the event happened.

1	# Headless browser
2	
3	Driving a real browser from your own process — a page loaded, faked, driven and captured by code
4	rather than by a user. True whether the output is a golden image, a build artifact, or an
5	assertion about behaviour, and whether the driver is Playwright or Puppeteer.
6	
7	This pack is the browser itself, and deliberately restates none of the ground either side of it:
8	**which** engine a UI golden should be rendered with, what tolerance it may carry, and the approval
9	gate before re-baselining one are testing decisions, and wiring the run into a workflow is a
10	workflow one.
11	
12	## Getting a browser
13	
14	- **Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container
15	  or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry
16	  download is slow, often blocked, and pins a build you did not choose. Look for an explicit
17	  override variable first, then the image's browser root, then fall through to the driver's own
18	  resolution — and prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all. The
19	  image's build number need not match the driver's own pin for the browser to launch. Never
20	  hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the
21	  failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it.
22	
23	- **A fresh install of the driver package is the same danger from upstream.** Reinstalling the
24	  package to fix an import error just as easily resolves to a newer release than the one paired
25	  with the environment's pinned browser — it then hunts for a browser build the image was never
26	  given and fails asking for a network install the sandbox cannot make. A reinstall run from the
27	  repo root instead of a scratchpad can dodge that failure outright (a version happens to
28	  resolve that works) and still cost you: it dirties the tracked `package.json`, its lockfile and
29	  `node_modules`, which then need a manual revert before anything can be committed. Resolve the
30	  already-installed package by its global path instead of adding a second copy, at any depth in
31	  the tree.
32	
33	- **When a page depends on a third-party library loaded from a CDN you have not vendored,
34	  stub the library's own API surface rather than trying to make the CDN reachable.** A default
35	  network abort (above) leaves the page's global for that library undefined, so every call into
36	  it throws and the render comes back empty — indistinguishable from a product bug unless you
37	  know the cause. Grep the code under test for the handful of calls it actually makes (a mapping
38	  or charting library often boils down to a handful of constructors and methods) and install a
39	  minimal no-op implementation of just those as an init script, before the page's own scripts run.
40	
41	- **A committed pixel golden is only comparable under the exact build that rendered it.** Two
42	  browsers a version apart rasterise text and shadows differently, so a comparison across them
43	  measures the renderer, not the product. Where the output is compared pixel by pixel, read the
44	  installed driver version at launch and **refuse to run** on any other, naming the pinned one in
45	  the error; where it is not — a build artifact, a behavioural assertion — let the build float
46	  and spend nothing on pinning it.
47	
48	- **Pinning is what buys a zero-diff browser golden — budget for the whole recipe or accept a
49	  tolerance.** A browser screenshot is not bit-stable across machines by default, which is why
50	  the general advice is a small tolerance. It *can* be made bit-stable, and the price is this
51	  pack's next two sections in full: the pinned build, a font jail, and the rasterisation flags.
52	  Take all of it or take the tolerance; a half-applied recipe gives a zero-diff gate that fails
53	  on someone else's machine for reasons no one can read off the diff.
54	
55	## The page's world is an input — replace all of it
56	
57	- **Serve the page from a fake origin you fulfil from disk, and abort anything you did not
58	  name.** Intercepting at the browser needs no server process, no port and no free-port race,
59	  and it reaches *every* request the page makes rather than the ones an application-level mock
60	  happens to know about. Make the default arm an abort: a new external dependency then breaks
61	  the run loudly instead of quietly adding real network to a run meant to be hermetic.
62	
63	- **Use an `https` fake origin.** Geolocation and several other capabilities exist only on a
64	  secure origin, and a page served over `http` silently takes the denied path instead. Routes
65	  are fulfilled before any connection is attempted, so no certificate is involved and nothing
66	  has to be trusted.
67	
68	- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
69	  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
70	  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
71	  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
72	  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.
73	
74	- **Know which knobs are fixed at context creation and which are per page.** Locale, timezone,
75	  viewport, device scale factor, geolocation and permissions belong to the browser *context* and
76	  cannot be changed once it exists — so proving that a product reads a fixed zone rather than
77	  the device's takes **two** contexts, not one page reconfigured twice. The clock, seeded
78	  randomness and injected scripts are per page.
79	
80	- **A command-line window-size flag is not a viewport — a narrow one does not test the narrow
81	  layout.** Ask a browser's *CLI* for a phone-sized window and it renders the page at a clamped
82	  width and crops the overflow, without applying the media queries the width should have
83	  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
84	  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
85	  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
86	  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
87	  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
88	  when they are fine.
89	
90	- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
91	  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
92	  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.
93	
94	- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
95	  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
96	  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
97	  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.
98	
99	- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
100	  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
101	  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
102	  has no timers to advance.
103	
104	## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts
105	
106	- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
107	  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
108	  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
109	  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
110	  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
111	  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
112	  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.
113	
114	- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
115	  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
116	  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
117	  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
118	  one machine.
119	
120	## Capturing
121	
122	- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
123	  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
124	  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
125	  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.
126	
127	- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
128	  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
129	  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
130	  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
131	  deliberately before measuring anything.
132	
133	- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
134	  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
135	  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
136	  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.
137	
138	- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
139	  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
140	  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
141	  is an error, not a crop.
142	
143	- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
144	  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
145	  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
146	  meant to show yourself.
147	
148	- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
149	  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
150	  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.
151

1	# core — working with Claudinite itself
2	
3	Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration, adoption and
4	the self-refresh. The contract a scheduled task is written to is claudinite-growth's.
5	
6	- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
7	  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
8	  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.
9	
10	- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
11	  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
12	  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
13	  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
14	  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
15	  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.
16	
17	- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
18	  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
19	  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.
20	
21	- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
22	  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.
23	
24	- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.
25	
26	- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
27	  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
28	  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
29	  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.
30	
31	- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `engineVersion` and
32	  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` or `ref`: the versioned flows stamp versions and
33	  nothing else, so those two hold the provenance of the last full re-vendor rather than of this
34	  mount, and a member converging nightly reads as weeks stale.
35	
36	- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
37	  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
38	  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.

1 # HTML 2 3 Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. 4 5 - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**. Read `element.nextElementSibling`. 6 - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. (2) Failing that, **read the declared locale** (``, `og:locale`): default **month-first** (the order `Date` and most JS parsers assume) and flip to day-first only on a *positive* non-US signal — a non-US region in `lang` / `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` with unknown region stays month-first. The `.` / `-` separators are day-first regardless. 7 - **When code must react to how a real page actually behaves, investigate it live before you ship — don't deploy a hypothesis you can only test after release.** If a change hinges on the real DOM, computed styles, or runtime state of a page you can't see, hand the user one JavaScript snippet to run in the browser DevTools console and read its output back. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. 8 - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. 9
