1	# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
4	**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
5	be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
6	subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.
7	
8	It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
9	algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
10	user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
11	iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
12	examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
13	anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
14	read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.
15	
16	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
17	rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
18	drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
19	project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
20	project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
21	non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
22	ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
27	
28	This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
29	optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.
30	
31	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
32	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
33	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
34	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
35	   it** — do not guess.
36	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
37	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
38	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
39	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
40	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
41	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
42	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
43	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
44	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
45	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
46	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
47	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
48	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
49	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
50	
51	### Show, don't just tell
52	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
53	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
54	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
55	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
56	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
57	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
58	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
59	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
60	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
61	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
62	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
63	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
64	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
65	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
66	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
67	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
68	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
69	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
70	- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
71	  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
72	  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
73	  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
74	  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
75	  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
76	  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
77	  trustworthy.
78	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
79	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
80	
81	### Interaction cadence
82	Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
83	when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
84	work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
85	and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
90	
91	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
92	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
93	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
94	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
95	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
96	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
97	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
98	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
99	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
100	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
101	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
102	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
103	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
104	  loudly.
105	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
106	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
107	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
108	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
109	  are requirements, not incidental.
110	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
111	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
112	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
113	  the review overlays.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
118	
119	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
120	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
121	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
122	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
123	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
124	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
125	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
126	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
127	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
128	  in scope.
129	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
130	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
131	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
132	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
133	
134	---
135	
136	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
137	
138	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
139	if it improves a metric.
140	
141	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
142	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
143	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
144	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
145	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
146	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
147	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
148	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
149	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
150	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
151	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
152	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
153	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
154	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
155	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
156	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
157	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
158	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
159	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
160	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
161	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
162	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
167	
168	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
169	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
170	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
171	
172	An iteration note captures:
173	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
174	  showed it).
175	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
176	  possible).
177	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
178	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
179	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
180	
181	### A metric's definition is part of its identity
182	
183	Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
184	one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
185	silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
186	under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
187	definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
188	the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
189	the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
190	the failure this rule exists to prevent.
191	
192	### A raw measurement is comparable only inside one calibration
193	
194	When each input carries its own scale (a per-image conversion factor, a per-run
195	sampling rate, a per-source unit), a raw absolute quantity means something
196	different in every input. **Aggregate and compare only normalized quantities** —
197	a density, a ratio, a per-unit rate — never the raw number, and never a mean
198	spanning two sources that differ in more than scale (a different instrument,
199	subject or protocol changes *what* is measured, not just how much of it fits in
200	frame). Group the rollup by source and say what the grouping is for.
201	
202	The conversion factor is a **measurement of that input**, not a constant: read it
203	off the input itself, never infer it from a stated setting or borrow it from a
204	neighbour. It lives in exactly one place in the code — a second copy is a second
205	calibration, and whichever copy a given script happens to read wins silently. An
206	input offering nothing to measure the factor from is **not** quietly dropped:
207	mark it uncalibrated *with the reason*, report only its scale-free quantities,
208	and leave it visible as a known gap.
209	
210	### Definition of done for an accepted change
211	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
212	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
213	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
214	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
215	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
216	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
217	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
218	  changed**.
219	
220	---
221	
222	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
223	
224	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
225	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
226	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
227	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
228	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
229	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
230	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
231	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
232	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
233	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
234	
235	---
236	
237	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
238	
239	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
240	
241	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
242	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
243	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
244	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
245	- **Capture the method that exists only inside a figure.** Part of a source's
246	  actual procedure is often drawn rather than written — a panel's inset, an
247	  annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
248	  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
249	  until someone re-opens the source.
250	- **Write down what the source *fails* to say**, as an explicit gap list — the
251	  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
252	  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
253	  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
254	  a stated gap is part of that.
255	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
256	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
257	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
258	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
259	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
260	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
261	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
262	
263	---
264	
265	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
266	
267	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
268	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
269	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
270	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
271	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
272	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
273	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
274	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
275	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
276	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
277	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
278	
279	---
280	
281	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
282	
283	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
284	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
285	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
286	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
287	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
288	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
289	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
290	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
291	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
292	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
293	    nothing finer.
294	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
295	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
296	  mask-free validation path for those sets.
297	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
298	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
299	  covered.
300	
301	---
302	
303	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
304	
305	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
306	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
307	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
308	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
309	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
310	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
311	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
312	  exhausted first.
313	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
314	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
315	  warm-up doc.
316	
317	---
318	
319	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
320	
321	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
322	first-class experiments:
323	
324	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
325	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
326	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
327	  couldn't.
328	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
329	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
330	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
331	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
332	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
333	  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
334	  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
335	  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
336	  the very structure you are measuring.
337	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
338	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
339	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
340	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
341	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
342	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
343	
344	---
345	
346	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
347	
348	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
349	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
350	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
351	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
352	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
353	substantially change a sub-step.
354	
355	---
356	
357	## 13. Continuity across sessions
358	
359	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
360	**resumable** state.
361	
362	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
363	  clean checkout.
364	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
365	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
366	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
367	  codebase.
368	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
369	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
370	  metrics current in it.
371	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
372	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
373	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
374	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
375	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
376	  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
377	  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
378	  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
379	  isn't captured yet.
380	- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
381	  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.
382	
383	---
384	
385	## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)
386	
387	Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
388	Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
389	such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
390	revived session:
391	
392	> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
393	> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
394	> the research task itself.**
395	> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
396	> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
397	> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
398	> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted
399	> on; how they want articles summarized, images extracted, and external data
400	> fetched; environment constraints they flagged; and how they hand off algorithm
401	> ideas. For each item, strip out anything specific to this project's subject
402	> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over

2	name: writing-tests
3	description: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
4	---
5	
6	# Testing practices
7	
8	Portable practices for writing tests you can actually trust — proving a test fails before relying on it, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, and how to gate a fuzzy quality metric. These are project-agnostic; a consuming repo's own test *mechanics* (runner, layout, which suites exist) stay in its own docs. (General software-engineering practices live in [the basics pack's RULES.md](../../RULES.md); CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md).)
9	
10	- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work.
11	- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
12	- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
13	- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. (A hostname-apex helper passed its tests but mis-stripped `tel-aviv.gov.il` → `gov.il`; the gap only surfaced when the function was run over the actual list of existing URLs.) Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once.
14	- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
15	- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
16	- **Never pin a declaration to itself.** Asserting that a config/manifest field equals the literal it is declared with (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'open-pr')`, `assert.equal(pack.id, 'thing')`) restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and, worse, teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. Assert what can actually come apart — a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set. If a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test.
17	- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
18	- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
19	- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (A UI-snapshot coverage gate parked behavioral leaves `9.1`–`9.3`/`3.4` and an unreachable `8.6` on cases that render none of them — issue #429.)
20	- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
21	- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
22	- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
23	- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
24	- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
25	- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
26	- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (The SPA-render fallback's CI test renders a `data:` URL whose script fills an empty root, not a real SPA — #310.)
27	- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
28	- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
29	- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
30	- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
31	- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
32	- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
33	- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

1	---
2	name: file-placement
3	description: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
4	---
5	
6	# File placement
7	
8	Where a file *lives* in a repository is a design decision, not a clerical one. This doc gives a portable rule for judging that placement: keep files close to the files they actually depend on. It is project-agnostic — the consuming repo's own docs own any project-specific layout conventions (where tests go, where generated output lands, framework-mandated folders, etc.). This is about the *shape* of the dependency graph relative to the folder tree, not about naming.
9	
10	## The reference-distance metric
11	
12	Treat the repository as a tree of folders. For any reference one file makes to another (an import, an include, a relative-path link, a sibling asset it reads), measure the **distance** between them as the number of folder edges you traverse in that tree to get from one file's folder to the other's:
13	
14	- **Distance 0** — both files are in the **same folder**. The reference is local.
15	- **Distance 1** — the target is **one folder up or one folder down** (a parent or a direct child folder). One edge.
16	- **Distance 2** — the target is in a **sibling folder**: a different child of the same parent. You go **up one** edge to the shared parent, then **down one** edge into the sibling. Two edges.
17	- **Distance _n_** — in general, the count of folder edges on the shortest path between the two folders in the tree. Each "up to a common ancestor" step and each "down into a subfolder" step is one edge.
18	
19	> A sibling reference is **distance 2** (up one, then down one) under this edge-counting model — not 3. Keep this consistent: the distance is just the length of the shortest folder-to-folder path in the tree.
20	
21	Distance 0 and 1 are *cohesion*: the file and what it needs are neighbors. Anything 2 or higher is *reach* — the file is grabbing across the tree.
22	
23	## The rule
24	
25	**A file should mostly reference files at distance 0 or 1.** Same folder, the folder above, or a folder below. That is the healthy case: a module knows its neighbors and its parent/children, and little else.
26	
27	It is a **code smell** when:
28	
29	- many of a file's references are at distance 2+, or
30	- a single reference is at a large distance (reaching across several folders to a far corner of the tree), or
31	- a whole folder's files all reach into the same distant folder — that pair of folders probably wants to be adjacent, or merged.
32	
33	High average reference-distance means the folder structure and the dependency structure disagree. The tree is supposed to *encode* what depends on what; when files routinely reach far away, the tree has stopped telling the truth.
34	
35	## What to do about a smell
36	
37	Don't treat a long reference as something to suppress — treat it as a signal that placement is wrong. Options, roughly in order of preference:
38	
39	- **Move the file** next to what it depends on, so the reference collapses to distance 0 or 1.
40	- **Move the dependency** the other way, if the dependency is the thing that's misplaced and several files want it nearby.
41	- **Lift a shared dependency** to the nearest common ancestor when several sibling folders all reach for it — distance 2-from-each becomes distance-1 from a parent everyone already touches.
42	- **Introduce a boundary** (a small public entry point / index for a subtree) so outsiders reference *one* near file instead of reaching deep into the subtree's internals. This converts many deep references into one shallow one.
43	- **Accept it, deliberately,** for genuine cross-cutting concerns (a top-level shared/util/config that everything legitimately depends on). These exist; the point is they should be *few and named*, not the accidental norm.
44	
45	## A file used by exactly one unit belongs inside that unit
46	
47	The distance metric asks *how far* a reference reaches. This asks *how many* things reach at all, and it is the sharper question when the answer is **one**.
48	
49	**A file — code or prose — whose only consumer is a single self-contained unit lives inside that unit's folder.** A "unit" here is any directory the project treats as one thing: a scheduled task, a command, a plugin, a feature module. If exactly one of them imports the file, reads it, or links to it, then the file is part of it, and the folder should say so.
50	
51	This is not the distance rule restated. A helper one level up from its only caller scores a perfectly healthy distance 1 and is still misplaced: sitting outside the unit it advertises itself as shared, so the next author treats it as a public surface, and it accumulates callers it was never designed for. Deleting the unit also leaves the helper behind as orphaned code nobody dares remove, because its location implies someone else might need it. Moving it inside makes the unit **self-contained**: everything it owns travels, and is deleted, with it.
52	
53	Apply it in both directions:
54	
55	- **Two or more units use it** → it is genuinely shared. Lift it to their nearest common ancestor and leave it there; that is the shared-dependency move above, and the location is now telling the truth.
56	- **Exactly one uses it** → move it in, even when the reference was already short.
57	
58	The usual exemptions still hold — a mandated location wins, and a project's test-location convention wins. Split a file whose *parts* have different audiences rather than leaving the whole thing outside for the sake of one shared export: move the single-consumer body inside the unit, lift the shared function to the common ancestor.
59	
60	## Special case: files whose location is mandated
61	
62	Some files **cannot** live next to what they relate to, because a tool or platform dictates exactly where they go. A GitHub workflow must sit under `.github/workflows/`; agent/config files live under `.claude/` (or `.cloud/`, `.vscode/`, `.devcontainer/`, etc.); many ecosystems require a manifest at the repo root (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `Dockerfile`). Their placement is fixed by an external contract, not chosen by you.
63	
64	**Exempt these from the distance metric.** A mandated-location file that "reaches far" into the code it acts on is not a smell — it has no choice, and moving the code to satisfy the metric would be backwards. Don't refactor to shorten a reference whose distance is forced by a tool's required path.
65	
66	But the exemption is **narrow and one-directional**:
67	
68	- It covers only the **mandated** file and **only the references the mandate forces.** A workflow under `.github/` referencing a script elsewhere is fine. Ordinary code reaching *into* `.github/` for something that didn't have to live there is still a smell — the metric applies normally in that direction.
69	- Keep the mandated file **thin**: a launcher that references one near entry point, not a file that reaches deep into many distant internals. Put the real logic in a normally-placed file at distance 0/1 from what it uses, and have the mandated file point at *that*. This keeps the long, forced reference single and shallow instead of spraying deep references from a corner of the tree.
70	- The exemption is for **truly mandated** locations, not merely conventional or convenient ones. "It's customary to put it here" is not a mandate — if you could place the file nearer its dependencies and the tooling wouldn't care, the normal rule still applies.
71	
72	## Special case: test files
73	
74	Tests are a common source of long references that are **not** placement smells. A project's test-location convention — a mirrored `test/` or `tests/` tree, a `__tests__/` folder, a `*_test.go` sibling, a `spec/` root — fixes where a test file lives, and that location is often far from the file under test. The resulting long reference from the test to the tested file is **forced by the convention, not by misplacement.**
75	
76	**Don't move files to shorten a test reference, or vice versa.** Where a project already has a standard for test locations, that standard wins: leave the tested file where its production neighbors are (distance 0/1 from *them*), leave the test where the convention puts it, and accept the distance between them. Relocating production code to sit nearer its test — or scattering tests next to code when the project mirrors them into a separate tree — trades a real, project-wide standard for a metric the standard already overrides.
77	
78	Apply the same narrowness as the mandated-location case: the exemption covers the **test → tested-file** reference that the convention forces, and it presumes the project *has* such a convention. Absent any standard, ordinary placement judgment still applies — co-locating a test with the code it exercises is a perfectly good distance-0 choice.
79	
80	**When picking a test-location convention from scratch, mirror the source tree — one test per source file at the same relative path** (`src/<area>/<name>` tested by `test/<area>/<name>.test`). The path *is* the link: a source file never has to name its own test in a comment, and a missing or misfiled test is obvious at a glance. Keep departures (whole-interaction tests, tests with no single source file to mirror) few and deliberate.
81	
82	## Special case: a plugin contract's shared lib
83	
84	The two exemptions above cover a file whose *own location* is fixed. A third case fixes **both ends of a reference**: a framework that discovers extension modules at a mandated path *and* publishes the shared lib those modules must import at another mandated path. Every extension takes the same import, at whatever distance the two mandated paths happen to sit apart — a plugin importing its host's plugin API, a check module importing the engine's finding constructor.
85	
86	**Exempt that reference too.** It is not a placement decision at either end: the extension can't move without ceasing to be discovered, and the lib is usually code the project doesn't own to restructure. The tell is universality — *every* extension of that kind takes the reference, in every repo, so a project can only ever waive it, never fix it. A waiver each adopter has to write is a rule flagging a constant.
87	
88	Apply the same narrowness as the other two:
89	
90	- It covers the **extension → published lib** direction only. Code reaching *into* an extension's folder, or an extension reaching somewhere other than the published lib, is judged normally.
91	- It covers the framework's **declared** surface — the paths it tells extensions they may import — and nothing past it. Reaching around that boundary into internals is not exempt; that's the reach-deep-into-a-subtree smell, and the boundary the framework already drew is what makes it visible.
92	- **Universal, not merely common.** A dependency several files happen to share is the lift-to-a-common-ancestor case above, and it is still fixable. This exemption is for the one every extension takes by construction.
93	
94	Take the surface from wherever the framework already defines it, rather than restating it. If some other rule enforces "an extension may import only X," that same X is what placement should exempt — one definition, so the two can't drift apart and disagree about the same import.
95	
96	In this corpus that means a pack module under `packs/` or `.claudinite/local/packs/` importing the engine surface (everything under `engine/` — `engineSurface()` in `engine/checks/helpers/module-imports.mjs`, the allow list the `pack-independence` barrier enforces; vendored under `.claudinite/shared/` in a consuming repo). The `basics/file-placement` check implements this exemption, so a pack rule's `findings.mjs` import is never flagged at all. A pack reaching into *another* pack, or deep into its own subtree, is judged normally.
97	
98	## Tooling acts on paths: encode act-on-able distinctions structurally
99	
100	A file's path is an interface not only for developers but for automated processes — build globs, linters, and access rules often act on a file by its location alone, without reading its content. When two kinds of file must be treated differently by tooling that reads only paths, make the distinction **structural**: give each kind its own folder so the path itself carries the signal.
101	
102	Keep such a split fail-safe: name the narrower or less-protected kind explicitly, and let the safer behavior be the default, so a misplaced file lands on the safe side rather than the dangerous one.
103	
104	This complements the reference-distance metric, which asks *what a file depends on*. This axis asks *what acts on the file by path* — and for path-driven tooling, placement is the only interface it sees.
105	
106	## Why this works
107	
108	- **Locality of change.** Edits ripple to neighbors, not across the repo. When related files sit together, a change and its blast radius share a folder.
109	- **The tree stays honest.** Folder structure should be a readable map of the dependency graph. Low reference-distance keeps the map matching the territory.
110	- **Cheaper navigation.** A reader following a reference travels a short path, not a tour of the tree.
111	- **Refactors localize.** Moving or deleting a subtree is safe when its outside references are few and shallow; it's perilous when half the repo reaches in.
112	
113	## How to apply it
114	
115	- When **placing a new file**, put it where its distance-0/1 neighbors are — with the files it will import and that will import it. If no such home exists, that's a hint the structure needs a new folder, not that the file goes "somewhere."
116	- When **reviewing**, scan a file's imports/links and ask how far each reaches. A cluster of distance-2+ references is a refactor prompt, not a nit.
117	- Use it as a **direction, not a hard gate.** The goal is low *average* reach and no surprising *far* reach — not a mechanical ban on distance ≥ 2.
118	- The check that measures this is **advisory and stays advisory.** It never fails a run and takes no acceptance entry in `.claudinite-settings.json`: a finding is a placement question to answer in the tree — move the file, lift the dependency, introduce an entry point, or judge the reach deliberate and leave it. Writing config to release it would be paying review cost to silence something that was never holding anything up.
119

1	# Spec-Driven Product Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a spec-driven product project run**, as a **bootstrap to
4	drop into a new project of this class** from day one. The class: **build and ship a small end-user
5	product against an executable specification — every requirement is a numbered leaf claimed by exactly
6	one executable proof of the right kind, expected results are owned by the owner, and releases cut
7	automatically while `main` stays green.** The archetype is a UI-centric product (a browser-extension
8	panel, a small web or mobile app) and the examples lean that way, but the discipline applies wherever
9	observable behavior can be specified leaf by leaf — read "surface", "render", and "server" as whatever
10	they mean for your project.
11	
12	It is written to be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
13	product, stack, or harness specifics of any particular project. Those live elsewhere — platform
14	gotchas in the project's technology packs, release mechanics in its release pack or release doc, and
15	the concrete spec, harness, and commands in the project's own docs. General test-trust practices
16	(see-it-fail, snapshot hygiene, the re-baselining approval procedure, capture-artifact-first) are
17	corpus canon in the writing-tests skill; this pack assumes them and adds the class's development loop
18	on top.
19	
20	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**: when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and drop it;
21	when the project needs a rule this document lacks, add it in the project's own docs first. The
22	non-negotiable is the spirit: **the spec is executable, the expecteds belong to the owner, the real
23	code produces every actual, and the product ships on green.**
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. The executable spec is the backbone
28	
29	- **One numbered requirements document states what the product must do**, leaf by leaf: what each
30	  surface must render, how it must behave, the exact copy and semantics it must carry. Not prose
31	  aspirations — specific, testable statements.
32	- **Keep the spec's boundary crisp: a leaf is what the harness can assert.** The feature-level story —
33	  what the product does and why — lives in the product's prose docs; the spec holds the specific,
34	  testable statements (exact strings, placement, semantics). A statement no kind can prove isn't a
35	  leaf yet: it stays prose, or it's the trigger to add the kind that can prove it.
36	- **Every leaf carries a stable id.** Add new requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse
37	  a retired one — the ids are what cases, commits, and review discussion key on.
38	- **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf with no executable proof fails the build until a case
39	  claims it.
40	- **The spec drives the tests, never the other way around.** A behavior change starts by editing the
41	  leaf, watching the gate go red, then changing product and proof to match. A test changed without its
42	  leaf — or a leaf reworded to match what the code happens to do — inverts the authority.
43	
44	## 2. Every leaf ⇄ exactly one proof, of the right kind
45	
46	- **Enforce the bijection with a committed coverage gate**: each leaf claimed by exactly one case,
47	  each case claiming exactly one leaf, and every discovered kind of case actually executed by a
48	  runner. The gate is part of the project's own suite.
49	- **A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted** — a rendered-state snapshot, a driven gesture,
50	  a pure rule, a boundary-enforced rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually observe what it
51	  asserts. Keep kinds **extensible** — adding one is a self-contained drop.
52	- **A kind may be a singleton.** "The product loads in the real environment" is a perfectly good leaf
53	  whose mechanism is one end-to-end case; the kind names the *way of asserting*, not a population of
54	  cases.
55	- **Give each kind's runner a named lane, and keep the default lane fast and deterministic.** Heavy
56	  real-environment kinds gate the merge from CI without slowing the inner loop; their trust rules
57	  (twice-green before merging, self-diagnosing on failure) are canon in the writing-tests skill.
58	- **Actuals come from the real code.** Whatever the kind, the proof drives the shipped entry points
59	  under a faithful harness — never a parallel re-implementation of what production "should" do (the
60	  writing-tests skill owns the general rule).
61	
62	## 3. Expected results are owner-owned
63	
64	- **The committed expecteds are the owner's approval record of the product.** A case's success
65	  criterion encodes what the owner accepted.
66	- **The contract takes two honest shapes.** *Artifact-expected* (a committed render, an exact-values
67	  file): the owner approves a committed file — an agent may **propose** the expected for a brand-new
68	  leaf, but never modifies a committed one to make a failing case pass. *Coded-expected* (an
69	  assertion, a `verify()`): the expected **is** the assertion — keep it outside the write surface of
70	  whatever writes the product code, so passing by weakening the check isn't even expressible.
71	- **On a mismatch, surface actual vs. expected (and the diff) and ask.** The re-baselining procedure —
72	  diff shown, owner approves, only then re-baseline — is canon in the writing-tests skill, and it
73	  applies uniformly: to a moved render, a changed values file, and a failing assertion alike.
74	- **Expected changes ride the normal review flow** — they land in the diff like code, so the owner
75	  approves the product change and its new expected together, once.
76	
77	## 4. State a requirement once; prove it at every boundary that enforces it
78	
79	- **A product rule with more than one enforcing tier gets sibling leaves under one statement** — e.g.
80	  "only signed-in users can post": the surface's half (the client sends credentials) and the
81	  boundary's half (the server rejects an unauthenticated write) are separate proofs of one
82	  requirement.
83	- **The proof lives where the rule is actually enforced.** A surface-side test of a server-enforced
84	  rule proves only that the client cooperates, not that the boundary holds; if the real enforcement is
85	  the backend, a leaf must exist there, exercised against the real handler.
86	
87	## 5. A supported-targets matrix is spec, not folklore
88	
89	- **When part of the product's value is breadth over external targets** — supported sites, file
90	  formats, providers, locales — each supported target is its own leaf, so dropping a target is a
91	  visible spec change, not a silent regression.
92	- **Prove each target against a committed, real sample of it** (a captured page, a genuine file), with
93	  the owner-reviewed exact-values expectation committed beside it — capture the sample first and read
94	  the expecteds off the committed bytes (canon in the writing-tests skill). A hand-invented sample
95	  proves support for a target the world doesn't actually serve.
96	- **Adding a target is a documented, repeatable flow** that lands the new leaf, its real sample, and
97	  its reviewed expected together.
98	
99	## 6. Green means "claimed", not "fully verified" — track the gap honestly
100	
101	- **Say what the harness cannot reach, naming the exact boundary of each stub.** A faithful harness is
102	  still a model of the platform; the honest sentence pattern is "this proof confirms our code *asks*
103	  for the action, not that the platform *performs* it". Put that statement where readers of the spec
104	  will see it — a banner on the requirements doc, linking the issue that tracks closing the gap —
105	  rather than in a test README footnote.
106	- **Deliberate gaps are marked at the leaf and committed, never remembered.** A leaf that can't be
107	  faithfully verified yet stays in the spec, visibly provisional (a loud "to be decided" marker, and a
108	  pointer to whatever covers it meanwhile), and is listed in a committed allowlist the coverage gate
109	  checks — the allowlist is the burn-down list, shrunk deliberately. Prefer a real validation; reach
110	  for the marker only for a genuinely undecided edge case or a not-yet-wired harness.
111	
112	## 7. The owner reviews the product surface, not the internals
113	
114	- **Embed regenerated renders of the real states in the spec itself** — the requirements document
115	  doubles as a gallery of what the product actually shows, generated from the shipped code, so
116	  approving the spec *is* approving the product's appearance.
117	- **Regenerate, never hand-edit.** The gallery is derived output of a committed generator; fixing it
118	  means fixing the source (or the generator) and regenerating.
119	- **The deterministic golden-image method this leans on is canon in the writing-tests skill** —
120	  matching the render engine to the surface (a bit-exact rasterizer for inline-styled/SVG surfaces, a
121	  headless browser for pages that use grid/vars/emoji/form-widgets), bundled fonts, capturing a
122	  host-page surface with styles inlined, and a drift gate on the embedded gallery.
123	
124	## 8. Ship automatically while `main` stays green
125	
126	- **`main` is releasable at all times, and automation does the releasing** — a release (and, where
127	  the platform has one, store publication) cuts from `main` on its own cadence without a human build
128	  step. Keeping `main` green *is* the release gate: a red `main` is a shipping outage, fixed before
129	  new work.
130	- **The version users see moves deliberately.** Automation may patch-bump to ship, but a meaningful
131	  version change is a decision made on `main`, not a side effect. The concrete release contract —
132	  workflows, artifacts, store procedures — belongs to the project's release pack or release doc, not
133	  here.
