5	
6	# Releasing a Chrome extension to the Web Store
7	
8	Every Chrome-extension repo of ours ships the **same** release pipeline: same workflows, same
9	Chrome Web Store API usage, same secrets, same versioning and artifact rules, same README install
10	sections. This skill is that contract, the setup steps for a new extension repo, and the manual
11	Chrome Web Store actions the automation can't do. The workflow **logic** is authored once, in this
12	pack's [`stubs/`](../../stubs/) — the [orchestrator](../../stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml), the
13	five `workflow_call`-only **reusable workflows**, and the
14	[report-failure](../../stubs/actions/report-failure/action.yml),
15	[read-release-config](../../stubs/actions/read-release-config/action.yml) and
16	[bump-extension-patch](../../stubs/actions/bump-extension-patch/action.yml) composite actions — and
17	**vendored into each extension repo's own `.github/`**, where the whole pipeline runs with no
18	cross-repo dependency. GitHub only resolves a reusable workflow or composite action from a repo's
19	own `.github/`, so "the logic lives in the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each repo
20	hosts a *managed* copy: the pack keeps every copy in sync — baselining re-materializes on drift via
21	the `chrome-release-vendoring` migration — so a repo **hosts** the pipeline without **owning** it.
22	Treat the vendored `.github/workflows/` + `.github/actions/` set as generated: edit the pack, not
23	the copy. A repo adds only its **required** `.github/release.config` (five explicit keys, **no
24	defaults**). A merged canon change reaches every extension repo through the nightly baselining, not
25	a live `@main` reference. Everything a repo used to carry as workflow values — the version files, the
26	zip location, the test gate, the shipping set, and the previously per-repo `bump`/`filter` scripts
27	— is either pack logic (the bump, and `npm run build`) or an explicit `release.config` key, so no
28	repo ships a bump or filter script any more. Reference implementation:
29	`missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`; also adopted by `TLDR` and `CrosswordChat`.
30	
31	Naming in the flat `.github/workflows/` namespace: Chrome-specific logic carries the
32	`chrome-extension-` prefix (future publish standards — other stores — will live beside it);
33	genuinely platform-agnostic pieces (`deploy-privacy-page.yml`, the `report-failure` action) keep
34	general names so other standards reuse them as-is. When in doubt, prefix.
35	
36	## The contract
37	
38	**Versioning**
39	
40	- The extension manifest's `version` (`X.Y.Z`) is the single source of truth. The extension's
41	  `package.json` `version` must equal it, enforced by a CI-run guard (a unit test or an inline
42	  workflow check — the repo picks the mechanism, the invariant is fixed).
43	- **The bump belongs to the change, not to the pipeline.** A change that touches a shipped file
44	  (anything under the repo's `ship_paths`) raises the **patch** in the same PR, across the manifest
45	  and `package.json` together. `cer/version-bumped` is what holds that line, and
46	  `node .github/actions/bump-extension-patch/bump.mjs <manifest_path> <package_json_path>` is what
47	  writes it. Merging that PR *is* cutting the release. A change that ships nothing — a README, a
48	  test, a workflow — needs no bump and cuts no release.
49	- **Minor and major are deliberate, and belong to no single change**, so they are the one bump the
50	  pipeline still performs: dispatch **Release to Chrome Store** with `mode: bump` and `part:
51	  minor|major`, which raises the version, pushes it to `main` and packages the result. **"bump
52	  version"** means that dispatch, or the same edit by hand on a branch.
53	- **No workflow writes a version on its own.** The daily run and "Release: Create Package" alike
54	  ship whatever version is on `main`, and no-op when it has already been released. So a shipped
55	  change that forgot its bump is never released — which is the failure `cer/version-bumped` exists
56	  to catch on the PR instead.
57	
58	**Artifact**
59	
60	- `npm run build` produces the zip at the **forced-uniform** standard location
61	  `dist/<kebab-cased repo name>.zip` (e.g. `dist/google-calendar-event-creator.zip`, `dist/tldr.zip`,
62	  `dist/crossword-chat.zip`) — the place/name is derived, not a config choice; a repo's build must
63	  write there. Stable, never version-stamped, so
64	  `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>` is a permanent
65	  newest-build URL. `manifest.json` sits at the zip's top level.
66	- The zip's contents come from a single shipping-set source of truth in `dev/build/release/`,
67	  drift-guarded by a test — nothing dev/test-only ships, and a renamed runtime file fails the
68	  build rather than silently dropping out of the package.
69	- A release is GitHub Release **`vX.Y.Z`**, tagged at the released commit, with auto-generated notes
70	  and **two** assets built from the one tested tree, differing only in the injected `API_BASE_URL`:
71	  the headline **`<zip>`** (the permanent `…/releases/latest/download/<zip>` URL) is built with
72	  `API_BASE_URL` **cleared**, so it keeps the committed **dev** default — the downloadable build is
73	  dev, never prod; **`<zip>-prod.zip`** carries the injected prod `API_BASE_URL` and is the store's
74	  source of truth (the publish job downloads it). So **only the store submission is prod-pointed**;
75	  the signing key + client id are injected into both. (A repo with no `API_BASE_URL` — no backend —
76	  produces two byte-identical zips; the split is a no-op there.)
77	
78	**Workflow** — **one** orchestrator per repo, [`chrome-extension-release.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml), named exactly
79	`Release to Chrome Store`. It owns only the triggers; its three `if:`-guarded jobs each call a **local**
80	reusable workflow (`./.github/workflows/…`, all vendored alongside it). The failure reporter keys
81	tracking issues on the **per-operation** names baked into the reusable workflows (`Release: Create
82	Package`, `Release: Publish to Chrome Web Store`, `Release: Daily Auto-Release`) — not on the
83	orchestrator's `name:` — so collapsing to one entry point loses no per-operation triage:
84	
85	| job (trigger) | reusable workflow it calls — what it does |
86	|---|---|
87	| `create-package` (push to `main`; dispatch `mode: package`) | `chrome-extension-create-package.yml` — version guard (a clean no-op unless the manifest version was bumped, so ordinary pushes don't cut a release) → full test gate → build the dev headline `<zip>` + the prod `<zip>-prod.zip` → GitHub Release |
88	| `publish` (dispatch `mode: publish` — the default — with `tag`, `auto_publish`) | `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` — download the prod `<zip>-prod.zip` (falls back to `<zip>` for pre-split releases) → upload via the store API (publish to users unless `auto_publish: false` → dashboard draft) → refresh the `/privacy/` page (via the `deploy-privacy-page.yml` reusable) |
89	| `daily` (schedule `30 0 * * *`; dispatch `mode: daily`) | `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` — has the version on `main` been released yet? → if not, calls the two reusable workflows above on `main`'s tip |
90	| `bump` (dispatch `mode: bump` with `part: minor\|major`) | `chrome-extension-bump-version.yml` — raise the minor or major across the manifest + `package.json`, push it to `main`, then `create-package` on that commit |
91	
92	The `create-package` job triggers on **every** push to `main` (no per-repo manifest path in the
93	trigger) and relies on the version guard to no-op unless a bump landed. The privacy page has **no
94	job of its own** and no dedicated option: it redeploys as part of **every** publish, from the same
95	`PRIVACY.md` the listing points at. The publish workflow runs that deploy leg even when the store
96	upload fails (so the `/privacy/` URL goes live before the first publication too — see below). The
97	platform-agnostic `deploy-privacy-page.yml` reusable workflow is vendored alongside the others and
98	called by the publish reusable — a repo never dispatches it directly.
99	
100	- Repo-specific values do **not** travel as `with:` inputs — the reusable workflows read them from
101	  the repo itself via the `read-release-config` action, so the orchestrator is copy-verbatim. They live in a
102	  **required, fully explicit** `.github/release.config` (dotenv) — **five keys, no defaults**, because
103	  a default that "happens to match" a repo's layout silently ships the wrong thing when the layout or
104	  the default later changes:
105	  `manifest_path`, `package_json_path`, `setup_command` (`""` = no install, stated),
106	  `test_command`, `ship_paths`. Two things are **not** keys because they are **forced-uniform
107	  structure**, not a per-repo choice: the **build** is always `npm run build`, and the **zip** lives
108	  at `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip` (both `zip_path` and the asset name are derived).
109	  `cer/release-config` fails the review on a missing file, a missing required key, or an unknown
110	  (typo'd) key.
111	- The one value that stays in the **orchestrator** (not the config file) is `build_env` — KEY=VALUE lines a
112	  repo whose build bakes in release config passes on the `create-package` and `daily` jobs, because
113	  it must reference `${{ vars.* }}` statically. Every listed key must be non-empty or the run fails,
114	  so a repo can't ship a placeholder-configured zip. These are the genuine per-**environment**
115	  values that must not be committed; they live in repository **variables** (Settings → Secrets and
116	  variables → Actions → Variables). Store secrets travel via `secrets: inherit`.
117	- Every unattended workflow (all of the above; not PR CI) reports failures through the
118	  `report-failure` composite action baked into the reusable workflows — a red run must reach a
119	  human, never sit unseen in the Actions list. Each failure opens a **fresh** `workflow-failure`
120	  issue, and any earlier open failure issues for the **same** workflow are closed as duplicates of
121	  it, so the newest failure is always the single open bug to triage. Repos no longer carry a
122	  `report-failure.yml`; a repo's own non-standard unattended workflows use the vendored action
123	  directly (`uses: ./.github/actions/report-failure`).
124	- Daily auto-release semantics: it asks the **release list**, not a file diff — has the version
125	  currently on `main` been released? That is self-healing by construction (a failed day retries the
126	  next with nothing to undo, and a day whose merges shipped nothing carries the version that is
127	  already out and no-ops), and it leaves no window in which the pipeline and the repo disagree about
128	  what the current version is. Release + publish are invoked via `workflow_call` because a
129	  `GITHUB_TOKEN` push triggers no workflows.
130	- `ship_paths` is what `cer/version-bumped` reads to decide whether a change owed a bump, so the
131	  declaration that used to be the daily filter is now the check's scope — one statement of what
132	  ships, read on the PR instead of a day later. A repo whose shipping set is a curated subset (not a
133	  whole directory) lists it there and keeps its build's own ship-set test honest against that list.
134	- The bump is **pack logic**, not a per-repo script: the `bump-extension-patch` composite action
135	  (token-replaces the version in `manifest_path` + `package_json_path`; `part` selects patch, minor
136	  or major, and `--print` reads the current one). It, and the `read-release-config` action, are
137	  dependency-free and run on a bare runner (no `npm ci`). The directory keeps its older
138	  `bump-extension-patch` name because it is vendored into every extension repo, where a rename would
139	  strand the old copy.
140	- Until the four store secrets exist, the publish leg fails **loudly** (a fail-early step lists
141	  the missing names, and the tracking issue nags) — that is the designed state for a repo that
142	  hasn't finished its first manual publication; releases and zips still work.
143	
144	**Chrome Web Store API** — uploads go through `chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3`
145	(`npx --yes chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3 upload --source dist/<zip> [--auto-publish]`), which
146	reads env `EXTENSION_ID` / `CLIENT_ID` / `CLIENT_SECRET` / `REFRESH_TOKEN` — set from the four
147	repository **secrets**, same names in every repo:
148	`CHROME_EXTENSION_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN`.
149	
150	**Privacy page** — the policy source is `dev/build/release/store_artifacts/PRIVACY.md`; a Jekyll
151	`permalink: /privacy/` pins the public URL `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/privacy/`
152	independent of the file's location. The store listing's Privacy-tab URL points **there**, never
153	at a `blob/main` link. The page redeploys on every store publish — the publish workflow's
154	privacy-deploy leg runs regardless of whether the upload leg succeeds, so it also brings the URL up
155	for the very first publication.
156	One-time: repo Settings → Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions".
157	
158	**Store listing & permission justifications live in the dashboard, not the repo** — the listing
159	copy (name, summary, detailed description, category), the graphic-asset choices, and the
160	Privacy-practices answers (single-purpose statement, a justification for **every** permission the
161	manifest requests — `permissions`, `host_permissions`, and `optional_*` alike — the remote-code
162	answer, data-usage declarations, reviewer notes) are all Chrome Web Store dashboard state. We keep
163	**no** repo copy of them: a mirror only drifts from the dashboard it duplicates. They are authored
164	once, at the first publication (tracked by a one-time issue — see setup below), and edited in the
165	dashboard thereafter. What the repo *does* hold and enforce is the privacy policy and its
166	agreement with the manifest:
167	
168	- `dev/build/release/store_artifacts/PRIVACY.md` is the privacy policy, deployed verbatim as the
169	  public `/privacy/` page the listing points at.
170	
171	**Store assets & icons** — required inventory: a 128 px store icon; the manifest icons the
172	extension ships (16/32/48/128), living inside the extension source where the manifest points;
173	at least one 1280×800 (or 640×400) screenshot; optionally 440×280 small and 1400×560 marquee
174	promo tiles. Listing-only images live in `store_artifacts/`; shipped icons live in the extension
175	source. Every asset comes from a **committed, deterministic generator script** — regenerate and
176	commit, never hand-edit a generated PNG. The generator's tech is the repo's choice (the
177	reference repo draws with stdlib-only Python; CrosswordChat rasterizes SVG/HTML with headless
178	Chromium); what's fixed is that every asset is reproducible from the repo.
179	
180	**Layout** — release machinery lives in `dev/build/release/`: the zip builder + shipping-set
181	module (with its test), and `store_artifacts/` (`PRIVACY.md`, listing screenshots, icon/asset
182	generators). No per-repo bumper or shipped-paths filter: the bump is vendored pack logic, and
183	`ship_paths` in `.github/release.config` is the one statement of what ships. No per-repo release doc: the concrete names and paths live in
184	`manifest.json`/`package.json` and the required `.github/release.config`, and the shared procedure
185	lives once, in this guide — a repo copy would only drift from it.
186	
187	## README template
188	
189	Every extension repo's README carries these two sections, same wording, repo values filled in:
190	
191	```markdown
192	## Install
193	
194	**[Install from the Chrome Web Store →](<store listing URL>)**
195	
196	Or load the latest development build:
197	
198	1. Download [the latest release zip](https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>)
199	   and extract it — it unpacks to a folder with `manifest.json` at its top.
200	2. Open `chrome://extensions`, enable **Developer mode** (top right), click
201	   **Load unpacked**, and select that folder.
202	
203	## Releasing
204	
205	The version users see is [`<manifest path>`](<manifest path>)'s `version`. A change that touches a
206	shipped file raises it in the same PR; merging that PR cuts GitHub Release `vX.Y.Z` with `<zip>`
207	attached, and the daily auto-release ships that version to the Chrome Web Store on its own.
208	```
209	
210	Until the extension's first store publication, replace the store line with:
211	
212	```markdown
213	*Not yet on the Chrome Web Store — the listing goes live after the first manual publish (tracked
214	in the repo's first-publication issue).*
215	```

217	## Setting up a new extension repo
218	
219	1. Declare the pack in `.claudinite-settings.json`; baselining then **vendors the release set** — the
220	   [orchestrator](../../stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml) plus the reusable workflows under
221	   [`stubs/workflows/`](../../stubs/workflows/) and the composite actions under
222	   [`stubs/actions/`](../../stubs/actions/) — into this repo's own `.github/`. (Setting up before the next
223	   nightly pass? Copy those two trees yourself; there are no tokens to replace.) Then write the
224	   **required** `.github/release.config` (dotenv) with **all five** keys, explicitly — no defaults:
225	   `manifest_path`, `package_json_path`, `setup_command` (`""` = no install), `test_command`,
226	   `ship_paths`. (The build is always `npm run build`, and the zip lives at the derived
227	   `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip`, so neither is a key.) If the build bakes in per-environment config,
228	   uncomment the `build_env` block on the `create-package` and `daily` jobs of the orchestrator (the
229	   only vendored file a repo edits) and set the matching repository **variables** (see step 5).
230	2. Create `dev/build/release/` — zip builder + shipping-set module (with its test) and
231	   `store_artifacts/` with `PRIVACY.md` and the icon/asset generators — adapting from the reference
232	   repo's `dev/build/release/`. **No** per-repo bumper or shipped-paths filter (the bump is
233	   vendored pack logic); a curated shipping set is expressed as `ship_paths` in `release.config`, kept honest
234	   against the build by the repo's own ship-set test. No `releasing.md` and no `STORE-LISTING.md`:
235	   the release procedure lives in this guide, and the listing copy / permission justifications are
236	   dashboard state (above).
237	3. Wire `npm run build` to produce the zip at the standard `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip` (a monorepo
238	   sets a root `build` that delegates, e.g. `npm --prefix client run build`) and set `test_command`
239	   to the repo's full release gate. Add the two README sections above.
240	4. One-time GitHub setup: Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions". The four `CHROME_*` secrets come
241	   later, after the first manual publish. (No cross-repo Actions access to configure — the whole
242	   pipeline is vendored, so it never calls another repo's reusable workflows.)
243	5. Open the **first-publication tracking issue** (idempotent — search the tracker first, skip if
244	   one already exists, open or closed) so the one-time manual setup below is tracked as state, not
245	   carried as a repo file. Its checklist:
246	   - Set the four `CHROME_*` **secrets** (minted below) — Settings → Secrets and variables →
247	     Actions → Secrets.
248	   - **Only if the orchestrator uses `build_env`**: set the repository **variables** it references. These
249	     are automatable where API access exists — the issue carries a ready-to-run script, e.g.
250	     `gh variable set API_BASE_URL --repo <owner>/<repo> --body "https://…"` (repeat per key) —
251	     rather than a click-through, so the one manual part is minting the store credentials, not
252	     copying config into Settings.
253	   - Do the "First publication" steps below, then close the issue. From then on the daily pipeline
254	     owns routine shipping.
255	
256	> A repo's **own** first-publication runbook — a go-live checklist, an account/credentials setup
257	> guide — is the same do-then-close artifact by another name: first-publication *guidance*, not
258	> standing reference. Once the extension is live it's spent; fold anything durable into the
259	> standing architecture/README docs it already defers to, then remove the file. (That a cleanup
260	> makes you fix references *into* such a doc is the cue to ask whether the doc itself is in scope
261	> for removal — not to polish it.)

263	## Manual actions — publishing to the Chrome Web Store
264	
265	The steps the automation cannot do, distilled from the path actually run for the reference
266	extension; the upstream reference is
267	[Using the Chrome Web Store Publish API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/using-api).
268	
269	### First publication (once per extension)
270	
271	1. Register a developer account at the
272	   [developer dashboard](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole) (one-time $5 fee).
273	2. **Add new item** → upload the release zip. If the extension pins its ID with a manifest
274	   `key` (needed when OAuth redirect URIs depend on a stable ID — see
275	   [the chrome-extension pack RULES](../../RULES.md)), the **first** upload must NOT contain the
276	   `key`: the store assigns the ID at first upload, and you copy the dashboard's Package-tab
277	   public key back into the build afterwards. Record the 32-char item ID → the
278	   `CHROME_EXTENSION_ID` secret.
279	3. Complete the listing — 128px store icon, name, summary, detailed description, category,
280	   ≥ 1280×800 screenshot — authoring the copy **directly in the dashboard** (this is where it
281	   lives; the repo keeps no copy). Screenshots and icons come from `store_artifacts/`.
282	4. Privacy tab: write the single-purpose statement, a justification for **every** permission the
283	   manifest requests, and the data-usage declarations, directly in the dashboard; set the
284	   **Privacy policy** field (bottom of the tab) to the `/privacy/` Pages URL — the same policy
285	   `PRIVACY.md` deploys. **Before submitting**: bring the privacy page up by running the **Release**
286	   workflow once with **mode: publish** — its privacy-deploy leg runs even though the store-upload leg
287	   fails at this stage (no store item or secrets yet — the designed pre-publication state), so the
288	   `/privacy/` page goes live. Load the URL in a browser to confirm it's live, and paste that exact
289	   permalink — never a guessed path. Google re-fetches this URL on **every** publish, and an
290	   unreachable link fails the publish (see [When a store publish fails](#when-a-store-publish-fails)).
291	5. Submit for review — approval takes hours to a few days (`ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW` = success).
292	   While the item is **pending review the API rejects uploads** — hold the pipeline dry run
293	   until the first review completes. Every subsequent upload must carry a **strictly higher**
294	   version, which is why every shipped change raises one (`cer/version-bumped`); a "version must be
295	   greater" rejection on a dry run is a **pass** — it proves the credential wiring works
296	   end to end.
297	
298	### Minting the API credentials (once per extension)
299	
300	Browser-only — no local tooling needed. Two standing rules for every step below:
301	
302	- Every "sign in with Google" must use the **same Google account that owns the store listing**,
303	  and will hit a **"Google hasn't verified this app"** interstitial — click **Advanced** →
304	  **"Go to \<app\> (unsafe)"** → **Allow**. That's fine and permanent: you are this OAuth app's
305	  only user, so **ignore every verification prompt and never start verification** — an
306	  unverified app's tokens work indefinitely.
307	- Before acting on any Cloud-console page, confirm the **top-bar project picker** shows the
308	  project created in step 1.
309	
310	**Google Cloud setup:**
311	
312	1. **Create a project**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate> — any name, keep
313	   "No organization" → **Create**. Confirm the top-bar project picker switched to it.
314	2. **Enable the Chrome Web Store API**:
315	   <https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/chromewebstore.googleapis.com> → **Enable**.
316	3. **Configure the OAuth consent screen** (the console now brands this "Google Auth
317	   Platform"): <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/overview> → **Get started** → app name +
318	   support email → Audience: **External** → contact email → agree → **Create**.
319	4. **Publish the app to production**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/audience> →
320	   **Publish app** → **Confirm**. Left in "Testing", refresh tokens silently expire after
321	   7 days — the unattended daily release dies a week later.
322	5. **Create the OAuth client**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/clients> → **Create
323	   client** → type **Web application** (NOT Desktop — Desktop clients can't take custom
324	   redirect URIs; the client type makes no difference to `chrome-webstore-upload-cli`, the
325	   refresh-token grant is identical) → add authorized redirect URI exactly
326	   `https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground` → **Create**. The client ID and secret are
327	   `CHROME_CLIENT_ID` / `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`.
328	
329	**Mint the refresh token in the OAuth 2.0 Playground:**
330	
331	1. Open <https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground> → gear icon (top right) → check
332	   **Use your own OAuth credentials** → paste the client ID + secret.
333	2. In Step 1, ignore the API list: type `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/chromewebstore` into
334	   **Input your own scopes** → **Authorize APIs** → sign in as the listing owner → past the
335	   unverified interstitial → **Allow**.
336	3. Step 2 → **Exchange authorization code for tokens** → copy the **Refresh token** (starts
337	   `1//`). Ignore the access token — it expires hourly; the CLI mints its own.
338	4. **Empty Refresh-token field?** Consent wasn't force-prompted: in the gear panel set
339	   **Force prompt: Consent** and redo the authorize step.
340	
341	Add all four values as repository secrets at
342	`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/secrets/actions/new`:
343	`CHROME_EXTENSION_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN`.
344	
345	**Alternative — local Node**: `npx chrome-webstore-upload-keys` walks the same flow from a
346	terminal (it needs the client to be a **Desktop app**, whose `http://localhost` redirect it
347	uses). Use it only when a Node-equipped machine is at hand; the Playground route above is the
348	default because it assumes nothing about the operator's machine.
349	
350	### Routine shipping
351	
352	- Nothing to do for accumulated work: each shipped change landed with its own patch bump, so the
353	  daily auto-release ships whatever version is on `main` the moment it is not yet released.
354	- A deliberate release now: merge the shipped change (which carries its bump, and cutting the
355	  GitHub Release is what merging it does) → run **Release to Chrome Store** with **mode: publish**
356	  from its dispatch page,
357	  `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/actions/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml` (blank tag = latest release).
358	- A new feature set or a new generation: **"bump version"** — the same workflow with **mode: bump**
359	  and `part: minor|major`, which raises it, pushes it and packages the result.
360	- Once the store approves, Chrome auto-pushes the update to installed users within hours — no
361	  reinstall.
362	
363	### When a store publish fails
364	
365	- **HTTP 400 `Publish condition not met: Privacy policy link is not reachable.`** — Google
366	  fetches the listing's privacy-policy URL at publish time, and re-checks it on **every**
367	  publish. Fix it on the item's **Privacy** tab in the
368	  [developer dashboard](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole)
369	  (`https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole/<publisher-id>/<item-id>/edit/privacy`,
370	  bottom field, "Privacy policy"): set it to the exact live `/privacy/` permalink → **Save
371	  draft** → re-run the publish.
372	- **Upload rejected while `ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW`** — the API can't upload while a review is in
373	  flight; wait for the review to complete, then re-run.
374	- **"version must be greater" than the live one** — expected whenever the zip's version isn't
375	  strictly higher; on a credentials dry run this is success. Otherwise the version on `main` is one
376	  the store already has: the change that needed shipping never raised it, so raise it in a PR (or
377	  dispatch `mode: bump`) rather than re-running the publish.
378	
379	### When a change touches the extension's permissions
380	
381	Any PR that changes the manifest's `permissions`, `host_permissions`, or `optional_*`:
382	
383	1. Adding a permission trips `cer/permission-added-store-issue` (advisory): open a tracking issue
384	   for the manual dashboard step — the Privacy-practices tab must carry a written justification
385	   for the new permission, and the store blocks publishing the new version until it does, so the
386	   next store publish (daily or manual) stalls on it. (If the daily pipeline hits it first, the
387	   failed publish lands on its `workflow-failure` tracking issue; the proactive issue beats the
388	   reactive one.) After updating the dashboard, re-run the publish.
389	2. Expect deeper store review than a plain code update — permission changes re-open scrutiny.
390	3. A new **required** permission that carries an install-time warning disables the extension
391	   for existing users until each one re-approves it — prefer `optional_permissions` /
392	   `optional_host_permissions` requested at runtime (`chrome.permissions.request`) when the
393	   feature allows.

6	# Merge to main
7	
8	If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
9	points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.
10	
11	1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
12	2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
13	3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
14	4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
15	   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
16	5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
17	6. Capture the conversation:
18	   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
19	   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
20	   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
21	7. Run the basics pack's
22	   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
23	   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
24	   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
25	   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
26	   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.
27	
28	Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

1	---
2	name: git-github-advanced
3	description: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
4	---
5	
6	# Portable git & GitHub procedures
7	
8	The project-agnostic half of how we drive GitHub: the branch/commit-history rules for PR work, the CI-trigger rules, and how we keep merge-conflict churn cheap across parallel branches. (The issue → branch → PR task lifecycle that every task follows is baseline prose every session already loads — it's not task-gated, so it doesn't live here.) Project-specific GitHub procedures (the merge-to-main command, when to open a PR early, the merge-cheaply poll loop tuned to the local environment, and the generated-file merge rules) live in the consuming repo's own GitHub-procedures doc.
9	
10	## Updating an issue's status: comment, don't overwrite
11	
12	To post a **status update** on an issue (the lifecycle's "update the issue's status" step), use `add_issue_comment`. **Don't** reach for `issue_write` with `method: update` — that edits the issue itself and **replaces the whole body**, silently wiping the original description. Reserve `issue_write`/`update` for genuinely editing the issue (retitling, rewriting the body on purpose).
13	
14	## An auto-merge refusal is not a verdict — read the PR's state, then act
15	
16	`enable_pr_auto_merge` only accepts a PR whose required checks are still **pending**, so its refusals answer *timing and configuration*, never the change. Take each at face value and stop:
17	
18	- *"already in clean status (all checks passed)"* — the checks finished before you got there. That's the green light: `merge_pull_request` directly.
19	- *"in unstable status (required checks are failing)"* — this same wording covers a check that is **queued** or **held at an approval gate**. Resolve it by reading the PR's check runs and looking at **`status`**, not `conclusion`; a check that hasn't `completed` has no verdict.
20	- *"Protected branch rules not configured"* — auto-merge is a protected-branch feature, so a repo with no rule on its default branch can never arm it. Final; don't let an earlier refusal's wording talk you out of it.
21	
22	Never re-arm on a loop hoping the answer changes — observed runs answered "unstable" then "clean" seconds later with nothing changed in between, and one spent ~6 minutes of a 13-minute budget circling a single PR without merging it.
23	
24	## Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same commit that deletes what produced its artifacts
25	
26	Removing a toolchain invites tidying away its ignore rules alongside it — but the artifacts it already produced are usually still sitting untracked in the worktree (`__pycache__/` from an earlier run, `build/` from an earlier build). The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps the junk *into* the commit that was supposed to remove it, and nothing complains: the commit is valid and the tests still pass. Delete (or `git clean`) the artifacts first, then drop their ignore lines. And after any bulk `git add -A`, read `git diff --cached --stat` — staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops telling you about.
27	
28	## Branch and commit history
29	
30	### Commit often, in layers
31	
32	While working a branch, commit frequently rather than landing one big commit at the end — small, ordered commits let the owner follow the work as it develops. Use commits to *layer* the work in the order you'd want it reviewed:
33	
34	- Write the failing test(s) first, commit them, **then** implement the feature — so the history shows the contract before the code that satisfies it (and you've seen the test fail before trusting it).
35	- Keep any documentation update as its own commit *after* the feature, not folded into it.
36	
37	There's no cost to a branch carrying many commits when the project uses a **squash** merge to `main` (one commit per PR): the squash collapses them into a single commit on `main`, so `main`'s one-commit-per-PR history is unaffected no matter how granularly the branch is committed.
38	
39	- **One caveat, at merge time: before rebasing an *unmerged* multi-commit branch onto a *moved* base, collapse commits that rewrite the same lines into one.** When your own commits churn the same lines (build X → refactor → remove X, common in an iterative design session) and the base has advanced, rebasing the stack replays *every* intermediate conflict against the new base. The squash-merge discards those commits anyway, so collapse them first — `git reset --soft $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)` then one fresh commit, and rebase that single commit: one conflict pass, not N. Lossless (unlike `reset --hard` + redo) and simpler than `--onto` when you want a single commit anyway.
40	
41	- **When a rebase or a review round drops part of a branch, amend the commit message in the same step** — then read it back against `git show --stat` before merging. Under a squash merge the branch's commit body *becomes* `main`'s permanent record, while the explanation of what was dropped, if it lives in a PR comment, is not carried by the squash at all. A commit describing a change to files it never touched sends the next reader of `git log -- <path>` hunting for work that isn't there.
42	
43	- Don't rewrite published/shared history to satisfy a tooling or authorship check (e.g. a hook flagging "unverified" commits): only amend your own un-pushed branch commits. Commits already on a shared branch — including ones merged in from `main` — belong to that history; reset-authoring or rebasing them forks your branch away from it.
44	- After your commit is **squash-merged** to `main`, a *reused* feature branch still carries that original commit (the squash created a *new* commit on `main`, so the branch's own is unreachable from it) — and the next PR off the branch re-includes it in the diff, because the three-dot merge-base predates the squash. Sync the branch to `origin/main` before opening the next PR (`git rebase origin/main`, which drops the commit as an already-applied cherry-pick, or a hard reset): it's your own un-merged branch, so this is the amend-your-own-commits case above, not rewriting shared history.
45	  - **`git rebase origin/main` only drops the old commit cleanly when the branch carried a *single* squash-merged commit.** When it carried *several* commits that `main` squashed into *one* (then kept developing), git can't match them to the squash as already-applied, so it replays them and conflicts mid-rebase. Replant only the genuinely-new commits instead: `git rebase --onto origin/main <last-squash-merged-commit>` (then `git push --force-with-lease`). If the new work is small, a `git reset --hard origin/main` + redo beats fighting the replay.
46	  - **If the merge auto-deleted the remote branch, start follow-up work on a new branch off `origin/main`** rather than reusing the old name — it has no stale tracking ref and no rebase dance. If you do reuse the old name: `--force-with-lease` actively *fails* — `git push --force-with-lease` rejects with `stale info` then `couldn't find remote ref <branch>` because the lease expects a remote branch that no longer exists. There's nothing to overwrite, so `git fetch --prune` (drop the stale tracking ref) then a plain `git push -u origin <branch>` just recreates it.
47	
48	## An automated commit-nag is not authorization to commit drift
49	
50	An automated prompt to commit the working tree (a stop-hook, a CI nag) tells you the tree is dirty — not that the changes are yours or intended. Before obeying, inspect what actually changed (`git status` / `git diff`): if it's environment/setup drift — a submodule pointer moved by `git submodule update` at clone time, a lockfile a setup script regenerated, generated artifacts — revert it rather than committing it onto your branch. Committing drift slips an unintended dependency or generated-file bump into an unrelated change.
51	
52	## Open a PR early when the reviewable artifact only exists on CI
53	
54	The default is to hold a PR until asked. Reverse that when a change's only reviewable output is produced by CI — an e2e/heavy-browser run, or a rendered artifact (a UI-snapshot pixel diff, a generated gallery) that can't be exercised in the local sandbox. Opening the PR is how the change is seen working and how failures surface, so doing it up front — rather than iterating locally first, which proves nothing for these classes — is the faster path to a working, reviewable result. Each CI iteration costs a full round-trip, so get the first one running as early as possible.
55	
56	## Never `git checkout <ref> -- <paths>` to carry uncommitted edits onto another branch
57	
58	It reads those paths out of `<ref>`'s **committed** tree and writes them over the working copy — so the uncommitted edits you were trying to move are destroyed, silently and unrecoverably (no reflog, no stash). Move in-progress work either by branching in place (`git checkout -b <new>`, which carries a dirty tree with it) or by committing/stashing first and then restoring on the new branch. In particular never put the checkout in the same `&&` chain as the branch creation: by the time it runs, the edits are already the only copy.
59	
60	## Sync early to keep merge conflicts small
61	
62	Conflict size scales with how long a branch lives and how far it drifts from the default branch. Sync early rather than at the end: when starting work on a branch — and periodically while it's open — bring the latest default branch in first, so the branch carries current sources instead of discovering the gap at merge time. A one-commit-per-PR squash history already keeps each branch a single reviewable unit, so shorter-lived, freshly-synced branches are the norm.
63	
64	**In a repo that forbids merge commits on the branch — the `squash-merge-history` check, or squash-only merging generally — sync by *rebasing*, never `git merge` the base in.** A `git merge origin/main` (even just to resolve conflicts) leaves a **merge commit** the check blocks, forcing a redo; `git pull --rebase` / `git rebase origin/main` replays your work with no merge commit. GitHub's **"Update branch"** button — and the `update_pull_request_branch` API behind it — is this same base-merge in disguise: it adds exactly the merge commit the check blocks, so refresh with a local rebase + `git push --force-with-lease` instead. The merge-conflict-resolution gotchas below apply to a rebase's conflicts exactly the same way.
65	
66	## A local git-mutation refusal after a merge already succeeded server-side is not worth a second variant
67	
68	Once an API call reports the merge done (`merged: true`), syncing your local checkout afterward is a convenience, not part of landing it — so if the session's own permission/auto-mode classifier denies a mutating git command (`git checkout main`, `git pull`, `git reset --hard`), take one attempt and stop; a differently-phrased retry (a plain `checkout`, then `fetch origin main`, then `reset --hard`) hits the same classifier and burns minutes on a step with nothing downstream of it. State plainly that local `main` is behind and move on, or confirm what's needed **read-only** (`git log`, a file-contents fetch against the server) instead of continuing to mutate.
69	
70	## The sandbox checkout can be shallow, and a shallow history breaks `git merge-base`
71	
72	A shallow clone (or a shallow default checkout in a sandboxed session) carries a truncated history graph with synthetic grafts, so `git merge-base <default> <branch>` fails for branches that predate the shallow point — even ordinary, cleanly-merged ones — and any check that reads that failure as "orphaned" or "unrelated" produces false positives at scale. Before trusting a merge-base result (or any cross-branch history comparison), run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`; if it reads `true`, unshallow first: `git fetch origin '+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*' --prune && git fetch --unshallow`.
73	
74	## Prefer `git commit && git push` over the MCP file-write tools for a file already correct on disk
75	
76	`push_files`/`create_or_update_file` take the file body as a literal string the model composes for the call, so what lands is a **transcription** of the file, not the file — a truncated JSON config and a stray inserted blank line have both landed this way on real PRs, each caught only by chance. Reserve the MCP write path for what genuinely needs it (a file a scoped token can push but the session's own git remote can't — e.g. `.github/workflows/` under a `GITHUB_TOKEN` that's forbidden to push it), and when you do use it, read the result back with a file-contents fetch and diff it against the local copy before moving on.
77	
78	## A run that never executed the repo's own steps is infrastructure, not a CI failure to wait out
79	
80	Two tells: a check stuck `queued` that auto-cancels around 15 minutes with its job logs then 404ing, or a job that dies in an early platform-provided step (e.g. "Prepare all required actions" / "Failed to resolve action download info … Service Unavailable") before your own workflow's steps ever start. Recognize the pattern and say plainly that it's a platform outage rather than continuing to poll or hunting for a repo-side cause — re-running (once) is the whole remedy; waiting longer or diagnosing the workflow file spends more time on an outage neither can fix.
81	
82	## After a remote-side merge, fetch before branching off origin/main
83	
84	A GitHub API/UI (or any remote-side) merge does **not** advance your local `origin/main` — it stays at the pre-merge commit until you `git fetch`. Branching off `origin/main` immediately after a remote merge forks the pre-merge state, silently missing the just-merged work; symptoms surface later as a missing file or a failed `git mv` on the new branch. Fix: `git fetch origin main` before creating the branch.
85	
86	## `git pull` failing "refusing to merge unrelated histories" usually means upstream re-rooted
87	
88	When syncing a long-lived local clone's default branch fails with `refusing to merge unrelated histories` (often alongside `ahead N, behind M`), the usual cause is that upstream **re-rooted** the branch — a history rewrite replaced the root commit — not repository corruption. Do **not** reach for `--allow-unrelated-histories`: that "fix" welds the two histories together into a merge nobody wants. Instead inspect what the local side uniquely holds (`git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` — typically just the old root), keep anything real by rebasing it onto the new history, then `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`. A work branch created from *fetched* refs is unaffected; only stale local refs from before the rewrite hit this.
89	
90	## A conformance finding on history you didn't write may be a stale diff base — refresh before fixing
91	
92	A Stop-hook or CI conformance check diffs your branch against `origin/main`. In a fresh cloud sandbox that ref can be **stale** — behind real `main` by whole merged PRs — so the check reads the wrong base and can flag findings on commits or code you never touched. Before acting on a finding you don't recognize, `git fetch origin <default-branch>` and re-run: a stale-base phantom disappears, and whatever survives against the current base is real — fix that. (The same stale ref bases new work on outdated product code, so fetch before building against `main`, too.)
93	
94	The same reflex applies when a **real** (not phantom) red check blocks *your* PR and you've correctly pinned it as pre-existing and unrelated to your diff: that "not mine" diagnosis is a **sync-the-base** signal, not a fix-it-yourself-or-ask-the-user one — `main` has often *already fixed* it since you branched, so merge/rebase the latest base into your branch and re-check before proposing a fix or escalating.
95	
96	## In a squash-merge repo, "commits ahead of main" does not mean "unmerged"
97	
98	A squash-merge creates a new commit on `main` that the branch's own commits are unreachable from, so a branch whose work has already landed still shows ahead by N. **"Ahead by N" never alone means unmerged.** Determine real status by content, not raw count:
99	
100	1. **PR state** — a merged PR means the work is in `main`; safe to delete however many commits show ahead.
101	2. **Content diff** — `git diff --stat main..branch`: if everything the branch adds is already in `main`, the work landed (catches a squash with no surviving PR).
102	3. **Superseded elsewhere** — the branch's work may have landed in `main` under a *different path or form* (a doc distilled into another, a feature re-implemented), so a file/line diff still shows its additions as branch-side and it reads as unmerged. Before concluding so, check whether its *intent* already exists in `main` — grep for the concept, not just the exact path.
103	4. **No merge-base** — `git merge-base` fails when a force-push rewrote `main` and orphaned the branch; can't be proven in or out mechanically; needs human review, never an automatic delete.
104	5. Otherwise — genuine unmerged work.
105	
106	## A push or PR made with the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not start another workflow
107	
108	GitHub suppresses workflow runs triggered by the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to prevent recursion, so a workflow's own `git push` or `gh pr create` won't fire another workflow (e.g. a `test` or cache-refresh workflow). The one exception is `workflow_dispatch` / `repository_dispatch` — which is why an automation pipeline that needs the downstream checks to run must dispatch them explicitly. A run dispatched against a branch executes on its head commit, so its checks still attach to the PR. The same suppression covers a Claude session's own app-scoped pushes: creating a PR through the API does fire its `pull_request` run, but a follow-up push to that PR gets **no** `synchronize` run — so don't wait for checks that will never start on the new head; gate by running the CI commands locally, and rely on the post-merge run (merging through the merge API does fire the `push` workflow on the default branch).
109	
110	**"Suppressed" is not always "absent", and the difference decides whether a PR can merge.** Where the repo requires approval for a workflow run, GitHub *creates* the `pull_request` run and parks it at conclusion `action_required` with **zero jobs**, waiting for a human "Approve and run" that unattended automation never gets. The run never executes and never reports, yet it still counts against the PR: `mergeable_state` stays `unstable` and auto-merge refuses to arm, even though the explicitly dispatched run on the same head sha passed. Nothing inside the workflow file can prevent it — `branches`/`branches-ignore` on `pull_request` filter the **base** branch (a bot branch's PR still targets the default branch), and the approval gate is applied to the whole run before any job-level `if` is evaluated. So treat a gated run as **no verdict rather than a failure**, and land the PR on the evidence of the run that actually ran.
111	
112	## A workflow definition only takes effect once it's on the default branch
113	
114	A `workflow_dispatch` or scheduled workflow runs from the copy on the **default branch**, and a `pull_request` run uses the workflow files from the PR's **base** branch — so a workflow you only added on a feature branch isn't dispatchable, and a build/CI change doesn't apply, until it's merged. Merge workflow and build-script changes *before* the release or run that depends on them, or that run executes the *old* definition (shipping a stale build, or silently skipping a check you thought you'd added). This is distinct from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` recursion rule above: even a human-triggered run reads the definition from the default/base branch, not your feature branch.
115	
116	## A CI OIDC `sub` claim is matched case-sensitively by the cloud trust policy
117	
118	GitHub's OIDC `sub` uses the repository's **canonical casing** (`repo:Owner/Repo:ref:…`), and a cloud trust policy compares it exactly — AWS IAM `StringEquals` is case-sensitive — so a trust policy written with the wrong case fails with a bare `Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` and **no** hint that casing is the cause. Match the exact canonical `owner/repo` (or list both casings in the condition). The same exact-match caution applies to any OIDC-federated cloud, not just AWS.
119	
120	## An automated job needs a unique branch per run
121	
122	An automated or scheduled job that derives its branch name from a non-unique key (e.g. the date) collides with itself on a repeat run for that key — `git checkout -b` fails when the branch already exists, and a push to the diverged remote branch is rejected non-fast-forward (so the run can't even open its PR). Give every run its own branch: append a per-run-unique suffix (`$RANDOM` / a short token) to the readable prefix.
123	
124	## An unattended workflow must escalate its own failure to a human-visible state
125	
126	A workflow with no human watching the run — scheduled, triggered by a push/merge, or a fire-and-forget manual dispatch, with no other path that reaches a person — must converge a failure to something a human will see (e.g. open a `workflow-failure` issue for it) rather than merely exiting red in the Actions list, where nobody looks. Skip this only when the failure is already loud: a `pull_request`/push CI run that blocks merge with a red required check the author is watching, or a workflow that already flags the triggering issue itself on failure. The canon's [report-failure](../../../../.github/actions/report-failure/action.yml) action does exactly this — a **fresh** issue per failure, with earlier open failure issues for the same workflow closed as duplicates of the newest — so the current failure is always the single open bug to triage; a standing per-workflow issue appended to on each failure is an equally valid shape, the invariant is only that the red run reaches a person.
127	
128	When the escalation is itself a separate reusable workflow invoked via `workflow_call`, permissions don't propagate implicitly through the chain: the job that calls it needs the permission explicitly granted (e.g. `issues: write`), and if that reusable workflow in turn calls another one, the middle workflow must forward the same grant to its own call — a caller two levels up granting it once is not enough.
129	
130	## A CI job that inspects commit shape must check out the PR head, not the merge ref
131	
132	On `pull_request`, `actions/checkout` checks out the synthetic `refs/pull/N/merge` commit by default — an ephemeral merge of the PR head into the base — so `HEAD` is itself a merge commit, not the branch tip. Any job that reasons about commit *shape* or history (merge commits, commit count, `--first-parent`, commit messages) reads that synthetic merge and misfires: a "no merge commits" check false-positives even on a linear branch, since `HEAD` is a merge. Check out the head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}`) so CI evaluates the same branch tip a local run does.
133	
134	## To read a PR's CI result, look at its check runs — `get_status` misses Actions
135	
136	GitHub **Actions** reports results as **check runs**, not the legacy **commit statuses**, so `pull_request_read` `method: get_status` returns `state: pending`, `total_count: 0` for a PR whose Actions CI has already **passed** — reading falsely as "no CI / not started," which can skip a real gate or trigger an endless wait. Gate on CI by reading the **check runs for the PR head SHA** (`get_check_run`, or the workflow run for that SHA) instead. Target the head SHA directly rather than `actions_list`-ing the repo's runs — that returns every run, its output is huge, and a specific check-run/SHA query is both correct and cheap.
137	
138	## To confirm a non-PR run (push / dispatch), read its job logs — it has no PR check runs
139	
140	A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. `get_job_logs` needs more than a bare `run_id`: it rejects with "job_id is required when failed_only is false" unless you pass `failed_only: true` or fetch a `job_id` first (`list_workflow_jobs`), and it 404s for a job still `in_progress` — wait for the job to finish. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.
141	
142	## A deleted workflow's old runs outlive it, and no session tool can clear them
143	
144	Removing a `.yml` from every branch does not remove its run history — the workflow stays listed in
145	the Actions tab, a ghost registration attached only to runs that already happened. Clearing it
146	needs `DELETE /repos/.../actions/runs/{run_id}`, an `actions: write` endpoint outside the read/
147	list/get-logs/dispatch surface the GitHub MCP toolset exposes. Don't hunt for a session-side fix
148	that doesn't exist — hand the cleanup to the owner (their own UI, or a one-time sanctioned
149	workflow) instead.
150	
151	## A green run is not evidence its job ran — read the job's own conclusion
152	
153	A workflow that gates a later job (an `if:` on changed paths, a mode flag, a preceding job's output) concludes **success** with that job **skipped** — so "the release workflow is green" is not evidence the publish step ever executed, and most green runs may never have reached it. Read the conclusion of the **job that does the thing**, never the run's. The corollary for closing an issue: the only closing evidence is a run that actually reached that job and went green, or the external system showing the effect. Fixing a repo-side defect that merely co-occurred with the failure verifies nothing, and a failure caused by state in an external service has no fix in the repo at all.
154	
155	## Mark large committed fixtures `linguist-vendored` to fix language stats
156	
157	Large committed fixture files (full-page HTML, generated data dumps) can dwarf actual source by byte count and cause GitHub to mislabel the repo's primary language. Add a `.gitattributes` entry for each such path (e.g. `test/fixtures/*.html linguist-vendored`) to tell Linguist to ignore it; apply the same annotation whenever you add another large generated or fixture file.
158	
159	## Renaming a directory that houses a submodule
160	
161	`git mv` on a directory containing a submodule rewrites `.gitmodules` and the index correctly but leaves `.git/config` stale — its old `[submodule "<old/path>"]` entry lingers, so any operation that consults `.git/config` (submodule status, checkout) sees the old path until you fix it. Run `git submodule sync && git submodule update --init` after the move to propagate the new path and re-register the submodule.
162	
163	## GitHub Markdown inside a `<td>` requires surrounding blank lines
164	
165	In a GitHub-rendered Markdown file, cmark-gfm re-enters Markdown mode inside a raw `<td>` only when blank lines surround the cell's content — without them the cell is treated as a raw HTML block and its content is shown verbatim (no `![img]()`, no `**bold**`, no links). GitHub's sanitizer strips `style` / CSS, so a flexbox two-column layout won't render; use a plain `<table>` with `align` / `valign` / `width` instead. GFM pipe-table cells can't hold multi-line prose — use the raw-`<table>` form when a cell needs it. A leading inline `<!-- … -->` comment also opens an HTML block, so keep any such marker as the *last* token on the line, leaving the line to *start* as Markdown.
166	
167	## `commit.gpgsign = true` does not cover merge commits
168	
169	`commit.gpgsign = true` signs ordinary commits but does not apply to `git merge` — each merge produces an unsigned commit even with signing fully configured. In a repo that enforces commit verification, this requires a fix-up after the fact. Cover merges proactively: either pass `-S` to every `git merge` call, or set `merge.gpgsign = true` globally so merges are signed the same way commits are.
170	
171	## When access is scoped to an explicit repo list, query per-repo — never an org/user-wide search
172	
173	A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.
174	
175	## Cap *and* qualify every list/search call — an unbounded one blows the tool-result limit
176	
177	A list or search API call that isn't bounded returns a full page of full-bodied records and overruns the agent's tool-result cap, which costs two or three further calls to dig the answer back out of the spilled result — a pure-overhead round trip on a call whose wanted answer was a single record. Two independent bounds, both needed:
178	
179	- **Qualify the query so it matches what you mean.** A bare string handed to an issue/PR search is a *full-text* search over the whole repo — title, body, and comments — so a lookup for one known issue returns every issue that merely mentions the phrase, each with its whole body. Anchor it to the field (`in:title "<exact title>"`), or use the narrower tool (a label-filtered `list_issues`, a run-id or head-SHA query) instead of a search.
180	- **When you already know the exact title, don't search at all — list and match it yourself.** Field anchoring is a *GitHub search API* feature, and an MCP layer in front of it may match **semantically** instead, ranking by resemblance and honouring no qualifier: the title you named can then rank below unrelated issues or be absent from the page entirely, and `in:title` changes nothing. Enumerate with `list_issues` (a narrow field list, a large page size, no state filter — a log issue is often deliberately closed) and compare the string in-session. Reserve search for what it is good at: finding items you can only *describe*.
181	- **Trim the fields, not just the page size.** The per-object field set is what governs the payload, so capping the page can leave the response byte-identical — measured, the same call at two page sizes returned output identical to the character. Ask for the fields you need (`["number","title","state"]` covers most lookups); dropping the body alone is usually the whole difference. Where a tool offers no field selection, narrow the query instead, or take the overflow as the answer and read the spilled result file directly rather than retrying it smaller.
182	- **Pass a small explicit page size.** Default page sizes are tuned for a browser, not a tool result; when the answer wanted is one issue or one run, ask for 5–10, never a bare unpaged call.
183	
184	All of them, not one: a qualified query still returns a full page, a small page of unqualified matches is still the wrong records, and a small page of full-bodied records still overruns the cap.
185	
186	## Merging gotchas
187	
188	These conflict/merge traps are independent of any one project's file layout.
189	
190	### Merging across a file relocation
191	
192	git's rename detection re-applies your content edits onto the moved files, but it does *not* fix *references* to the moved paths — an npm script, a `.gitattributes` glob, or a doc link naming the old location keeps pointing there and breaks with no conflict (a green local test on the old layout won't catch it either). After such a merge, grep the files your branch touched for the old paths.
193	
194	### Merging in content that predates a branch-wide invariant
195	
196	When your branch establishes a cross-cutting invariant — a renamed term, a "mentioned only in X" containment rule — a branch you merge in that *predates* it can silently reintroduce violations: its independent additions (a new file, a new section) auto-merge clean, no conflict, while still using the old form. Resolving the marked conflicts isn't enough. Re-run the check that *defines* the invariant (the grep) over the whole tree after the merge, not just the conflicted files.
197	
198	### Porting old work forward across a changed invariant
199	
200	The converse direction: when you re-implement or cherry-pick an *older* change onto current `main`, check each part against the invariants `main` has added since — not just whether it still applies. A part that violates a now-enforced guarantee becomes a **silent no-op** if taken verbatim (e.g. a guard that reverts any write outside an allowed set leaves the patch landed but doing nothing), so drop or redesign it rather than copy it.
201

2	name: github-actions-scheduling
3	description: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
4	---
5	
6	# GitHub Actions cron is best-effort
7	
8	GitHub's `schedule:` trigger is a **request to queue**, not a promise to run. A cron'd workflow
9	routinely fires minutes to tens of minutes late, and under load GitHub **drops** a firing
10	outright — the run never happens, with no failure, no notification, and nothing in the run
11	ledger to look at. The effect is worst at `:00` and other round minutes, where everyone's cron
12	lands at once. GitHub's docs concede only that a schedule "may be delayed during periods of high
13	loads"; the behaviour is measured across a fleet in
14	[Upptime's write-up](https://upptime.js.org/blog/2021/01/22/github-actions-schedule-not-working/).
15	Same family, different mechanism: GitHub **disables** a repo's scheduled workflows entirely
16	after 60 days without repository activity.
17	
18	## Building for it
19	
20	- **Never let correctness depend on a firing happening, or on when it happened.** Derive what is
21	  due from durable state the run can read — the Actions run ledger, a timestamp in the repo, the
22	  world the job inspects — never from "this fired, so it must be time". Wall-clock equality with
23	  the cron minute is not a test any real run passes.
24	- **Idempotent and self-catching.** A scheduled job does whatever is outstanding *now*, so a
25	  missed firing costs latency rather than data. Per-scheduler run bookkeeping — counters, "the last hour's
26	  changes", a queue advanced one step per run — loses information the first time a scheduler run vanishes.
27	  If a job cannot catch up, say so where it is declared and design the miss as an accepted loss.
28	- **Catch up the most recent slot only.** A job that backfills every missed slot turns an outage
29	  into a storm on recovery; one catch-up evaluation per frequency is the shape that survives a
30	  multi-day gap.
31	- **Spacing two jobs apart is not an ordering.** "B is an hour after A, so A has finished by
32	  then" holds only while the fires land on time — and when a poll is dropped, the catch-up run
33	  finds *both* due and does them together, which is precisely the run where B most needs A to
34	  have gone first. If the order actually matters, assert it in the run: have the run do A and
35	  defer B, or have B check for A's result and skip when it is missing. Spacing is a preference;
36	  a check is a guarantee.
37	- **Pick a minute off `:00`.** Anywhere in `:10–:50` dodges the stampede and stays clear of the
38	  hour boundary any slot math anchors on; across a fleet, hash the repo name into that band so
39	  members spread rather than collide.
40	- **Deadline-bound work does not belong on a cron.** If something must happen *at* a time, drive
41	  it from the event, not an hourly poll that may skip.
42	
43	## Talking about it
44	
45	- **Say "about hourly, best-effort", never "hourly".** Stating an interval the platform does not
46	  honour turns ordinary jitter into a bug report.
47	- **A late or missing run is not a defect until proven one.** First question: did GitHub fire at
48	  all — check the workflow's run list, not the job's logic. Then: has the repo been quiet for 60
49	  days? Only after both does the code become a suspect. A single missed slot is expected
50	  behaviour.
51	
52	Claudinite's own scheduler is built to this: a repo-hashed `:10–:50` minute, and an hourly scheduler run
53	that reconciles a queue of issues rather than replaying a ledger — a missed fire leaves the queue
54	exactly as it was, so the next one catches up by looking at it. See
55	[the writing-tasks skill](../../../claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md) for the task-authoring side.
56

1	# Static website
2	
3	A static site that releases on push and serves from GitHub Pages. The full contract — the pipeline, the config, the setup — is [the static-site-releases skill](skills/static-site-releases/SKILL.md); these are the things a session touching such a repo has to know before it edits anything.
4	
5	- **A published file is a file the publish set names — adding a page is two edits.** The Pages artifact is assembled from `.github/site.config`'s `publish_paths` and nothing else, so a new page, stylesheet or data file that isn't under a published path (or named in the list) is simply absent from the live site, with no error anywhere: the build is green, the deploy succeeds, the page 404s. When you add a file the site serves, put it under an already-published directory or add it to `publish_paths` in the same change. The list is additive on purpose — the alternative, "publish the repo minus what we remember to exclude", publishes every draft, note and key nobody thought to hide.
6	- **The version moves with the change.** A change touching the published site raises `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` in the same PR — `node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs $(version_files)` computes it from the previous version and the UTC date, and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds the line. Never hand-write the `ymmdd` or the counter: a typed value either collides with a released one or is dated in the future, and the next bump refuses. The release flow writes no version of its own — it ships what it finds on `main` — so a shipped change without a bump is never released at all. The one deliberate human part is the **major**, a "this is a new generation of the site" statement; the owner's **"bump version"** means exactly that, and the release workflow's `bump: major` dispatch is what performs it.
7	- **The pipeline files under `.github/workflows/static-site-*` and `.github/actions/{read-site-config,bump-site-version,assemble-site}` are managed copies of the pack's `stubs/`.** Fix the pack and re-vendor; an edit to the copy is overwritten and, until it is, makes this repo's pipeline differ from every other site repo's. The repo's own values all live in `.github/site.config`, which is what the copies read.
8	- **The site is served from a subpath, not a domain root.** GitHub Pages serves it at `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/` (unless a custom domain is configured), so a root-relative URL — `/style.css`, `/img/logo.png`, a `fetch('/data.json')` — resolves above the site and 404s in production while working fine in a local `file://` or `python -m http.server` preview. Write links, asset paths and fetches **relative** to the page.
9	- **Freshness is a published manifest's job, not a per-file TTL's.** There is no server here to vary `Cache-Control` per file, so the freshness policy moves into the client — and the shape it reaches for first, giving each file a lifetime matching how fast you think it changes, reprices the same bet on every file and gets it wrong in both directions at once: too long and visitors read stale data, too short and they re-download what never changed. Publish one small manifest naming every downloadable asset and a hash of its contents, fetch *that* on each load, and evict exactly the entries whose hash moved. It buys longer caching **and** fresher data, which no TTL can offer together, and the extra request is the one you are probably already making for a version string. Expect a mismatch mid-deploy — the manifest is fetched, a deploy lands, the asset that follows disagrees — so refetch once and carry on; only a disagreement that survives fresh copies of both is a fault worth surfacing.
10	- **Nothing can attest to its own freshness, and size attests to nothing at all.** A stale file carries a perfectly valid hash *of itself*, and an internal `"version"` field states which generation it is, never whether that generation is still current — so the expected hash has to come from a file fetched fresher than the one being judged, which is what makes the manifest the one asset that may never carry a TTL of its own. Caching it saves no round-trip; it moves the staleness up a level and hides it better. Nor is length a cheap stand-in for a hash: a correction applied uniformly across a file is routinely byte-length-neutral — a timezone fix rewriting every `16:25` to `17:25` moved **0 bytes** of a 3.1 MB catalogue while changing the meaning of every record in it. And record the manifest's hash beside the entry as you write it, so the check is a string compare; re-hashing the stored body means pushing megabytes through a digest on the critical path of every load to answer a question the bookkeeping already knows.
11	- **Two files cached on separate clocks and later joined *will* be joined across generations — make them a verified set or don't split them.** Splitting a payload so each half caches on its own schedule is a sound instinct and it has this cost: every visitor eventually holds one half from Tuesday and the other from Thursday. Content-addressed keys ("name the row by its date and time, not its position in the array") survive rows being *added and removed*, which is what they are usually chosen for, and not a systematic *correction to the key itself* — a timezone shift, a rounding change, a rename — which moves every key at once and joins the two halves to nothing. Have each half record the generation of the other and refetch both on a mismatch. Then assert on the join *rate*, because a partial join is silent by construction: a missing key returns "no data for this row", which is indistinguishable from a row that genuinely has none yet, and a check written as "at least one row joined" passes at 6%.
12	- **Don't call missing data survivable until you have followed it to the pixel.** "The fetch is allowed to fail — it'll just show as unknown, which we already handle" is a claim about every consumer downstream, and it is usually wrong: an absent value reaching a boolean, a comparison or a status lookup is very often indistinguishable from a real negative, so the page renders a confident falsehood with nothing logged and the visitor acts on it. Trace the missing value all the way to what it draws before deciding a failure is tolerable. Where it isn't, the file is required — fail the load and show the error state, because a wrong answer with no error is worse than an error.
13
