2	name: writing-tasks
3	description: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
4	---
5	
6	# Writing a task
7	
8	The contract a task is written to. How a repo's own Claudinite work runs: A repo schedules **itself**, and
9	every occurrence of every task is an **issue in that repo** — a `[claudinite-work]`
10	work item whose labels are its state. That is the work-item queue; what follows is
11	the contract a task is written to, not how the queue works internally.
12	
13	**A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is.** A task is a
14	unit of the repo's own work with a precondition, a code-work phase and optionally an
15	agentic-work phase; `frequency` says only how often the queue offers to run it, and
16	`manual` — no cadence at all — is a first-class value. Work that fires on an event,
17	on a condition, or on a force is a task in exactly the same sense as work that fires
18	nightly, and reads the same contract. Anything reachable from the executor belongs
19	here rather than in a workflow of its own; see the cron rule below for the narrow
20	case that genuinely cannot be.
21	
22	Three responsibilities, strictly separated (owner, 2026-08-06):
23	
24	1. **The scheduler run** — a vendored hourly Action
25	   (`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) that is pure label mechanics
26	   over the issue list: **instantiate** each recurring task's standing item when
27	   its anchor comes, **ready** blocked items whose wait has passed, **reclaim**
28	   dead executor claims. It evaluates no precondition and collects no signal.
29	2. **The executor** — a pull worker over the queue (the scheduler run's post-scheduler run drain,
30	   and a `labeled`-event run for latency) that picks the next ready item, claims
31	   it, evaluates **that one task's** precondition, runs its code-work, and either
32	   converges the item or hands off to an agent session.
33	3. **The task-janitor** — an ordinary daily task (`basics/task-janitor`,
34	   `agent_model: none`) that owns everything about the queue that is *nobody's
35	   task*: items stuck ready past their period, items wearing no state label after
36	   a torn transition, and a health review of the open set.
37	
38	The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics
39	pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
40	scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
41	declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.
42	
43	There is no watermark and no per-run state: an occurrence exists because its
44	issue exists, which is why an outage self-heals by looking at the queue rather
45	than by replaying a ledger.
46	
47	## What the checks guard
48	
49	- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
50	  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
51	  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
52	  `engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
53	  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
54	  `workflow_dispatch` trigger (whose one `wake` input is how a task is forced,
55	  here or from another repo), and a call into the vendored scheduler run — no logic of its own
56	  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
57	  is the repo's **only** cron; the executor's workflow beside it carries none. Work
58	  that had its own cron'd workflow becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted
59	  — its steps move into the task's worker. So does work with no cron at all: an
60	  event-driven or condition-gated job becomes a task on `frequency: 'manual'`, woken
61	  by whatever knows the event happened. Don't keep either as a dispatch-only workflow
62	  for the task to fire: that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a
63	  workflow whose only caller is the thing that replaced it. (The exception is narrow,
64	  and it is **not** about privilege. An Actions-only secret is reachable from
65	  code-work, which runs Action-side — `required_secrets`, below. A deploy target's
66	  OIDC identity is one `permissions:` line in the executor's own workflow, not a wall.
67	  A one-shot external effect is handled by `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`, not by
68	  escaping to a workflow. What genuinely does not fit is the Actions **composition
69	  model**: a `uses:` step is resolved by the runner out of workflow YAML, and code-work
70	  is itself a step's subprocess, so no task — in any language — can invoke one. Work
71	  built on marketplace or composite actions, a Pages deploy being the standing example,
72	  keeps a workflow for those steps. Even then the task owns the trigger and the
73	  decision to run; the workflow carries only the `uses:` steps.) Off-band or multiple
74	  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
75	  safety, or manual runs.
76	
77	- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`
78	  default-exports `id` (matching its directory), `frequency` (`hourly | daily-2h
79	  | daily-1h | daily | daily+1h | weekly | monthly | manual`), `precondition_signals` (the collector
80	  vocabulary), `agent_model` (`opus | sonnet | haiku | none`), `expected_outcome` (`none |
81	  open-pr | merged-pr`), and a `precondition`. An agentic task (`agent_model !==
82	  none`) also carries `agent_instructions`, the worker file the agent reads; a
83	  `none` task runs no agent, so the field is not applicable and is omitted. The
84	  scheduler run and executor read agent_model/expected_outcome/frequency from this file — never from the work
85	  item — so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
86	  or writes past its declared ceiling. The same contract
87	  (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`) is re-validated at run time, so the
88	  static and runtime views can't drift. A task declares **no session scope** — see
89	  the next entry.
90	
91	- **A task's code reads only the environment code-work is handed.** Code-work runs as
92	  a subprocess with a fixed set of `CLAUDINITE_*` variables — `REPO_ROOT`, `REPO`,
93	  `DEFAULT_BRANCH`, `ITEM`, `PACK`, `TASK`, `CONTEXT`, `REQUEST_AGENT` — and
94	  `task-code-work-env` (blocking) rejects a read of anything else. A variable nobody
95	  sets is `undefined`, the parse of it yields empty, and the run goes green having
96	  quietly done something other than what it was asked: that is how three fleet
97	  tasks kept taking their parameters through a channel the queue had stopped
98	  setting, leaving a fleet-wide sweep unable to be scoped or dry-run. **Operator
99	  parameters ride the item's Context** (`CLAUDINITE_CONTEXT`, one line per bullet),
100	  which is the only channel a task may take them from.
101	
102	- **Session scope is retired, and `session_scope` is now inert** (owner ruling,
103	  2026-08-09; the field's last reader went with the slot scheduler). Reach is a
104	  property of **which endpoint the hand-off calls** — `invocation_endpoint`, below
105	  — so a task needing wider access names a different endpoint and nothing else in
106	  the system has a concept of scope. A declaration still carrying `session_scope`
107	  validates and does nothing at all; `task-declaration-shape` raises it as an
108	  advisory rename (advisory on purpose: a member's vendor refresh must not turn its
109	  CI red over a file nothing has edited yet). Drop it, and name an endpoint if the
110	  task actually needed the reach.
111	
112	- **Every run is bounded.** An agentic task (`agent_model !== none`) declares
113	  `agent_execution_timeout` — seconds bounding the agentic run
114	  (task-code-work design §2, §6 — see issue #394).
115	  There is no platform wall-clock kill for a launched agent session, so the
116	  bound is best-effort: the hand-off surfaces it into the session's brief ("fail
117	  after N minutes") and the agent leash catches a session that never converges its
118	  item. Set it generously — extreme protection against a runaway, not a scheduling
119	  knob.
120	
121	- **A task says which repo secrets it needs.** Code-work runs Action-side, so repo
122	  Actions secrets are reachable there and nowhere else in a task's life (an agent
123	  session carries none). A task lists what it needs in `required_secrets`; the
124	  wiring converge stamps each name into the workflows that run code-work — the scheduler run's
125	  drain and the executor — so a worker reads it as ordinary environment. A declared
126	  secret the repo has not configured is **named, not guessed at**: code-work is the
127	  only code that sees a secret's value, so the executor parks the item at
128	  `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-action` saying exactly which one is missing. Nothing else fails; the task
129	  that needs the secret just doesn't work yet. The consequence worth designing
130	  around: **a workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant** — fold its
131	  work into the task's code-work rather than dispatching and polling a second
132	  workflow from an agent.
133	
134	- **A standing tracker belongs to the task that keeps one, not to the machinery.**
135	  Nothing in the contract declares a tracker and no task is expected to want one. A
136	  task that keeps an aggregated record across runs resolves the issue in its **own**
137	  code-work and passes the number to its agentic phase the ordinary way — the hand-off
138	  payload's `delivered.issue`, which the executor renders into the work item as an `Issue:` line
139	  the worker doc points at. The exact-title lookup and the create-then-close pair are
140	  a library that code-work may call (`engine/scheduler/tracker.mjs`), never a phase:
141	  whether a run with nothing to say should mint a tracker at all is the task's own
142	  judgment, and tidy-repo's three answer no.
143	
144	`task-declaration-shape` and `task-md-only-when-agentic` are **relevance-first**:
145	both key off a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs` existing, so on a repo that carries no tasks
146	they are a no-op.
147	
148	## The task folder
149	
150	One directory per task — `<pack>/tasks/<name>/` — holding **`task.mjs`** (the
151	self-contained declaration + `precondition(signals, config, item)`, the eligibility
152	gate as pure code) beside its worker, plus any deterministic helpers. The
153	precondition both asserts need-to-run and pre-decides scope: its `context` lines
154	join the item's own Context as binding constraints the agent may not re-litigate.
155	
156	**The worker is code by default, and the agent is the escalation.** An
157	`agent_model: none` task's worker is a sibling `.mjs` the executor runs as
158	code-work: the item closes on that subprocess's outcome and no session is ever
159	started, which is how a repo runs a deterministic job in Actions without
160	authoring a workflow for it. An agentic task adds **`task.md`**, the spec its
161	session follows, and may still do its own code-work first — escalating the
162	remainder for **work code-work could not do**, never for a re-check of whether
163	the run should have happened.
164	
165	`task.md` is that spec and nothing else, so an agentless task must not carry one
166	(`task-md-only-when-agentic`, blocking): the file's presence is what the rest of
167	the corpus reads as "an agent runs here" — the routine contract judges the folder
168	by it, and every work item names it as the file its run is about. What an
169	agentless task's worker does is documented in a **`README.md`** beside it.
170	
171	**`task.md` describes only what this task must do — never how anything outside it
172	works.** A session opens the file already dispatched, already at its model, already
173	holding its item; restating that machinery teaches it nothing and is read as
174	instruction, so a later run generalizes the description into a rule and acts on it.
175	Keep out how the task is invoked (the executor, the hand-off, the queue's labels),
176	what model it was dispatched at, and what downstream consumes what it produces.
177	Where such a fact carries a constraint the run must obey, state the **constraint**
178	and drop the mechanism: not "you run from a work item the executor handed off whose
179	Context is binding scope", but "the Context section is binding scope"; not "never
180	merge — the executor enforces it in code", but "never merge". The declaration is
181	where the mechanics belong: `agent_model`, `schedule_after` and `expected_outcome` live in
182	`task.mjs`, and `task.md` never repeats them.
183	
184	This is the task-folder shape of the unattended-agents routine-folder convention; the
185	issue-driven-dispatch security rule (the issue is data, the task path is
186	code-validated, agent_model/expected_outcome come from the repo) lives with that
187	skill's agent practices.
188	
189	### Three optional declarations
190	
191	Declare one only when its rule applies.
192	
193	- **`schedule_after: ['<pack>/<task>']`** — this task yields while a named upstream's item is live
194	  *this cycle*, and picks up the moment it converges. Declare it when your task
195	  reads what another task produces; never as a general priority hint. It is not a
196	  `Blocked-by` edge and must not be described as one.
197	- **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`** (default `requeue`) — declare `needs-human`
198	  only for a genuinely one-shot side effect (a store submission, an external notification):
199	  it makes every recovery path that would re-execute the task converge to triage instead.
200	- **`invocation_endpoint: '<name>'`** — a key into the repo's `taskScheduler.endpoints`, for a
201	  task whose agentic phase needs reach the repo's ordinary sessions lack. **Never a URL**: a
202	  task declaration is vendored verbatim into every consuming repo, so deployment detail and
203	  anything adjacent to a credential stay in that repo's own config.
204	
205	One field is **not** yours to declare: `model_from_request`, which lets a task run
206	at the model its ITEM names rather than the one it declares. Exactly one task
207	declares it — the engine's own built-in request implementer, which no pack can be —
208	and every other task names its own `agent_model`.
209	
210	A task's `code_work_timeout` must stay under the executor's one-hour claim leash — a code-work
211	that can outlive it is reclaimed while still running, and the item livelocks. The declaration
212	contract enforces this; do not raise a timeout past it, split the work instead.
213	
214	## The precondition is the ONLY decision point
215	
216	Task execution is **two similar, consecutive phases**: deterministic **code-work**
217	(a subprocess the executor runs, Action-side) and **agentic work** (the session
218	the executor hands off to, following task.md). Neither phase is "preparation" for the
219	other, and — the rule that matters — **neither may decide whether the task
220	runs**. That decision is the precondition's alone:
221	
222	- **The precondition sees the occurrence, not just the repo.** Its third argument is
223	  this item's own facts, for a verdict about one target where the signals describe a
224	  window of activity — a fan-out item's precondition can tell which target it is
225	  about. Declare the argument only if you read it.
226	- **A precondition that cannot answer says so**, with `{ error: '…' }` rather than a
227	  decline: a decline is a decision about the world, and one taken on an API that
228	  would not answer is a guess. The item parks open in the failure lane and the
229	  ordinary re-queue lever retries it.
230	- A task that passes its precondition **runs**. The later phases must not find
231	  "new reasons to skip" — not timing, not repo state, not "already handled", not
232	  an open PR elsewhere. If a condition should stop the run, it belongs in the
233	  precondition, as code over signals, its verdict binding via the item's
234	  Context.
235	- **Failures may stop a run** — a crash, a timeout, an API error park the
236	  item at `needs-human`. Discretion may not.
237	- **A failing worker may say why it failed.** The executor sees an exit code and
238	  nothing more, so it cannot tell a token missing a scope (a person's five-second
239	  fix) from an exception in the worker's own code (a bug). A worker that knows
240	  prints one line on either stream before exiting non-zero, and the park is routed
241	  by it:
242	
243	  ```
244	  claudinite-needs-human: action — FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN lacks Actions: write
245	  ```
246	
247	  The kind is `action`, `decision`, `approval` or `failure`; the last marker in the
248	  output wins, so a worker sweeping many targets may revise its verdict as it goes.
249	  No marker — and every worker written before this existed — parks at `failure`,
250	  which is the lane that means "someone reads the trace".
251	- **"The work ran and produced nothing" is always legal** — that is an empty
252	  outcome, not a skip. The line: did the phase *do* the work and find it empty,
253	  or *decline* to do it?
254	- The conditional agent hand-off (a code-work worker requesting the agentic phase
255	  via `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`) escalates on **work code-work could not do** —
256	  never on a re-check of whether the run should have happened.
257	
258	The `task-phase-discipline` world check (advisory, heuristic) hunts for tasks
259	that escape this — skip-language in task.md, cycle-skip strings in code-work
260	workers.
261	
262	## Ordering between tasks is `schedule_after`, not a claim on the run
263	
264	A task that reads what another task produces declares **`schedule_after:
265	['<pack>/<task>']`**: its item yields while that upstream's item is live this
266	cycle, and picks up the moment the upstream converges. Nothing else
267	orders tasks — there is no run to claim, because there is no run: each item is
268	picked, decided and executed on its own, so a task that must go second says which
269	task it goes after and the queue holds it there.
270	
271	Declare it only for a real read-what-it-produces dependency, never as a general
272	priority hint, and never describe it as a `Blocked-by` edge — that is a different
273	field with different semantics. A yielded item is not spent: it waits, and runs in
274	the same cycle once the upstream is out of the way.
275	
276	## The queue labels are the item's state, and only the queue writes them
277	
278	A work item's **state is its labels**, and there is exactly one state label on it
279	at a time: `task:blocked` (waiting on a `Not-before` or a `Blocked-by`),
280	`task:ready` (available to pick), `task:executing` (an executor holds the claim),
281	`task:agent` (a session owns it). Beside them: `task:urgent` (pick before anything
282	non-urgent) and the terminal set — `task:done`, `task:obsolete`, `needs-human`.
283	(A closed item may still wear the retired `outcome:*` spellings of the first two,
284	or `outcome:delivered`, which nothing writes any more; every reader accepts them.)
285	
286	Whether an item is a task's **standing occurrence** or an **ad-hoc run** is not a
287	label but a property of the item: the standing one is titled with the task and
288	nothing else, and its task is on a calendar. A `manual` task's item and every
289	qualified one — a fan-out target, a request naming its issue — are ad-hoc, which
290	is what lets them run beside the schedule rather than consuming it.
291	
292	Two rules follow, and both are about not borrowing the vocabulary:
293	
294	- **Never put a queue label on an ordinary issue**, from a task or by hand. The
295	  scheduler run and the executor read them as state, and a label on an issue that is not a
296	  `[claudinite-work]` item is either ignored or misread — neither is what the
297	  person applying it meant.
298	- **A task that wants its own tracking issue owns that issue's whole lifecycle**,
299	  in its own vocabulary. `needs-human` is the one word shared with the queue, and
300	  a task reusing it is on the hook for clearing it: nothing sweeps an issue that
301	  is not a work item.
302	
303	Label writes are always **granular** — add and remove named labels, never write
304	the label set. A set-write replaces from a stale snapshot and clobbers a
305	concurrent transition, and with a scheduler run and several executors moving labels at
306	once that is a correctness rule rather than a style preference.
307	
308	## An item's identity is its issue number, and a hand-off carries a nonce
309	
310	There is no slot id and no occurrence id beside the issue: **`#<n>` is the
311	occurrence**. It is what a `claudinite-task-exec` record's bracketed field
312	carries, and the only thing tying that record back to the work it describes.
313	
314	A hand-off is an **API call**, not a label event — the executor invokes the
315	session directly and stamps a nonce on the item first. So a session proves it is
316	this item's session in code before acting: the task file exists at HEAD, its pack
317	is declared, the title names that task, the item carries `task:agent`, and the
318	newest hand-off comment carries the nonce it was given. A nonce mismatch means
319	the fire named a hand-off that is not the current one — the item belongs to
320	someone else, or to an earlier episode — and the session stops without labelling,
321	closing or running anything.
322	
323	## Item lifecycle — every exit is terminal, and nothing keeps updating
324	
325	- **Succeeded, nothing pending** → `task:done`, one comment, issue closed.
326	- **Parked for a human** → `needs-human` **plus one sub-label naming what is being
327	  asked for**, one comment, issue left open. Nothing keeps updating a parked issue:
328	  one visible convergence, then it is a person's to look at. Re-queueing it by hand
329	  (`create-work-item --wake #<n>`) is the sanctioned road back, and the
330	  precondition is re-evaluated at that pickup — which is what makes the retry safe
331	  even when the failed run half-did its work. The four:
332	  - `task:needs-human-approval` — succeeded, and deliberately left an unmerged PR
333	    for a person to merge or close. The only park that is not a fault.
334	  - `task:needs-human-action` — something outside the code must change before this
335	    can run: a secret set, a scope granted, a routine rewired, an input supplied.
336	  - `task:needs-human-decision` — the run stopped mid-flight and the next step is a
337	    choice: re-queue or abandon, does the half-done work stand, was the ceiling
338	    violation acceptable.
339	  - `task:needs-human-failure` — the run broke. A bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a
340	    malformed item. The default when nothing else fits.
341	
342	  **An open item is the task's standing item, and a `failure` park therefore stops
343	  the task being scheduled** — no further occurrence is filed until it is woken or
344	  closed. That is deliberate: a queue of items that will break the same way helps
345	  nobody, and the silence is the signal. The other three do **not** hold the lane —
346	  they are one person's inbox, not a fault in the task, so the schedule carries on
347	  around them.
348	- **Never ran** → `task:obsolete`, closed as not planned: the precondition
349	  declined, or the task is gone (file removed, pack undeclared). An obsolete item
350	  is not an anomaly and gets no `needs-human`. A scheduled task's next occurrence
351	  is the scheduler run's ask at its next anchor — and most declines never make an
352	  item at all: the scheduler run asks the precondition when the anchor comes,
353	  files an item only on a yes, and records a no as a row on the repo's schedule
354	  board (the one open `[claudinite-schedule]` issue).
355	- Every terminal state is recorded in code as a `claudinite-task-exec` line
356	  (`record-exec.mjs`), so the usage fold counts task statuses out of the captured
357	  conversation logs deterministically.
358	
359	## A dormant project runs nothing
360	
361	A project nobody is working on declares itself dormant in `.claudinite-settings.json`:
362	
363	```json
364	"dormant": true
365	```
366	
367	The scheduler run instantiates, readies and reclaims nothing, and the executor picks
368	nothing up; the fleet sweeps skip it; sessions are unaffected. Delete it to wake — a dormant spell is not replayed, so the repo
369	simply starts scheduling again from now.

5	
6	Adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite. Whole-repo bootstrap and the on-demand
7	refresh are [adopt-claudinite](../adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md); this is the narrower act of turning
8	one or more packs on. The declaration is authoritative — declaring is the project's call — so the
9	work is: declare, answer what the pack asks, materialize its content, satisfy what it now demands.
10	
11	## 1. Declare
12	
13	The full directory of adoptable packs — every canon pack with what it covers, how it activates,
14	and what it requires — is vendored in the mount at `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md`
15	(canon-side: `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`); read it when choosing, or when the owner asks what
16	could be added. **Match the owner's plain-words name to a pack id yourself** before asking them to
17	disambiguate — pack ids rarely read like how people describe them, so read the candidate's entry
18	there and confirm the fit.
19	
20	Add each chosen pack's id to `packs` in `.claudinite-settings.json`. A pack that only makes sense
21	alongside another names it in `requires`; `resolveDeclaredPacks` pulls that closure in when the
22	declaration is written, so you declare what you *chose* and its dependencies follow (e.g.
23	`spec-driven-product` pulls `executable-requirements`). An unknown pack name — or an unknown
24	property on an entry — is a blocking **settings** error, not a conformance finding; fix the name.
25	
26	## 2. Interview — the part that is easy to skip and must not be
27	
28	A pack that needs the project's intent before it can provide value declares `questions` on its
29	manifest (see [packs/README.md](../../../README.md) and the machinery in
30	[../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs](../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs)). For **every** newly
31	declared pack that asks questions:
32	
33	- Where a question says the repo may already hold the answer (a product brief, an existing
34	  requirements doc, the issue tracker), **read that first and confirm** rather than asking cold.
35	- Otherwise ask the owner directly (`AskUserQuestion`), one question at a time, at the point of
36	  adoption — when a human asked for the adoption, they are present by construction.
37	- Record each answer **verbatim** on that pack's entry as `answers: { "<question-id>": "<text>" }`.
38	  `"n/a — none wanted"` is a valid answer and stops the asking. Where the question carries a
39	  `distill` note, derive the entry's `config` from the answer (e.g. `executable-requirements`'s
40	  spec path → `config.spec`).
41	
42	### When nobody is there to ask
43	
44	Adoption also runs **unattended** — a scheduled task acting on a recommendation, the
45	fleet-add-missing-packs task's agent stage, any run with no human in the loop. The interview is then the hard stop, and
46	the order matters:
47	
48	1. **Never guess an answer, and never leave the question unrecorded.** A pack whose question is
49	   answered by inference carries a decision nobody made, in a file that then propagates by
50	   `requires` closure and outlives whoever could have corrected it. `"n/a"` is an *owner's* answer,
51	   not a default you may write on their behalf.
52	2. **Finish everything the question does not gate, first** — declare, re-vendor, refresh the badge
53	   row, scaffold, and get the checks green (§4, §5). Stopping at the question with a red repo hands
54	   the owner a broken tree *and* a question; stopping with a green one hands them only the question.
55	3. **Then stop, and hand off in the open.** Open the PR with what is settled, name each unanswered
56	   question in the PR body under a heading that says the adoption is incomplete, and say the same
57	   on whatever issue prompted the run. Do **not** merge, do not proceed to a next pack's interview,
58	   and do not re-run the adoption on a later firing hoping the answer appeared — an unanswered
59	   question is a human's, and re-asking it weekly is nagging.
60	
61	A pack that asks nothing adopts fully unattended; this section costs it nothing.
62	
63	## 3. Re-vendor
64	
65	The new packs' prose, checks, and skills must land under the tracked `.claudinite/shared/` mount,
66	**and the repo must be stamped with the version it is now at.** Fetch a fresh canon to scratch and
67	run its install runner against the checkout — sessions never fetch:
68	
69	```
70	node <canon>/updates/install.mjs --target . <pack-id> [<pack-id>…]
71	```
72	
73	**Do not hand-roll this with `apply-vendor-set.mjs`.** It lays the files down correctly and does one
74	thing that nothing notices for weeks: it stamps **every declared pack** at the newest version,
75	whether or not the records between were ever applied. `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, so once
76	the stamp reaches a record's own version that record stops applying — not for this cycle, but
77	permanently. Re-vendoring a repo to add one pack therefore silently burns every pending record for
78	the packs it *already* had, and the repo is left claiming a version whose shape it was never
79	migrated into.
80	
81	That is correct behaviour at version zero, where there is no older state to skip; it is wrong
82	everywhere else, and adding a pack to a live repo is everywhere else.
83	
84	The runner declares each pack, vendors its content, stamps it and every pack in its `requires`
85	closure at the newest version, runs any one-shot seed ops, and gates on the converged tree's own
86	self-test. It exits non-zero on a refusal or an unanswered interview — a pack already installed is
87	**refused**, because reinstalling would restamp the repo to the newest version while skipping every
88	record in between.
89	
90	Then **refresh the README pack-badge row**, from the mount you just rebuilt:
91	
92	```
93	node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges
94	```
95	
96	Declaring a pack is what makes that row wrong, and adoption is the only moment anything derives it —
97	the nightly deliberately leaves a repo's README alone, so a row not refreshed here stays stale until
98	someone notices by eye. The converge rewrites the row in place between its
99	`<!-- claudinite:packs -->` markers, keeping whatever the repo wrote after the closing one, and is a
100	no-op when the row is already right. A repo that has deleted its row keeps it deleted only if you
101	skip this — dropping the row is a real choice, so don't re-seed one the repo removed on purpose.
102	
103	## 4. Scaffold what the pack now demands
104	
105	A newly active pack may require structure the repo doesn't have yet — deliberately, so the
106	declaration is a statement of intent that its own findings then guide you to satisfy. Run the
107	world sweep and let each finding name the file: e.g. `product-wiki` wants its index and the
108	reviewed `product-requirements/` sink before the isolation wall has anything to guard. Scaffold
109	per the pack's own README template; the pack's rules are the checklist.
110	
111	## 4b. File what adoption cannot do
112	
113	A pack may declare `adoptionHandover` — steps only a human can perform (a repository or
114	console setting, a permission, a secret). The install runner prints them; they are not
115	optional and they are not PR-body notes. **Open one tracking issue per adopting repo**,
116	a checkbox per step, carrying each step's `breaks` (what is broken while it is off) and
117	`done` (its closing condition) verbatim. Per-repo manual work reliably does not happen,
118	so an unfiled step is a capability that dies silently in that member.
119	
120	Say on the adoption PR that the issue exists and link it. If the repo already has an
121	open issue for the same steps, comment there rather than opening a second.
122	
123	## 5. Land
124	
125	World and work checks green (`.claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`; the Stop hook
126	carries the work checks). Commit referencing the task's issue, push, open one PR. Content a pack
127	seeds through this flow — a `product-wiki` wiki's first researched, cited pages — rides the same
128	review gate as any other change; it is never pushed straight to the default branch.
129	
130	**A failing check is your work, not the reviewer's.** Declaring a pack is what switched those rules
131	on, so every finding they now produce belongs to this change — fix it here, in the repo, before the
132	PR opens. Two things that are *not* fixes: silencing a rule by adding it to `rules`/`accept` in
133	`.claudinite-settings.json`, and undeclaring the pack to make the findings stop. Both turn a real
134	signal off on the repo's first exposure to it. If a finding genuinely cannot be satisfied — the pack
135	demands structure this repo has decided against — that is evidence the pack is **not** the right fit:
136	drop it from the declaration, say why on the PR, and let the smaller adoption land.
137	
138	**Never leave the repo red.** Whatever stops you — a check you cannot satisfy, an unanswered
139	interview question, a scaffold that needs a decision — get the tree green first and open the PR on
140	what is settled. An incomplete adoption in a green repo is a handoff; an incomplete adoption in a
141	red one is a bug report against you.
142

1	---
2	name: create-release-plan
3	description: The Firebase release standard — two separate dev/prod projects with the committed default pinned to dev, prod config injected only by the release pipeline, App Check attestation gating, and deliberate promotion. Use when planning a Firebase-backed app's first release, splitting a project into dev and prod, or wiring prod config and App Check into a release pipeline.
4	---
5	
6	# Planning a Firebase release — environments, provenance, attestation
7	
8	The release standard for Firebase-backed apps. **Decided ahead of first exercise** (from TLDR's
9	worked AWS split + the design in ShoutsAndWhispers `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`); refine on the first
10	real release rather than treating this as settled canon.
11	
12	## 1. The committed default is dev, always
13	
14	- **Two fully separate Firebase projects** — dev and prod. Isolation is at the project boundary
15	  (data, auth, quotas, keys).
16	- **Everything committed points at dev**: `.firebaserc`'s `default` alias, the checked-in client
17	  `firebase_options`, every documented command. Strongest form: **no prod alias committed at
18	  all** until the release milestone — no command run from the repo can reach prod by accident.
19	- **Dev builds coexist with prod installs** (Android `applicationIdSuffix .dev` / iOS bundle-id
20	  suffix) so testing on a real phone never displaces the store app.
21	- **Guard tests pin the contract** once prod exists: the committed client config's projectId must
22	  be the dev project (TLDR pins the equivalent in `client/test/inject-config.test.mjs`), and seed
23	  scripts hard-refuse prod targets.
24	
25	## 2. Prod config is release-pipeline-injected
26	
27	- The store artifact gets its prod `firebase_options` (and any prod-only identifiers) from
28	  **release-workflow variables**, never from the tree. A plain/local/CI build physically lacks
29	  prod coordinates.
30	- **The release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset** — a dev-pointed or
31	  placeholder-configured artifact must be unbuildable, not merely unlikely.
32	- The same artifact that goes to the store is the release download — one prod build, one
33	  provenance trail.
34	
35	## 3. Attestation beats provenance
36	
37	- Provenance (only the pipeline holds prod config) is necessary but not sufficient — anyone can
38	  extract config from a shipped APK/IPA. Close the gap: **enforce App Check on the prod project**
39	  (Firestore, Functions, Storage) with Play Integrity (Android) / App Attest (iOS), so requests
40	  without a store-signed attestation are rejected server-side.
41	- **Dev keeps the App Check debug provider** so emulators, tests, and local builds stay
42	  friction-free; enforcement is a per-project switch, which is precisely why prod must be a
43	  separate project.
44	- Register the store apps in the Firebase console at first release; until enforcement is ON,
45	  treat prod as provenance-only and say so in the project's environments doc.
46	
47	## 4. Promotion is deliberate; dev deploys are automatic
48	
49	- Dev auto-deploys from `main` (it is the always-current sandbox); **prod deploys are a manual,
50	  explicit promotion** of something already verified in dev — a workflow dispatch or a named
51	  command, never a side effect.
52	- Per-environment deploy credentials: the prod deploy identity is distinct from dev's, so a
53	  compromised or misconfigured dev lane cannot touch prod.
54	- Data hygiene follows the project split: seed/backfill tooling targets dev by name and refuses
55	  the prod project id as a hard guard, not a convention.
56

1	---
2	name: static-site-releases
3	description: The release standard every static-site repo of ours ships — the date-anchored version scheme, release-on-push, the explicit publish set, .github/site.config, the vendored workflows, the Pages deploy, and the setup a new site repo needs. Use when setting up a site repo, changing or debugging its release pipeline or site.config, when asked to "bump version" on a site repo, or when a static-website check fires.
4	---
5	
6	# Releasing a static site
7	
8	Every static-site repo of ours ships the **same** pipeline: same workflows, same versioning, same
9	publish-set rules, same CI gate. This skill is that contract, the setup for a new site repo, and the
10	one-time GitHub settings the automation cannot turn on for itself.
11	
12	The workflow **logic** is authored once, in this pack's [`stubs/`](../../stubs/) — the
13	[orchestrator](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml), three `workflow_call`-only **reusable
14	workflows** ([publish](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-publish.yml),
15	[deploy](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml),
16	[bump](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-bump-version.yml)), the
17	[CI gate](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml), and three composite actions
18	([read-site-config](../../stubs/actions/read-site-config/action.yml),
19	[bump-site-version](../../stubs/actions/bump-site-version/action.yml),
20	[assemble-site](../../stubs/actions/assemble-site/action.yml)) — and **vendored into each site repo's own
21	`.github/`**, where the whole pipeline runs with no cross-repo dependency. GitHub resolves a
22	reusable workflow or a composite action only from a repo's own `.github/`, never from the shared
23	mount, so "the logic lives in the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each repo hosts a
24	*managed* copy: edit the pack, not the copy. Everything repo-specific is the keys of
25	`.github/site.config`, so every vendored file is copy-verbatim across repos.
26	
27	## The contract
28	
29	### Versioning — `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>`
30	
31	The site's version is **date-anchored**, and it is computed, never typed. The scheme, and the code
32	that computes it, live together in [bump.mjs](../../stubs/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs):
33	
34	| Part | What it is |
35	|---|---|
36	| `major` | the wrap counter. Raised by hand only as a deliberate "new generation of the site" statement — and automatically on the decade wrap (below). |
37	| `ymmdd` | the **last digit of the UTC year**, then `MM`, then `DD`. 2026-12-31 → `61231`; 2027-01-01 → `70101`. |
38	| `n` | the day's release counter: `1` for the day's first release, the previous release's `n + 1` for each further release the **same** day. |
39	
40	**Why the year digit.** The bare `MMDD` form is not monotonic across a year boundary: December
41	31st's `1.1231.3` sorts *above* the next day's `1.0101.1`, so "later" stopped meaning "bigger" —
42	which is the one thing every reader of a version assumes. Prefixing the year digit restores it:
43	`1.61231.3` → `1.70101.1`.
44	
45	**The decade wrap.** One year digit means 2029-12-31 (`91231`) is followed by 2030-01-01 (`00101`)
46	— the one legitimate decrease. The major absorbs it: `1.91231.4` → `2.00101.1`, and the ordering
47	holds forever. Any *other* decrease (a version dated in the future — a hand edit, a wrong clock) is
48	an error and fails the bump loudly; burning a major to paper over it would hide a real problem.
49	
50	**The bump belongs to the change, not to the pipeline.** A change that touches the publish set
51	raises the version in the same PR — `node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs $(the repo's
52	version_files)` writes every record together — and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds that line. The
53	release flow writes no version at all: it releases whatever it finds on `main`, and no-ops when that
54	version already has a release. So the number a reviewer sees on a PR is the number that ships, and a
55	published change that forgot its bump fails on the PR rather than silently never deploying. A change
56	that publishes nothing needs no bump and redeploys nothing.
57	
58	**The major is the one bump the pipeline still performs**, because it belongs to no single change:
59	dispatch **Release static site** with `bump: major` and it raises the major, pushes it, and releases
60	the result. That dispatch is what **"bump version"** means on a site repo.
61	
62	**Moving an existing site onto the scheme** is a one-line edit, once: rewrite the current version
63	in place with the year digit inserted (`1.1231.3` → `1.61231.3`). The result is strictly greater
64	than what it replaces (`61231 > 1231`), so no tag or release ordering is disturbed and no major
65	bump is needed. Every version after that is the next change's bump.
66	
67	The version lives in the files the repo names in `version_files` — the first is the source of
68	truth, the rest must agree. `sw/version-scheme` holds them to the scheme and to each other; the
69	bump validates every record before writing any, so a failure never leaves a half-bumped tree.
70	
71	### The published artifact — an explicit list
72	
73	The Pages artifact is assembled from `publish_paths` under `publish_root`, **and nothing else**.
74	The rejected alternative is subtractive — "serve the repo except `.claude/` and `.claudinite/`" —
75	and it fails in the direction that hurts: it publishes every file nobody thought to exclude, and it
76	publishes each *new* one silently, the day it lands. An additive list can only publish what the
77	repo asked for, and its failure mode (a file that doesn't appear) is visible on the site and caught
78	on the PR. Two guards make that concrete, in [assemble-site](../../stubs/actions/assemble-site/action.yml):
79	a publish path that doesn't exist fails the run, and so does an assembled site with no `index.html`
80	at its root. Both also run on every pull request, so a broken publish set never reaches `main`.
81	
82	### `.github/site.config` — five required keys, no defaults
83	
84	A dotenv file, **every required key explicit**. A default that "happens to match" a repo's
85	layout silently publishes the wrong tree the day the layout or the default changes:
86	
87	| Key | What it is |
88	|---|---|
89	| `publish_root` | the directory the site is rooted at; `.` = the repo root. It becomes the site's `/`. |
90	| `publish_paths` | the publish set: space-separated files/directories under `publish_root`. |
91	| `version_files` | space-separated version records; the first is the source of truth. |
92	| `build_command` | what produces the publish set; `""` = nothing to build, stated. |
93	| `test_command` | the repo's gate; `""` = no tests, stated. |
94	
95	A command that needs dependencies installs them itself (`npm ci && npm test`) — that's why there is
96	no "setup" key and no assumption that a lockfile exists.
97	
98	#### `build_vars` — the one optional key
99	
100	`build_command` otherwise runs with no access to any repo configuration at all, which leaves a site
101	needing a build-time value (an analytics token, a base URL, a feature flag) with nowhere to put it.
102	`build_vars` is the declaration that closes that gap: space-separated names of **repo variables**,
103	exported into the build's environment before `build_command` runs.
104	
105	```dotenv
106	build_command=node tools/build.mjs
107	build_vars=SITE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN SITE_BASE_URL
108	```
109	
110	Three properties are load-bearing, and each is the opposite of a nearby easier choice:
111	
112	- **Optional, unlike the five.** The explicitness rule exists to stop a default from publishing the
113	  *wrong tree*; an absent `build_vars` can't do that — it means the build sees no variables, exactly
114	  what every site did before the key existed. So an untouched config keeps its exact meaning and no
115	  existing repo has to be migrated to stay valid.
116	- **A declared-but-unset variable fails the run.** Exporting an empty string instead would give the
117	  original failure one level down: the build succeeds, the page ships, and the feature that needed
118	  the value is silently dead on the live site. Better a failed deploy naming the variable.
119	- **Variables, never secrets.** The exporter is handed `toJSON(vars)`, a context that structurally
120	  cannot carry a secret — so a value that must not appear in a published artifact cannot reach the
121	  step that produces one. That boundary is a property of what the workflow passes, not a convention
122	  to remember. A build that genuinely needs a secret is doing something a published static site
123	  should not be doing.
124	
125	Declaring `build_vars` also holds the repo to a vendored copy new enough to honour it: `sw/release-workflows`
126	fails if the config names variables while the vendored action or workflows predate the exporter, since
127	that combination reads the key, ignores it, and builds with the variables unset.
128	
129	```dotenv
130	# A hand-authored site with no build step.
131	publish_root=.
132	publish_paths=index.html about.html assets data
133	version_files=package.json
134	build_command=
135	test_command=npm ci && npm test
136	```
137	
138	`read-site-config` fails the run on a missing file, a missing or empty required key, or an unknown
139	(typo'd) key; `sw/site-config` fails the same cases in the repo's own checks, plus a publish path
140	that matches nothing tracked, a tooling directory in the publish set, and a site with no
141	`index.html`.
142	
143	### The workflows
144	
145	**One orchestrator per repo** — [`static-site-release.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml),
146	named exactly `Release static site`. It owns only the triggers (push to `main`, plus a
147	`workflow_dispatch` with `force`) and calls the local publish reusable, which runs:
148	
149	| Stage | What it does |
150	|---|---|
151	| `check` | is a release due? The version on `main` has no release of its own yet — or `force`. Asking the **release list** for the current version (rather than diffing files against a tag) is what makes the flow idempotent: a failed run retries on the next push with nothing to undo, and a push carrying an already-released version is a clean no-op. |
152	| `verify` | the repo's `test_command`, on the tree being released — **before** anything is tagged or deployed. |
153	| `release` | GitHub Release `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` at that tree, auto-generated notes. |
154	| `deploy` | the Pages deploy of that exact commit, from the explicit publish set. |
155	| `report-failure` | any failure above opens a fresh `workflow-failure` issue and closes earlier open ones for this workflow as duplicates, so the newest failure is the single open bug to triage. |
156	
157	The `bump: major` dispatch pushes with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which fires no workflow — which is why the
158	orchestrator runs the release explicitly after it rather than relying on the push trigger, and why
159	the push cannot loop.
160	
161	A push carrying a version that is already released is a clean no-op: no tag, no redeploy.
162	
163	**CI** — [`static-site-ci.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml) runs on every pull request with
164	**no `paths:` filter**: the Claudinite world sweep, the repo's `test_command`, the build, and a dry
165	run of the artifact assembly. The missing path filter is deliberate — a path-filtered conformance
166	flow arms auto-merge and then never runs, so the repo's own maintenance PR waits forever.
167	
168	## Setting up a new site repo
169	
170	1. **Declare** `static-website` in `.claudinite-settings.json` and answer the pack's two adoption
171	   questions (where it's served; what's published). Re-vendor so the pack's tree lands under the
172	   shared mount.
173	2. **Vendor the pipeline** into the repo's own `.github/`: everything under
174	   [`stubs/workflows/`](../../stubs/workflows/) and [`stubs/actions/`](../../stubs/actions/). There are no
175	   tokens to replace. A repo whose site deploys somewhere **other** than Pages takes the CI stub
176	   and the versioning half only, and skips the orchestrator + the three reusables — every rule in
177	   this pack is gated on the orchestrator, so nothing here fires on it.
178	3. **Write `.github/site.config`** with all five required keys, from the adoption answers (plus
179	   `build_vars` if the build needs repo variables).
180	4. **Put the version on the scheme** — one hand edit in each `version_files` record (`1.1231.3` →
181	   `1.61231.3` for an existing site; `1.<today's ymmdd>.1` for a new one).
182	5. **Open the one-time settings issue** (below) — idempotent: search the tracker first and skip if
183	   one already exists, open or closed.
184	6. Run the world sweep; `sw/release-workflows`, `sw/site-config` and `sw/version-scheme` are the
185	   checklist for whether the wiring is complete. `sw/version-bumped` is work-scope and shows up on
186	   the first PR that touches the publish set.
187	
188	## The settings only a human can turn on
189	
190	Repository settings are not repo content: no workflow, check or agent can set them, and a pipeline
191	that silently depends on one is a pipeline that fails on its first run for a reason nobody wrote
192	down. So they are tracked as **state, in one issue in the adopting repo** — done once, then closed
193	— not as a standing file:
194	
195	```markdown
196	### One-time GitHub settings for the static-site release pipeline
197	
198	The release pipeline is vendored and green in CI, but the following are repository *settings* —
199	nothing in the repo can set them, so they are turned on by hand (Settings → …). Until they are,
200	the first release-on-push run fails and opens a `workflow-failure` issue.
201	
202	- [ ] **Pages → Build and deployment → Source = "GitHub Actions"** (not "Deploy from a branch").
203	      Without it `actions/deploy-pages` fails and nothing is served.
204	- [ ] **Actions → General → Workflow permissions = "Read and write permissions"**, so the pipeline
205	      can create the release and push a `bump: major` dispatch. (Not needed if the repo is already
206	      on read/write.)
207	- [ ] **Environments → `github-pages` → deployment branches** must allow `main` — the default
208	      "protected branches only" rule already does; check it if the repo renamed its default branch.
209	- [ ] Optional: **Pages → Custom domain**, if this site has one. Note that a custom domain moves
210	      the site from `/<repo>/` to the domain root — see the relative-URL rule in the pack's
211	      [RULES.md](../../RULES.md).
212	
213	Close this issue once the first release-on-push run has deployed successfully.
214	```
215	
216	## Routine work
217	
218	- **Ship a change**: raise the version in the same PR (it touched the publish set, so
219	  `sw/version-bumped` requires it) and merge to `main`. The site redeploys under that
220	  `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` on its own — that is the whole release procedure.
221	- **Redeploy without a content change** (a settings fix, a first deploy): run **Release static
222	  site** from its dispatch page with `force: true`. It redeploys the existing tag rather than
223	  cutting a second one.
224	- **"bump version"** on a site repo means the **major** — the deliberate "new generation" statement.
225	  Run **Release static site** with `bump: major`; it writes every `version_files` record together,
226	  pushes, and releases.
227	- **A failed release** leaves a `workflow-failure` issue with the run link. Nothing before the tag
228	  changes anything at all, and the version is already on `main` either way — so the next push (or a
229	  `force` dispatch) releases from there with nothing to unwind.

1	# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy
2	
3	The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own queue runs the
4	pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
5	the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
6	([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
7	[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
8	[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).
9	
10	The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**
11	
12	- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
13	  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
14	  ref's auto-generated name.
15	- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
16	  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
17	  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
18	  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive. A verdict
19	  identical to the one already posted on that issue is **not** an action — say nothing, or the
20	  comment becomes tomorrow's trigger.
21	- **Trackers — record changes, never scans.** A run reaches its tracker only with something to record:
22	  an action actually taken (issues), or a picture that differs from what the body already says (PRs,
23	  branches). A run that acted on nothing, or re-derived the same verdicts, leaves the tracker untouched
24	  and creates none.
25	
26	Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
27	**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
28	rewritten to today's state, a dated comment beside it). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
29	three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

1	# web-scraping — taking data from a site you don't own
2	
3	The facet: a project whose input is another organisation's website, reached without a
4	contract. There is no support channel, no changelog and no SLA, so every rule below is about
5	**reducing what you have to re-learn** — from the site, from the network, and from your own
6	pipeline — when it changes underneath you.
7	
8	A default to adapt, not a contract. Language-agnostic: "fetch", "parse" and "normalize" mean
9	whatever they mean on your stack.
10	
11	## Finding the data surface
12	
13	- **Adding a source, or deciding what to parse** — scraping rendered markup is the **last**
14	  resort. Prefer, in order: the hydration blob a server-rendered app embeds in the page, then
15	  the JSON/GraphQL endpoint a single-page app fetches its rows from, and only then the markup
16	  — where you prefer the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD, `og:` tags) over element
17	  positions, because metadata survives a redesign and `.results > div:nth-child(2)` does not.
18	  Finding that surface on a new site is a one-off reconnaissance job with its own procedure,
19	  the [`map-a-data-source`](skills/map-a-data-source/SKILL.md) skill.
20	
21	- **A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record** — rendered output is **not
22	  deterministic**, so treat the shift the way you'd treat a markup change: re-review it, don't
23	  assume a regression.
24	
25	- **Learning something non-obvious by probing the service** — write it down in a reference doc
26	  beside the scripts: endpoints, auth, the field surface, the enum values. Keep it complete
27	  enough that **nothing needs to re-probe the live service to answer a question**. The
28	  expensive part of this work is the knowledge rather than the code, and re-probing is slow,
29	  rate-limited, sometimes blocked, and occasionally the thing that gets you banned.
30	
31	## Fetching
32	
33	- **Writing the fetch itself** — browser-like headers, a randomized delay between requests, and
34	  exponential backoff on retry. Route **all** outbound page/API fetching through a single
35	  module, so swapping the vendor, the proxy or the credential is one edit with one place to
36	  test.
37	
38	- **Deciding whether to retry a failed request** — retry only what can improve. A gateway or
39	  proxy failure (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) is worth another attempt; any other 4xx is about
40	  your request and will answer the same way forever.
41	
42	- **Porting a fetch to a language-level HTTP client** — carry the retry policy across the
43	  rewrite. `curl --retry` covers exactly that status set and the port silently drops all of it,
44	  so the first transient 500 the old command would have ridden out kills the run.
45	
46	- **Setting the retry budget** — attempts times per-attempt timeout, plus the waits, must fit
47	  inside whatever hard limit kills the process, and the backoff should be injectable so tests
48	  exercise the retry path without sleeping through it.
49	
50	- **One item in a batch failing to fetch** — record and continue. Log the reason per item and
51	  emit a report; one unfetchable item should not abandon the batch.
52	
53	- **A sandbox refusing the target host** — an agent sandbox is commonly **bot-blocked**, and its
54	  egress proxy may refuse the host outright. That refusal is policy: **do not route around it**,
55	  not with a local fetch and not with an ad-hoc workflow spun up to reach the host. Give the
56	  fetch one sanctioned home — a scheduled job or workflow on a runner, with the credential in
57	  repository secrets — and let sessions read the committed raw records instead.
58	
59	- **A fetch that works on your machine and fails from CI** — a 403/400 or a CAPTCHA wall from a
60	  runner or a sandbox is usually the *datacenter IP* being blocked, not the headers, so tuning
61	  them is wasted work. **Reaching a commercial rendering proxy** is the standard answer: a
62	  residential lane clears the IP block, and these services usually execute JavaScript too, so a
63	  single-page app records real content. Ask it to render, and give it a wait-for-selector when
64	  the content you want arrives late. A target that stays blocked even through the proxy is
65	  un-cacheable: say so and stop, rather than hunting for another route.
66	
67	- **Needing many items from a service with no list endpoint** — no bulk endpoint is not the same
68	  as no bulk request. GraphQL lets one document alias the same field many times, and many REST
69	  APIs accept a multi-id parameter. The cap is usually undocumented, so **halve a rejected batch
70	  and retry** — that keeps batch size a throughput knob and never an accuracy one.
71	
72	- **A fetch that cannot produce a page at all** — a bot wall, a dead URL, an empty render is a
73	  dead end, not a pipeline failure: mark the item for a human and **exit successfully**. Failing
74	  the run converges on the same human signal while also implying the pipeline broke, when in
75	  fact it correctly declined. The rest of the batch should still land.
76	
77	## Reading what came back
78	
79	- **Deciding whether a fetch succeeded** — a 200 is not success. An anti-bot interstitial arrives
80	  as a normal-looking 200 (or a 403/503) whose body is a challenge page, and caching it stores
81	  garbage that looks like data. Match the known markers in the first few KB and report it as a
82	  distinct failure reason.
83	
84	- **Getting an empty body back** — nothing rendered. Treat it as a failure of that fetch rather
85	  than as an empty result, and don't retry it: a successful-but-empty response will keep being
86	  successful and empty.
87	
88	- **Choosing which field to read** — prefer the authoritative status enum over the summarizing
89	  convenience boolean, which is routinely wrong: an item can report "not sold out" while its
90	  status says there is nothing left to sell. Take the enum's legal values from the service's own
91	  options endpoint rather than from what you happened to see.
92	
93	- **Filtering rows by a status** — deny-list the bad statuses, don't allow-list the good ones,
94	  and log the set actually observed. A new status then defaults to usable and shows up in your
95	  logs, instead of silently dropping rows.
96	
97	- **Reading a numeric field** — numbers may arrive as strings. Parse; don't assume the JSON type.
98	
99	- **Reducing a set to its "cheapest" or "first"** — that value can be a special case rather than
100	  a value. Filter to what the field means before you reduce over it: a zero-priced accessibility
101	  companion band makes the cheapest ticket for every show free.
102	
103	## Normalizing what you read
104	
105	- **Converting an instant to the domain's local time** — instants usually arrive in UTC while
106	  your domain thinks in local wall-clock. Do the conversion in one function at the ingestion
107	  boundary and have everything downstream speak local time. Slicing digits out of the string
108	  files everything an hour off during daylight saving, and **the result looks completely
109	  plausible** — nothing throws, nothing is empty, the data is simply wrong. Because the failure
110	  is silent, keep a **known-answer probe**: an item whose correct value you know independently
111	  (something named after its own time, a figure published elsewhere), checked after every fresh
112	  pull. "Exactly once" cuts both ways — a stage downstream of the boundary that parses,
113	  re-offsets or re-reads a stored value as UTC is the same bug from the other end.
114	
115	- **Taking a "now"** — read it in the domain's zone rather than off the device clock. A reviewer
116	  in the same zone as the developer cannot see the difference, which is how a device clock
117	  survives review.
118	
119	- **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** — read it by what the page declares, centrally;
120	  never per-source, never guessed. A numeric slash date whose parts are both ≤ 12 (`05/07/2026`)
121	  has no intrinsic answer, so resolve it from a *positive* signal the document gives you (an
122	  explicit region in `<html lang>` or `og:locale`, a non-English language) and keep the default
123	  when the signal is absent or region-less, rather than inferring one from the host or the
124	  venue. Put that resolution in one helper the whole pipeline threads, so a new source cannot
125	  invent its own reading. A trailing `Z` or `+00:00` is *serialization*, not a claim about the
126	  subject's zone: it neither supplies the zone nor vetoes deriving one from what the page says
127	  about the place.
128	
129	- **Changing the conversion** — it is a **full-snapshot change**. Committed derived data is
130	  generator output, so the fix isn't done until the raw record is re-run through the new
131	  conversion and every downstream artifact regenerated. Expect the boundary to move records
132	  between partitions — items at the end of a day land in the next one, and may fall outside the
133	  range your day-partitioned files cover — and check that rather than reading it as data loss.
134	
135	- **Emitting a value your pipeline hasn't reached yet** — missing is its own state: *unknown*,
136	  never folded into *free*, *empty* or *false*. Sources keep adding rows after your last full
137	  pass, so gaps are normal and permanent. Carry unknown through the whole stack — omit the key
138	  rather than emitting a default — and let each consumer render it as its own thing.
139	
140	## What lands on disk, and when it refreshes
141	
142	- **Deciding what a fetch writes to disk** — two forms, separated deliberately. The fetched
143	  artifact (page HTML, raw response pages) is a **cache**: git-ignore it, since it is large,
144	  regenerable, and not what you reason about. The extracted raw record — the site's own object,
145	  before any of your normalization — is **committed**, and is the durable source of truth. That
146	  split buys three things at once: re-deriving your normalized output becomes an **offline**
147	  operation, so a parser change costs no requests; the committed record doubles as the fixture
148	  for a self-test of the transform that needs no network; and a field you didn't parse this
149	  month is still there next month, because you kept the whole object rather than the subset you
150	  needed at the time.
151	
152	- **Re-running a fetch that already ran** — **fetch only what's missing**, with an explicit flag
153	  to force a refresh, so repeat runs are a no-op. Note what "resumable" is measured against: the
154	  file on disk. On a CI runner that file is durable only once the job's commit step pushes it,
155	  so a resumable script still loses everything if the runner itself dies. Chunk the work if that
156	  matters.
157	
158	- **Scheduling the refresh** — give each field its own pass on the clock it actually moves on.
159	  The single biggest cost saving in a scraper is noticing that some fields are fixed once
160	  published, some gain rows daily and some move hourly: re-fetching everything on the fastest
161	  clock re-learns a static field nightly, thousands of requests for the same answer, and it is
162	  the part of your traffic most likely to get you blocked.
163	
164	- **Generating the artifacts downstream of the stored data** — make them a **pure function of
165	  the stored master**: refresh writes to the master, and everything else regenerates from it.
166	  Files whose inputs didn't change come back byte-identical and never enter the commit, so the
167	  diff of a scheduled run is exactly what actually moved.
168

Now I have enough to report.

## Findings

Most rules across these packs are either stubs (android, app-store-release — no prose yet), already mechanized (aws-sam's esbuild/CloudFront rules, chrome-extension's release/version/CORS/permission rules, claude-code-web-users-support's store rules, basics's suppression/task-lifecycle/catalog/generated-file rules, barriers which is check-only by design), or genuine judgment/runtime calls (deploy-role IAM scope, cache-vs-auth tradeoffs, token-storage discipline, CDP probing, most of writing-tests and file-placement). Only a few gaps stood out.

**1. packs/aws-sam/RULES.md — CORS `AllowOrigins` must never carry a non-http(s) origin**
> "API Gateway HTTP API (v2) rejects a `chrome-extension://` origin in CORS `AllowOrigins`... An API fronted by a browser-extension (or other non-`http`) origin must therefore set `AllowOrigins: ['*']` and rely on its JWT authorizer, not CORS, as the security boundary."
Working rule: it's a deploy-config gotcha about how a template must be written, not a product decision. Statically testable: same shape as the already-mechanized `aws-sam/cloudfront-authorization` check — scan `template.yaml`'s `AWS::Serverless::HttpApi`/`AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Api` `Cors.AllowOrigins` (or equivalent) for a listed value with a non-`http(s)`/non-`*` scheme (`chrome-extension://`, `moz-extension://`, etc.). Fixture: a template with `AllowOrigins: ['chrome-extension://abc...']` (violating) vs `['*']` (clean). Confidence: high — this is a real, deploy-time-rejected config shape, same pattern as an existing check.

**2. packs/chrome-extension/RULES.md — service worker importing must declare `"type": "module"`**
> "Declare the service worker `"type": "module"` and load page/side-panel scripts with `<script type="module">`; relative imports resolve within the packaged extension. Content scripts are the exception."
Working rule: a manifest/code-consistency convention, not a product feature. Statically testable, and it's the exact mirror of the already-shipped `content-script-module-syntax` check: resolve `manifest.json`'s `background.service_worker` file, check whether it contains a top-level `import`/`export` (parsed the same stripped-comments/strings way the existing check does), and require `background.type === "module"` when it does. Fixture: a service-worker file with a top-level `import` and manifest lacking `background.type: "module"` (violating) vs one with it set (clean). Confidence: high — same engineering pattern already proven safe in this pack's other checks.

**3. packs/chrome-extension/RULES.md — `web_accessible_resources` must cover a content script's whole transitive import graph**
> "Adding an import to a content-script module — list that module and its whole transitive import graph under `web_accessible_resources` ... Keeping that `web_accessible_resources` list correct — have a test walk the import graph from the entry module, so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list."
Working rule: an internal consistency/packaging discipline, not a product feature. Statically testable in principle: parse the dynamic-`import()` entry module(s) named by the classic-loader pattern, walk static imports transitively, and diff against `manifest.json`'s `web_accessible_resources.resources` globs. Confidence: medium — mechanically sound (mirrors the existing content-script-module-syntax parsing approach) but resolving arbitrary import specifiers against WAR glob patterns correctly, with no false positives on legitimate glob coverage, is more involved than the other two; worth a "see it fail" fixture pass before committing to it.

Everything else in these packs is either already covered by a declared check/worldRule, a stub with no prose, or fails gate 1 or 2 (judgment calls like naming, review discipline, CDP session mechanics; runtime-only effects like account verification, CloudFront cache-hit ordering, rollback-state cleanup; or product decisions like which store fields exist).

1	# Web Speech APIs
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for browser voice I/O — speech-to-text
4	(`webkitSpeechRecognition` / the Web Speech `SpeechRecognition` API) and
5	text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`) — true for any app that reads
6	or listens through the browser, read cold. These are runtime browser-behaviour
7	gotchas, knowledge you carry into the code rather than state a tool can read off
8	the repo.
9	
10	> Some of these APIs (`chrome.tts`) are extension-only; where a rule touches
11	> MV3 service-worker / content-script mechanics, only the speech-API facet is
12	> here — the general extension gotcha underneath is not.
13	
14	## Speech-to-text (`webkitSpeechRecognition` / Web Speech API)
15	
16	- **The recognizer owns its own microphone capture — you cannot hand it
17	  `getUserMedia` audio constraints.** `echoCancellation` / `noiseSuppression` /
18	  `autoGainControl` are `getUserMedia` *microphone* constraints, and the recognizer
19	  exposes no hook to set them on its internal stream (Chrome applies its default
20	  echo cancellation there regardless). To *warm* the device with a known processing
21	  state — and to read back whether echo cancellation actually engaged — run a
22	  separate preflight `getUserMedia({ audio: {…} })` capture and stop its tracks.
23	  (`suppressLocalAudioPlayback` /
24	  `restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia` *screen-capture* constraints and have no
25	  bearing on a mic — don't reach for them here.)
26	- **Read the whole n-best list, not just alternative `[0]`.** Set
27	  `maxAlternatives` > 1 and iterate `result[0..length]` for `{ transcript,
28	  confidence }`; the ranked alternatives are exactly where homophone / near-miss
29	  recovery lives.
30	- **`onresult`, `onend`, and `onerror` all fire — settle the cycle exactly once.**
31	  Guard a `settled` flag: interim results arrive before the final one, a cycle can
32	  end with no result at all (treat `onend`-without-result as `no-speech`), and an
33	  error and an end can both arrive.
34	- **With `interimResults` off, engines omit `isFinal` — treat a result as final
35	  unless `isFinal === false`.** Don't test `if (result.isFinal)` (it's `undefined`
36	  on those engines and you'll drop every result); test `result.isFinal !== false`.
37	- **The classic recognizer streams audio to a cloud service (Google's) — plan for
38	  it.** A `network` error means "offline / service unreachable", and audio leaves
39	  the machine. On-device recognition is opt-in and capability-gated: probe
40	  `SpeechRecognition.available({ langs, processLocally: true }) === 'available'`
41	  once and cache it, set `recognizer.processLocally = true`, and **never trigger a
42	  language-pack download** (only `'available'` counts, not `'downloadable'`). When
43	  the local path is absent, fall back to ordinary cloud recognition unchanged.
44	- **Contextual biasing (`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` + `recognizer.phrases`) works
45	  only on the on-device path** — gate it behind that same availability probe and
46	  apply it best-effort (any failure falls back to un-biased recognition rather than
47	  breaking the listen cycle). Only bias **closed vocabularies you control**
48	  (a command lexicon, known labels, a spelling alphabet) with **modest** boosts:
49	  over-boosting makes the recognizer hear a biased phrase when the user actually
50	  said a same-sounding free-form utterance.
51	- **Map the raw Web Speech error names to a small taxonomy** — `not-allowed` /
52	  `service-not-allowed` → permission-denied, plus `no-speech`, `network`,
53	  `aborted`, `audio-capture`, else `other`. In particular `aborted` is the
54	  *self-inflicted* stop (you called `recognizer.abort()`), so the caller should
55	  ignore it rather than surface it as a failure.
56	- **A missed endpoint mid-utterance needs a pause watchdog, not just `onend`.**
57	  If interim hypotheses exist but no final arrives, the engine may have lost the
58	  endpoint; a timer that fires after a pause discards the half-heard input and
59	  reopens a fresh cycle (preventing "heart heart" doubles when the user repeats
60	  themselves). Set the threshold **well above a natural mid-command thinking
61	  pause** — a tight window (~1.2 s) cuts real commands; a wider one (~1.8 s) keeps
62	  only the genuine missed-endpoint case.
63	- **Mic permission is per-origin, and the grant belongs to whatever page the
64	  recognizer runs in.** In a content script the prompt reads as the *host site*
65	  asking and the grant persists for that origin. Surface it in a controlled moment:
66	  preflight `navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'microphone' })`, then a one-time
67	  `getUserMedia` to raise the prompt. **Retry the capture bare** (`{ audio: true }`)
68	  if the first constrained call is rejected — a browser balking at the constraint
69	  *shape* must not be misread as a permission denial; only a second failure is a
70	  real "denied".
71	
72	## Text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`)
73	
74	- **Prefer `chrome.tts` over `speechSynthesis` — it's immune to page
75	  autoplay / user-activation gating.** `speechSynthesis` invoked from a content
76	  script is subject to the host page's autoplay policy and can silently refuse to
77	  speak; `chrome.tts` (extension-only, needs the `"tts"` permission, usable from the
78	  service worker) is not. Make `chrome.tts` primary and `speechSynthesis` the
79	  fallback for non-extension document contexts.
80	- **`chrome.tts` doesn't exist in a content script — relay speak/cancel to the
81	  service worker over a port.** Keep the same `speak()`/`cancel()` contract on both
82	  sides; the in-page port sends `{ speak }` / `{ cancel }` messages and the worker
83	  drives `chrome.tts`. On port disconnect, resolve every pending `speak()` promise
84	  so a dead worker never leaves the caller awaiting an utterance that will never
85	  finish.
86	- **Voice lists load lazily — an empty `getVoices()` means "not ready yet", not
87	  "no voices".** Resolve the preferred voice on the *first* `speak()` and don't
88	  cache an empty result: fall back to the default that turn and try to resolve
89	  again next turn.
90	- **Don't trust the OS/browser default voice — it's often the most robotic one
91	  installed.** Keep an ordered list of preferred voice names, take the first one
92	  actually installed, and fall back to the default only when none match.
93	- **Resolve a `speak()` promise on *any* terminal event, and never reject.** For
94	  `chrome.tts` that's `end` / `interrupted` / `cancelled` / `error`; for
95	  `speechSynthesis` it's `onend` / `onerror`. Resolving (not rejecting) on error
96	  keeps a spoken-prompt sequence from deadlocking on one bad utterance. Use
97	  `enqueue: false` so a new line interrupts the current one for turn-taking rather
98	  than stacking up.
99	- **Neither engine reliably supports SSML — you can't force intonation.** If a
100	  punctuation cue matters (a question's rising tone), speak the cue in words
101	  ("question mark") rather than relying on prosody the engine may not apply.
102
