1	# Evaluating and routing a new item
2	
3	The shared method for three decisions every proposed addition to this corpus must pass through: **is it worthy** of inclusion at all, **which mechanism** should carry it, and — only for prose — **where does it go**. Any routine or person that adds an item — the [growth promote stage](tasks/growth-promote/task.md), an owner-requested retrospective pass, a hand edit — applies this same protocol, so the decision-making lives here once instead of being re-derived per caller.
4	
5	This is a Claudinite-internal doc used by the growth lifecycle (see [the canon-curation README](README.md)): it is **not** part of the mounted corpus and consuming repos do not `@import` it.
6	
7	An "item" is one **distilled, portable rule** — not a transcript, not a narration of what happened. A candidate still phrased as "here's what we did" has not been distilled yet and is below the bar on form alone, before any of the tests below. This doc picks up once a distilled rule exists and decides its fate.
8	
9	## Worthiness — does it earn a place at all
10	
11	The corpus is read read-only by every consuming repo, so a **duplicative** item (already covered) or an **undistilled** one (a story or a truism, not a rule) pollutes shared canon and costs every future reader. The bar guards against *those* — it is **not** a bar on *scope*: an item useful to only one project today can still earn a place (see Portable). Admit an item only when **all** hold:
12	
13	- **Distilled.** It is a single tight rule in the imperative, not a story, a log, or a restatement of a generic truism.
14	- **Portable — would a *future* project benefit?** Not "useful to every project today." An item can help only **one** project right now and still belong here, so long as another project — **especially one with a similar tech stack or process** — would benefit when it arrives. Being specific to a technology or a process is **not** disqualifying: generalize it and route it to that technology's or practice's home. What disqualifies is leaning on *this* project's non-transferable particulars — a product requirement, or a one-off incident in how it happened to call some API. The test, a genuinely hard one: *if another project with a similar tech stack came along, would it benefit from this?* Yes → portable; only-ever-this-product → local. A rule mined from Claudinite's own test suite is the hardest case: it reads as generic testing craft even when it actually depends on Claudinite's own shape — the only project whose tests build git-repo fixtures because its checks take a repo as input. Before promoting one, grep the fleet's own callers of the pattern the rule is about; zero callers outside this project's own conformance tests means the lesson is local however general its wording (#857: a fixture-signing rule read as portable, was promoted to `writing-tests`, then reverted once every caller of the fixture helper turned out to be a Claudinite conformance test).
15	- **Durable and reusable.** It will still apply on a future, unseen task — not a one-off, not a situational detail, not something already implied by an existing rule.
16	- **Readable through the channel it lands in.** A rule whose premise is that the delivery channel
17	  itself failed cannot be carried by that channel. Promote #497 admitted "the tell that the SessionStart
18	  hook did not fire" as pack prose — and pack prose is what that hook delivers, so in the one situation
19	  the rule describes it is not in context to be read. Detecting a channel's own failure belongs in code,
20	  not in the payload the channel carries; reject such an item here rather than rewording it.
21	- **Not already covered.** The insight does not already exist **anywhere** in the corpus, even worded differently or owned by a different file. This is checked against the *entire* corpus, not just the file it would land in — see [Dedupe against the whole corpus](#dedupe-against-the-whole-corpus).
22	
23	Reject on any miss — but the misses that matter are *undistilled*, *already-covered*, or *genuinely one-off*, not merely *narrow*. When you're torn over a real, non-duplicate rule, lean toward **keeping** it — the goal is a broad library. When you're torn over whether something is a duplicate, or a rule at all, leave it out. The failure to avoid is padding the canon with restatements of what's already there; admitting a narrow-but-reusable rule is not that failure.
24	
25	### Dedupe against the whole corpus
26	
27	Before admitting anything, read across the corpus, not only the file you expect to own the item. The same insight is frequently already present under a different heading or in an adjacent group. If it sharpens an **existing** rule, fold it in with a minimal edit rather than adding a second bullet that says nearly the same thing — and never weaken or restate what is already there in the process.
28	
29	**Sweep last, and case-insensitively.** A dedupe pass is only evidence about the text it actually read, so it runs **after** every re-home, merge and edit the change makes — a sweep run early and never re-run reports clean on content that has since moved under it. Measured on #740 (the seven-PR promote consolidation): the sweep ran *before* two lessons were re-homed out of a folded-away skill file into `packs/basics/RULES.md`, and **three** copies of the same unknown-state rule reached the owner, who found them by reading. The re-run then surfaced a further pair the pattern had missed because it was case-sensitive and the survivors were capitalised. So: sweep as the last step, match case-insensitively, and state the similarity threshold you swept at so the "no remaining near-duplicates" claim is checkable.
30	
31	## Mechanism triage — prose is the fallback, not the default
32	
33	A worthy item next descends the **promotion ladder** ([../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) owns it): platform setting (always paired with its verifying check) → PreToolUse hook → conformance check → skill → prose. The *first* rung that can carry the item wins — a rule about repo state becomes a check whose failure message *is* the lesson; a bad action to prevent becomes a guard; a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger becomes (or joins) a skill. Only an item none of those can carry — judgment, in-flight behavior, signature-less knowledge — proceeds to the file routing below, and its landing **names that reason** in the promote log so conversion rates stay auditable.
34	
35	**"No universal signature" alone never routes an item to prose.** A rule converts to a check when a *narrow, file-scoped* signature covers the **grounded cases** — the concrete shapes the rule was distilled from — even though no signature covers every conceivable violation. Gate it relevance-first so it stays inert off-target, and document the genuinely signature-less residue in the rule's own comments as out of scope. The prose rung is only for an item whose grounded cases *themselves* have no reliable signature (pure judgment, runtime/in-flight behavior).
36	
37	## Routing — picking the right file (rung-5 items only)
38	
39	Routing is robust when it keys on **stable file groups**, not on the current roster of individual files (which grows over time). The corpus is organized into a few groups, each with its own selection rule:
40	
41	1. **The practice group** — durable, project-agnostic practices, each file a self-contained, reusable unit of know-how the agent applies whenever its subject comes up (engineering, agentic, git/GitHub, testing, investigation, discipline, architecture), partitioned **by kind of practice** with each file owning one recurring subject cluster. This group spans **two folders that differ only by *when* the rule loads**: `always/` for a rule that applies to essentially every task (the index `@`-imports it, so it's force-loaded every session), and `tasks/` for a subject-gated rule read on demand when its trigger fires. Route in two steps: first match the item's *kind* to the file whose cluster already owns that subject; then keep it in `always/` only if it genuinely isn't tied to one kind of task (the rare case — `always/` stays small), otherwise it belongs in `tasks/`. Read the group's own index (the root `CLAUDE.md`) to find the current owner for a kind — never from memory, since the set of clusters can grow.
42	2. **The per-user group** — interaction preferences and trigger phrases. This group does **not live in this repo**: an item of this kind routes out to the person it belongs to, never into the practice group and never back into the canon.
43	3. **The per-technology group** — practices specific to one technology, **one file per technology**. Route a technology-specific item to that technology's file. When **no pack homes that technology** (not even a stub), the item doesn't land in a loose doc — it **mints a fingerprinted stub pack** (a `packs/<tech>/`, delivered in its own PR), so the next project on that stack self-declares it; [promote](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)'s stub-minting floor and [the generate-project-instructions skill](../../../../packs/claudinite-growth/skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) own the mechanics.
44	
45	Pick **exactly one** owner. If an item plausibly fits two files, choose the single best one — never split one item across files, and never duplicate it into both. The group decides the *axis* (kind, person, or technology); the file within the group is then the one whose existing scope the item falls squarely inside.
46	
47	### When nothing fits
48	
49	An item that matches **no** existing file is **not** a reject signal by itself — a genuinely new category of lesson is meant to be learnable, so a worthy item that no file owns earns its own file. Resolve it in this order:
50	
51	- **Route into an existing owner** when one genuinely fits — the first choice. If the item belongs to a file's cluster and merely sits slightly off-center, a small stretch toward that owner beats spinning up a new file. A new file is for when no existing file's scope genuinely fits, **not** a way to dodge folding into an existing owner.
52	- **Open a new file** when the item clears the [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) bar in full — distilled, portable, durable and reusable, and not already covered anywhere in the corpus — **and** no existing file's scope genuinely fits it. That is the whole bar: nothing more is required. Do **not** also demand that you expect the cluster to recur, that forcing the item into the closest file would *distort* it, or default to rejecting when the new-file call is a close one — those extra hurdles are dropped. Creating a file obliges registering it where the corpus is indexed and in any routing table, in the **same** change, so it never lands orphaned (see [Keep the write surface bounded](#keep-the-write-surface-bounded)).
53	
54	The loosening above is **only** to the new-cluster hurdle, never to the per-item bar. An item that misses [Worthiness](#worthiness--does-it-earn-a-place-at-all) — a one-off, non-portable or project-specific, a restatement of a generic truism, or already covered anywhere in the corpus — is rejected whether or not a file already exists for it; for the per-item admission decision, the default-to-reject-when-unsure tiebreak still stands.
55	
56	## Keep the write surface bounded
57	
58	Once worthiness and routing are settled, the edit touches **only** the single owning file: add or sharpen one terse rule in that file's existing voice and format, and change nothing else. Do not "improve" unrelated rules while you are in there. The sole exception is the new-file path above, whose surface is itself bounded to the new file plus its index and routing-table registration.
59

175	- **Naming a new canon pack** — kebab-case, named for the surface it serves rather than the
176	  first feature you are building for it. A pack whose subject is a **Claudinite feature itself**,
177	  rather than a technology or a way of working, carries the `claudinite-` prefix
178	  (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-dashboard`) — owner, 2026-08-18.
179	  The directory name is the pack's public id, spelled in
180	  every member's declaration, so another casing costs a fleet-wide rename. `claudinite-growth`
181	  is grandfathered. (convertible → prose-to-checks)
182	
183	- **Starting a new Claudinite-facing capability** (a tool, a dashboard, anything meant to reach
184	  more than the current repo) — decide **which distribution model it is** before writing the
185	  first file: a member-local tool, always-on engine code, or an opt-in pack with its own
186	  adoption/scaffolding. Nothing prompts this choice on its own, and getting it wrong costs a full
187	  move-and-rewrite cycle per correction — one session paid it three times in a row before landing
188	  on "opt-in pack" (#934).

193	  whether its procedure applies.

196	  current `main` before merging: a whole-tree aggregate is judged post-merge, so a branch's own green
197	  never covers it. Never transcribe a corpus-wide total into a doc — `packs/README.md` states how to
198	  count checks and rules instead of quoting a number, so every pack change no longer edits it.
199	  (portable → `merge-to-main`)
200	
201	- **Writing a check's `fix` text** — name only remedies that match the enforced severity;
202	  sessions follow the words, not the `severity` field. An advisory finding's remedies are act on
203	  it or leave it, never a config-acceptance escape.
204	
205	- **Declaring a check, or adding a key to the vocabulary** — name the key so the declaration
206	  reads alone to someone who hasn't read the design doc (`scanFiles`, `matchLines`,
207	  `relevantWhen`): if it needs a comment to be read, it needs a better name. Declarations live in
208	  `packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json`, which cannot hold one, and borrow nothing from prose — no
209	  `description`, no `doc`; the line the agent reads is `failureMessage`.
210	
211	- **Writing a check that reads the session transcript** — screen the harness's own **plain-text**
212	  pseudo-turns, not only the tag-wrapped ones. `humanText` in
213	  `engine/checks/helpers/session-transcript.mjs` drops a user entry that starts with `<`, which
214	  lets a bracketed marker straight through: `comment-classification` blocked a session on
215	  `[Request interrupted by user for tool use]` as "the owner's latest comment". A conversation rule
216	  fires at the Stop hook, where a false positive spends a whole cycle on something no edit can
217	  clear — so its fixture carries an interruption marker beside a real owner turn.
218	
219	- **A doc reached only by following a link out of `RULES.md` or a check's `doc:`/`More:` line** —
220	  if it is a how-to wanted at authoring time rather than prose every session should carry, convert
221	  it into a skill (frontmatter + description) invocable by description, not a doc chained through
222	  links nobody follows cold (#975).
223	
224	- **A check declaration's `doc:` field** — nothing ever opens it; it only renders into a finding's
225	  `More:` line when the check actually fires. A stale pointer left by a file move can sit broken
226	  indefinitely with nothing to catch it — grep for and re-verify every `doc:` field by hand
227	  whenever you move or rename the file it points at (#975).
228	
229	- **A check built to catch a thing being missing or misnamed** — don't gate the check's own
230	  relevance on the single signal it exists to validate. Gating solely on "does the orchestrating
231	  file still have the expected name" makes the exact failure the check exists to catch (a rename)
232	  also the thing that silences the check — the run that should say "rename it back" never fires.
233	  Use two independent signals, either sufficient, so at least one survives when the other is the
234	  thing that broke (#1060).
235	
236	- **Deciding whether an enforced check still earns its keep** — measure its actual blocking-firing
237	  rate against what it buys, not vibes. A check whose firings are dominated by cases where the
238	  agent had already done the right thing, and the check only wants the exact tokens for it, is a
239	  demotion candidate (check → prose-only), justified by the firing-frequency data itself:
240	  `comment-classification` fired 204 times in 31 days, 21% of all blocking findings, each one a
241	  blocked Stop-hook turn spent re-emitting a line the session had already been told to emit
242	  (#1118).
243	
244	- **A documented multi-step procedure the agent re-derives interactively every time it runs** —
245	  that pattern, not the doc's polish, is the signal to mechanize it into a script the agent runs
246	  once. A nine-part prose bootstrap doc cost ~90 exploratory tool calls and ~11 minutes per
247	  adoption for work that runs in seconds once scripted. Part of that cost was sequencing, not
248	  exploration: the tracking issue was created only after the first commit had already failed the
249	  issue-reference check, costing a full amend/force-push/CI cycle — create the artifact a check
250	  will demand *before* the action it gates, not after (#1132).

257	  root, so a mount-shaped path works fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — where it
258	  surfaces last.
259	
260	- **Adding a module under `packs/`** — keep it import-light, and start work after evaluation
261	  completes (`check(…).catch(…)`), never in a top-level `await`. Discovery imports every
262	  `pack.mjs` and `checks.mjs` before activation is consulted, so a module that is also a CLI entry
263	  point is re-imported mid-evaluation and Node exits 13 having run nothing.
264	  `pack-discovery-entry-await` enforces the await half only.
265	
266	- **Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy** — first ask what carries it
267	  across the fleet. Vendoring refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only and a migration record moves
268	  paths, not schemas — so if the answer is "nothing", accept the legacy shape in
269	  `normalizeManifest` until a carrier exists. Never let a stale declaration degrade to *fewer
270	  checks running* rather than a failure.
271	
272	- **Renaming a pack whose config a member writes into their own repo** — the rename map fixes
273	  code-side id resolution, but it cannot rewrite a member's own already-committed config, which
274	  converges on its own separate schedule or never. A reader consuming that config keeps resolving
275	  both the new key and every legacy spelling explicitly and permanently: rewriting the write side
276	  to the new name (the fix for the fleet's own persisted data) only helps where the engine itself
277	  owns the write, not data a member wrote into their own repo (#1081).
278	
279	- **Checking whether an actor may trigger a privileged automated action off a GitHub issue/PR
280	  payload** — read the actor's permission from the collaborators-permission API
281	  (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/collaborators/{u}/permission`), never the payload's `author_association`:
282	  `MEMBER` covers any org member regardless of repo permission, and `COLLABORATOR` includes
283	  read-only collaborators — both broader than push access (#1067).
284	
285	- **Extending what a copied stub reads** — make the new config key optional, fail the run when
286	  it is declared-but-unset, and let declaring it trigger a staleness check (`build_vars` /
287	  `release-workflows` is the shape). Stubs are copied into a member's `.github/` once and never
288	  re-copied, so a new key is silently dead in every repo holding the old copy.
289	
290	- **Writing a migration record that needs engine behaviour newer than itself** — have
291	  `appliesTo` probe the member's own mount for that capability, by content rather than version,
292	  and stay inert until it reads back; an unreadable mount must read as "not capable". The record
293	  comes from a fresh canon clone but the worker executing it is the member's vendored one, so
294	  otherwise the converge fails, the mount never advances, and the fix can never arrive.
295	
296	- **Changing an export in `updates/*`** — empty it, never remove it. Fielded workers are stale
297	  callers of instantly-current flow modules, so a removal wedges every member permanently on its
298	  next run. Keep it callable, say at its definition that this is why, and pin the surface with a
299	  test carrying an expiry — the canary rehearsal cannot catch this class, since it drives the
300	  worker this ref ships. Retire it by reading the field: the condition is that no member's
301	  *vendored* worker calls it.
302	
303	- **Renaming or deleting an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports** — leave a shim at the old
304	  path re-exporting what it named, for the same reason and by the same rule as `updates/*` above:
305	  the engine lane and the pack lane deliver in separate PRs on separate cycles, and pack delivery is
306	  version-gated per pack, so every member spends a window holding the NEW engine beside an OLD pack.
307	  The failure is worse than a broken task — a pack that fails to load fails the mount's self-test,
308	  the converge then refuses to land AT ALL, and the member cannot receive the pack version that
309	  would have fixed it (#1004: a green run, an unmoved stamp, and a `needs-human` PR). Ask which
310	  symbols are fielded by walking the TRUNK's pack history, never `--all` — an import that only ever
311	  existed on an unmerged branch is not fielded, and scanning every ref fires on whatever is in
312	  flight.
313	
314	- **Changing a vendored stub** — edit the canon's own `.github/workflows/` copy in the same
315	  commit and diff the two whole files. The canon has no converge, so its copy drifts invisibly
316	  until it is a permission denial in production.
317	
318	- **Excluding files from the vendor set by pattern** — whitelist any operational file that
319	  matches by path, and pin it with a test against the real canon tree, not only a fixture. The
320	  nightly refresh re-runs the computation from canon HEAD, so a bug there is the one canon
321	  regression that is not self-healing. Assert that the **whole containing directory** vendors,
322	  not just the one file that broke — a test re-asserting only the known-missing file needs a
323	  fresh edit for the next file added there; one that walks the real directory doesn't (#907).
324	
325	- **Retiring or reshaping a protocol the engine exposes** (a dispatch input, a stub's declared
326	  interface) — sweep for callers **outside this repo**, not just what greps locally. `FORCE_TASKS`'s
327	  replacement broke Shepherd's only caller because the migration enumerated this repo's own
328	  callers and missed the cross-repo one (#929); two independently-maintained stub copies at the
329	  same path declaring different input names is the same failure from the other side (#801, #907)
330	  — the two spellings *are* the protocol, and they live in different trees.
331	
332	- **Branching on the result of an API write in fleet machinery** — read its status, not just
333	  the body: a body-only destructure turns a 403 into a plausible object and the run still logs
334	  `ok`. Judge the fleet by members' stamps, never by run conclusions — the stamp is the only
335	  artifact that moves when delivery actually worked.
336	
337	- **A single timeout bound covering two different waits** ("has this even started" vs. "is
338	  something already running about to finish") reintroduces the bug a prior fix closed, on
339	  whichever side crosses the shorter phase's real need. Split the bound to match what each phase
340	  is actually waiting on, sized from that work's own declared budget rather than a round number —
341	  and once a bound is hit, the give-up message must never read as a verdict on the work: "no
342	  successful run yet" is a statement about the clock, not about the runs, and collapsing the two
343	  sent a reader chasing a wrong repository-settings diagnosis for CI that was simply still running
344	  (#1027).
345	
346	- **Writing generated content into a size-capped GitHub API field** (an issue or PR body) —
347	  budget it explicitly, in two tiers: an always-complete compact summary plus best-effort detail
348	  rationed to a byte budget with an explicit omitted-count, never a single unbounded write that
349	  can 422 outright at the ~64KB cap. `growth-dedup`'s brief rendered 350KB against that limit and
350	  would have failed the run at its first step.
351	
352	- **Writing a generated title whose naive content scales with a variable-length list** (a PR
353	  title, a notification headline) — collapse the list to a count and keep the per-item detail in
354	  the body. A title is a summary surface, not a second body, and grows unreadable exactly where a
355	  long list makes every character compete for space (#1048).
356	
357	- **Preflighting a required grant or permission** — a probe is only as good as the environment it
358	  runs against; where the failure is conditional (a scope that 403s only under a specific
359	  condition, e.g. a private repo), a probe run where that condition isn't met reports a
360	  false-positive pass. Prefer attributing a real observed 403 to the permission that would fix it
361	  over guessing from an unrepresentative probe (#1052).
362	
363	- **Introducing a finer-grained classification of an existing catch-all state** — default
364	  whatever an older or unaware writer produces (or a future writer's not-yet-known category) to
365	  the most conservative member of the new set, not the most lenient. An unlabelled park now reads
366	  as the blocking `failure` lane rather than a soft one, so a writer that predates the split fails
367	  safe instead of silently landing in a lane nobody watches (#1051).
368	
369	- **Adding a fleet task** — fail loudly on a Context target it cannot reach rather than
370	  proceeding on a partial list, and treat a member as un-adopted until the routine's repo scope
371	  names it. The target list is enumerated over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` while the grant is hand-typed
372	  UI config no Action can read; the drift *completes*, filing a report that reads as a full sweep.
373	
374	- **Spawning a child process from a worker** — pass an explicit `cwd`, resolved to a root that
375	  cannot vanish (`--root`, then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then `cwd`). The converge deletes the tree
376	  its own code-work runs inside, so children die at `process.cwd()` before doing anything. Keep
377	  "could not run" distinguishable from "had nothing to run": a crash sharing a benign outcome code
378	  is unobservable.
379	
380	- **Diagnosing a member's maintenance PR that won't land** — `unstable` beside a green sweep
381	  is a parked `action_required` run, not a missing repo setting. Read the member's raw
382	  `.claudinite-settings.json` and the head sha's `pull_request` runs; propose a platform-settings
383	  change only as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.
384	
385	- **Judging whether a member is fresh** — read its `ref` (or `engineVersion` /
386	  `packVersions`), never `claudinite.updated` alone: a held stamp pins `updated` behind a pending
387	  note, so a mount converging hourly can look a week stale.
388	
389	- **Reading a uniform signal across every fleet member right after a shared mechanism changes**
390	  — a rate-limited, unauthenticated `api.github.com` probe can return a clean-looking uniform
391	  negative across every target, and a uniform stamp/ref shared by the whole fleet can mean "not
392	  yet past its nightly anchor" rather than "frozen." Check for a rate-limit signal explicitly
393	  before trusting a uniform empty sweep, and check timing — has each member's own convergence
394	  window actually passed — before generalizing one member's confirmed fault to the fleet. Never
395	  reuse a signal already known unreliable to corroborate a different theory (#801, #939: a "the
396	  entire fleet is frozen" claim stood uncorrected for ~10 hours).
397	
398	- **Retiring or migrating a dispatch/config parameter channel** — a parameter that stops being
399	  read must fail loudly, never silently default. A dropped safety knob (e.g. `DRY_RUN`) defaults
400	  to the operation's *most dangerous* mode — live, unscoped — not a safe one; audit that a
401	  parameter's producer and consumer still agree after every interface migration (#974,
402	  owner-authored).
403	
404	- **Relying on a push to trigger further Actions workflows** — a push authored with the default
405	  `GITHUB_TOKEN` (which every converge and auto-merge in this repo's own machinery uses) fires no
406	  `on: push` workflow; only a push carrying a real user or app credential cascades. A dashboard
407	  stuck showing a stale "hasn't converged" banner traced back to exactly this: the deploy
408	  workflow's trigger never fired for the pushes that actually moved a mount (#1094). The same
409	  platform fact is why `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push into — it lands
410	  only through a PR a human merges — so a renamed or removed entry point that a workflow file
411	  references by literal path needs a shim held open until every consumer's own copy has moved, by
412	  the same rule as an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports (#1108).
413	
414	- **A script written for one execution context silently breaking in another** — audit every
415	  script's environment assumptions (a real `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `gh`/`curl` reachability) whenever the
416	  execution context of its caller changes, not just at the one call site that surfaced the break.
417	  A script written when the queue ran as an Actions job (a real token, shell GitHub access) 401'd
418	  once the same work started running inside an agent session (MCP-only, a proxy-scoped token, no
419	  `gh`) — and per the owner, every other script built against the old assumption fails identically
420	  in the new context, not just the one that broke first (#1133).
421	
422	- **Finding a check that watches only one of two structurally-identical surfaces** — widen it to
423	  the sibling in the same change rather than filing it separately. A check exercising the
424	  scheduler's own vendored stub had never been extended to the executor's stub, which is just as
425	  much a fleet-wide vendored surface and just as capable of drifting unnoticed (#1138).
426	
427	- **Picking a compact date-encoded identifier** (a version stamp, a compact timestamp) — check
428	  the encoding's own rollover boundary years ahead, not just today's decode correctness: anchoring
429	  a year on its last digit wraps to 0 in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath every 2029
430	  one, so the anchor point matters (`year - 2020`, not `year % 10`). And keep the identifier
431	  string-typed everywhere it travels — `'60820.10'` and `'60820.1'` are different versions and the
432	  same float, so nothing in the corpus may parse one as a number (#1105).
433	
434	- **Designing text that instructs a model to echo an exact string** (a session-start directive, a
435	  generated title) — don't reference the payload anaphorically from later text ("that line," "the
436	  above"); state the instruction first, have it disclaim itself as instruction-not-payload, and
437	  put the literal string once, last, introduced by the instruction's own colon. Recency is what an
438	  LLM actually resolves ambiguous reference against: putting the directive *after* the payload
439	  line made "that line" read as the directive sentence itself, and a session opened two replies in
440	  a row reciting the instruction verbatim instead of the summary (#1126).
441	
442	- **A work-scope check that verifies "this PR bumped X" by diffing against `main`** — on a PR
443	  stacked on another still-open one, that diff already carries the lower PR's own bump, so the
444	  check reads it as *this* PR's and passes green even though this PR's own edits still need one.
445	  The false green survives only until the lower PR merges and this one rebases onto the real
446	  base. Re-verify (and re-bump if needed) after every earlier PR in the stack actually lands —
447	  never trust a stacked PR's check result against its pre-merge base (`pack-version-bumped`,
448	  #1119).

Good, that confirms `scope: 'work'` checks exist and have access to changed-file data (as used by `adoption-answers-pending` via `work.jsonPair`), so a "no PR may touch `.claudinite/shared/`" check is architecturally consistent with existing patterns.

## Findings

**1. `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md`** — *"Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite… Never edit anything there [`.claudinite/shared/`]: change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`."*
Working rule (governs how a vendored tree is treated, not a product fact) and statically testable: a work-scope check can flag any changed file path under `.claudinite/shared/` in a PR diff. Existing `claudinite-isolation` check only forbids *referencing* the vendored tree from consumer code — it does not catch a PR that directly edits vendored files. `conformance-work-scope` proves the work-scope machinery (`scope: 'work'`, changed-file list) already exists and is used this way (see `adoption-answers-pending`). Confidence: high — clean fixture (a PR touching `.claudinite/shared/foo.mjs` vs. one that doesn't) with essentially no false positives.

**2. `packs/flutter/RULES.md`** — *"Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins… A plugin type leaking into a screen… is a defect."* Named plugin examples: `geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`.
Working rule (architecture discipline, not a product fact) and statically testable: forbid `import 'package:geolocator...'`, `import 'package:firebase_...'`, `import 'package:google_sign_in...'` etc. inside `lib/ui/**` and `lib/screens/**`. flutter has zero worldRules/declared-checks today. Confidence: medium-high — clean violating vs. clean fixture, main risk is enumerating "plugin packages" without hardcoding an incomplete list (could scope to any `package:` import outside a small allowlist, which needs care to avoid false positives on legitimate value-type packages).

**3. `packs/firebase/RULES.md`** — *"Keep compiled output (`functions/lib/`) and `.firebase/` gitignored."*
Working rule (repo hygiene convention) and statically testable: check that no tracked file matches `functions/lib/**` or `.firebase/**` (or that `.gitignore` covers them). Not covered by existing `functions-node-pin`/`functions-predeploy-build` checks. Confidence: high — clean fixture, low false-positive risk (path patterns are exact).

**4. `packs/firebase/RULES.md`** — *"End every ruleset with an explicit catch-all deny and grant per collection; a collection nobody thought about must be unreachable."*
Working/security-discipline rule, statically testable: scan `firestore.rules`/`storage.rules` (resolvable via the pack's existing `projectConfigs` helper) for a catch-all `match /{document=**}` (or `/{allPaths=**}`) block containing `allow ...: if false`. Confidence: medium — the invariant is clear, but ruleset syntax variety (split `allow read:`/`allow write:` lines, nested matches) raises some false-negative/positive risk; would need a real fixture pass to be confident.

**Considered and rejected as not clean enough:** flutter's `pubspec.lock`-without-`pubspec.yaml` rule (the prose itself says a lockfile-only change can be legitimate — "unless you deliberately ran an upgrade" — so a static diff check can't distinguish intended from accidental without judgment); git-github's `linguist-vendored` fixture rule (no principled, false-positive-free size/path threshold); most of `git-github-advanced` and `writing-tasks` (session-time/runtime behavior, or already mechanized by existing `gha/*`, `task-declaration-shape`, `task-phase-discipline` checks); `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/RULES.md` and most of `claudinite-lifecycle/RULES.md` (judgment calls about interpreting sweep reports, not static repo shape).

1	---
2	name: single-pr-status
3	description: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
4	---
5	
6	# Single-PR status
7	
8	Assess **one** open pull request and return a verdict. **Assess-only — never close, merge, or comment
9	on it.** Read status from its **commits + diff**, never the PR title.
10	
11	`main` = the repo's default branch. Take the **first** that applies:
12	
13	1. Merged ⇒ **merged** (done).
14	2. `git diff --stat origin/main..<head>` empty ⇒ **stale** (already landed).
15	3. Its intent is present in `main` under another form ⇒ **superseded**.
16	4. `git merge-base` with `main` fails ⇒ **orphaned** — a human must look.
17	5. Else ⇒ **open** (genuine work that should stay).
18	
19	Return `{ status, note }` — `status` one of merged/stale/superseded/orphaned/open. For `open`, the
20	note says why it's live (`#N — why`); for merged/stale/superseded, recommend closing (never close it).
21	In a git-proxy-only sandbox, read over the API/MCP, never a clone.
22

1	---
2	name: map-a-data-source
3	description: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
4	---
5	
6	# Map a data source before you parse it
7	
8	This runs **once per source** (and again when a site is redesigned). Its output is
9	not code — it is a committed reference doc plus one saved raw payload. Everything
10	after it is ordinary parsing. The standing rules for the pipeline that follows live
11	in [the `web-scraping` pack's RULES.md](../../RULES.md).
12	
13	## 1. Fetch one page and look at what came back
14	
15	Save the raw response of a single representative page to disk and read it. You are
16	answering one question: **is the data in this document?**
17	
18	- If the interesting rows are present in the markup, you have a server-rendered page
19	  — go to step 2.
20	- If you got a small shell (a few KB of script tags and an empty root), the page is a
21	  single-page app and the data arrives separately — go to step 3.
22	
23	## 2. Look for a hydration blob first
24	
25	A server-rendered app framework almost always embeds the exact object it rendered
26	from in a script tag with a stable id. Search the saved document for a large inline
27	JSON payload and find the path to the record you want (it is usually nested a few
28	levels under a props/data wrapper).
29	
30	If one exists, **this is the surface**: it is the site's own typed record, one regex
31	and one JSON parse away, and it does not care about the layout. Save that object,
32	verbatim, as your first committed fixture.
33	
34	If there is no blob, the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD `<script
35	type="application/ld+json">`, `og:` meta tags) is the next-best target — it survives
36	redesigns that break element selectors.
37	
38	## 3. Find the client API
39	
40	Identify the request the page makes for its rows. Two ways in, and the second one
41	matters more than it sounds:
42	
43	- **Watch the page load** in browser devtools and read the request: URL, method,
44	  headers, auth, and the response shape.
45	- **Read the site's own JavaScript bundles.** Fetch the page, extract the script
46	  `src` paths (mind any asset prefix — the paths in the HTML already carry it),
47	  download them, and search for the operation names, query documents and field
48	  selections. For a GraphQL client the embedded query strings unescape into readable
49	  SDL, giving you the **complete** set of operations and fields the client was built
50	  against — the authoritative surface, short of introspection.
51	
52	  This path is worth knowing because it needs **only the public site host**. When the
53	  API host is blocked from where you are but the site itself loads, reading its
54	  bundle still tells you exactly what a request would look like. It cannot execute
55	  anything, so it is not a bypass of the block.
56	
57	Then note the auth story. A public listing is frequently reachable with anonymous
58	credentials the client itself ships — the same read access every visitor has. If
59	reaching the data requires a real account, stop and take that to the owner.
60	
61	## 4. Probe the shape, not just the happy path
62	
63	Before declaring the surface mapped, ask these of it explicitly, because each one has
64	silently corrupted a pipeline that assumed otherwise:
65	
66	- **Are timestamps UTC or local?** Take one item whose real-world time you can verify
67	  independently and check.
68	- **Which field is authoritative for state?** If there is both a status enum and a
69	  summarizing boolean, find an item where they disagree — there usually is one.
70	- **What are the enum's legal values?** Take them from the service's own options
71	  endpoint, not from the sample you happened to pull.
72	- **Are numbers numbers?** Amounts and counts frequently arrive as strings.
73	- **Is anything missing from this surface entirely?** A listing endpoint often
74	  carries flags but no amounts, with the real values behind a separate per-item
75	  query. Find that out now, not after you've shipped a catalogue of nulls.
76	- **Is there a bulk form?** If the per-item query has no list variant, check whether
77	  one *request* can still carry many items (GraphQL aliases, a multi-id parameter).
78	
79	## 5. Write it down, then stop
80	
81	Commit a reference doc beside the scripts holding: the endpoint(s) and auth, the
82	field surface, the enum values, each answer from step 4, and — explicitly — the
83	questions you could **not** answer and where they'd have to come from. State the
84	access constraint too: which hosts are reachable from where, and which sanctioned job
85	is allowed to do the fetching.
86	
87	The bar: **a later session should be able to write the parser from this doc without
88	touching the live service.** If it can't, the reconnaissance isn't finished.

---
name: jwt-minting
description: Issuing or signing JWTs — choosing the algorithm, generating keys, deciding the claims. Use when adding or changing code that creates tokens.
---

# JWT minting

- **Algorithm by trust shape.** HS256 only when signer and verifier are the *same party* — anyone who can verify an HMAC token can also mint one. One-to-many (APIs, federated identity) → RS256/ES256 (ES256: same strength, smaller keys and signatures).
- **Keys.** From a CSPRNG, never a password: an HMAC secret must be ≥ 256 random bits (32+ chars — RFC 7518 requires at least the hash-output length, and short/guessable secrets are practically brute-forceable). Asymmetric pairs:
  - RSA: `openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -out private.pem -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048`
  - EC P-256: `openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out ec_private.pem`

  Load key material from the environment or a secret store — never source. Use a **different key per subsystem/token type**; one shared key is what makes cross-service substitution possible.
- **Claims.** Always set `sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp` — and make `iss`/`aud` specific (the subsystem's URL, not the company name) so exact-match validation has something to bite on. Keep `exp` short; long-lived access rides a refresh token, not a long expiry. Use `typ` to separate application token types.
- **Payload is readable by anyone** — Base64 is encoding, not encryption. No secrets or private data in a signed-only token; use JWE when third parties must not read it, and in multi-party flows **sign first, then encrypt** the signed token.
- **Client-side sessions are still client data.** Size the token (every request carries it), store it `HttpOnly` when cookied, and pair with CSRF mitigations — a stolen token *is* the session.

6	import { normalizeEdges, barrierFindings, staleFindings } from './reference-scanning.mjs';
7	
8	// The declarative pattern-check engine: a rule whose whole logic is "these
9	// patterns over these files" is DECLARED as data — and data is JSON, not code.
10	// A pack's declarations live in `packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json` (a skill's
11	// in `<pack>/skills/<name>/declared-checks.json`), an array of specs the pack
12	// registry discovers structurally and compiles here into ordinary
13	// `{ id, severity, why, run(ctx) }` rule objects the runner treats like any
14	// other. Nothing wires them: dropping a declaration into the file adds it.
15	//
16	// The format admits no comments — the pattern plus its failureMessage/what/fix
17	// text IS the check — and no prose pointers: a declaration states its own case
18	// or it isn't finished. So a spec carries exactly:
19	//   id              the rule id settings and findings name it by
20	//   severity        'blocking' | 'advisory'
21	//   failureMessage  why this matters, printed on every finding the rule makes
22	//   …the assertions below, each with the `what` and `fix` it fails with
23	//
24	// REGEXES ARE STRINGS in `/body/flags` form — "/^\\s*schedule:/m" — compiled at
25	// load. Keys that accept a path instead (scanFiles, excludeFiles, pathExists)
26	// read any other string as an exact repo path; at every other pattern key a
27	// string that is not in `/…/` form is an authoring error, reported as one.
28	// The engine owns only the walking (the mechanism/policy line line-scanning.mjs
29	// draws): every pattern, file filter, and failure text stays in the declaration.
30	// Spec keys are deliberately wordy — a declaration must read as the whole check
31	// without this header.
32	//
33	// Built for MANY such rules at once: however many pattern rules a run holds,
34	// the engine makes ONE pass over the scanned tree — each file is read once and
35	// its lines split once, with every subscribing rule's assertions evaluated in
36	// that single visit — and the per-context results are cached, so the first
37	// pattern rule the runner reaches pays for the whole family and the rest are
38	// lookups. Regexes must be non-global (`.test` on a /g regex is stateful).
39	//
40	// Every key at every level is validated against the vocabulary at load — an
41	// unknown key is an authoring error (a typo'd key would otherwise assert
42	// nothing, silently), reported with the container's valid keys.
43	//
44	// The spec vocabulary — everything beyond the rule metadata is optional:
45	//   fix                rule-level default: any assertion declaring `what` but
46	//                      no `fix` of its own inherits this one (for rules whose
47	//                      every assertion shares one remedy)
48	//   scope              "work" = this declaration judges the CHANGE rather than
49	//                      the repo, so it runs in check_the_work and may carry the
50	//                      work assertions below. Absent = world scope, the default
51	//                      (the pack manifest's own two rule lists say the same
52	//                      thing for a coded rule — a declaration has no list to
53	//                      sit in, so it states its scope here)
54	//   scanFiles          which files the content assertions read, in one of three
55	//                      forms: a RegExp over repo paths, one exact path (read
56	//                      directly), or an object naming the files ANOTHER parsed
57	//                      document points at —
58	//                        { inParsedFilesMatching, whereFileContains,
59	//                          namedByField, defaultingTo, withSuffix }
60	//                      every tracked document `inParsedFilesMatching` (refined
61	//                      by the `whereFileContains` probe) is parsed, the string
62	//                      at `namedByField` read from it — an array anywhere along
63	//                      that field path fans out over its entries, and
64	//                      `defaultingTo` supplies the name when the field's own
65	//                      parent is there without it — and each name, plus any
66	//                      `withSuffix`, resolved against the NAMING file's
67	//                      directory. A name pointing outside the scan set is
68	//                      dropped silently: a check has nothing to say about a
69	//                      file this checkout does not carry
70	//   scanFileClasses    named shared file sets widening the scan scope (unioned
71	//                      with a RegExp scanFiles): javascriptFiles, pythonFiles,
72	//                      markdownFiles, workflowFiles, testFiles
73	//   excludeFileClasses named shared file sets removed from scope (the same
74	//                      class names — testFiles is the usual one)
75	//   scanIgnoringComments  true = content assertions (matchLines, checkEachFile,
76	//                      repoWide, and requireIndexCoverage's whoseTextMatches)
77	//                      read each file with its JS/TS comments blanked
78	//                      (string-aware, line count preserved — code-scanning.mjs
79	//                      stripComments), so a comment merely naming a forbidden
80	//                      token never fires
81	//   scanIgnoringMarkdownFences  true = content assertions read each markdown
82	//                      file with its fenced code blocks blanked (line count
83	//                      preserved — the view checkSections always gets), so an
84	//                      example inside a fence never satisfies or trips a
85	//                      pattern; non-markdown files are untouched
86	//   scanTracked        true = scan every git-tracked file (mode-independent);
87	//                      default is ctx.files (the run's scanned set —
88	//                      tracked+untracked minus vendored, and only the changed
89	//                      files under --changed)
90	//   excludeFiles       RegExp (or exact path) removing files from scope
91	//   relevantWhen       repo-level relevance, all parts must hold:
92	//                        pathExists / pathAbsent          a path present/absent
93	//                        trackedFileMatches               some tracked path matches
94	//                        noTrackedFileMatches             no tracked path matches
95	//                        exactlyOneTrackedFileMatches     exactly one tracked path matches
96	//                        someTrackedFileContains          { pathMatching, text,
97	//                                                           ignoringComments } — some
98	//                                                         tracked path matching the first
99	//                                                         has text matching the second
100	//                                                         (ignoringComments: true reads it
101	//                                                         with JS/TS comments blanked)
102	//                        scanningWholeRepo                true = only under a whole-repo
103	//                                                         sweep (mode 'all'), never a
104	//                                                         --changed run
105	//                        repoContains                     some in-scope file's text
106	//                                                         matches — evaluated only
107	//                                                         if findings exist
108	//   whenMissing        { what, fix } — fires when an exact-path scanFiles is absent
109	//   maxLines           { limit, what, fix } — fires past `limit` lines, anchored there
110	//   maxLineLength      { bytes, what, fix } — one finding per file whose lines
111	//                      run past `bytes` (UTF-8 bytes, so wide characters count
112	//                      what they cost), anchored at the first over-long line;
113	//                      {count}/{longest}/{bytes} interpolate
114	//   skipLinesMatching  RegExp — lines it matches are invisible to matchLines
115	//   matchLines         [{ match, andLineMatches, unlessLineMatches,
116	//                         unlessPreviousLineMatches,
117	//                         andIndentedBlockBelowMatches,
118	//                         unlessIndentedBlockBelowMatches,
119	//                         andWithinBlockOpenedBy, unlessWithinBlockOpenedBy,
120	//                         whenPathMatches,
121	//                         whenFileMatches, unlessFileMatches, what, fix }]
122	//                      flag each line `match` hits — provided `andLineMatches`
123	//                      (if declared) also hits it, `unlessLineMatches` does
124	//                      not, and `unlessPreviousLineMatches` does not hit the
125	//                      line above (the first line has none) — in files whose
126	//                      path matches `whenPathMatches` (absent = every scanned
127	//                      file), where every `whenFileMatches` matches the text
128	//                      and `unlessFileMatches` does not; per line, the first
129	//                      matching assertion wins.
130	//                      The four BLOCK relations read the indentation structure
131	//                      a line sits in, so an assertion can say "under this key"
132	//                      / "inside that section" instead of hand-walking the
133	//                      columns (the shape Semgrep spells pattern-inside and
134	//                      ast-grep spells inside/has). A line's indented BLOCK is
135	//                      every following line more indented than it, up to the
136	//                      first non-blank line at or left of its own column
137	//                      (blank lines belong to the block, and a YAML `|`/`>`
138	//                      scalar's body is just such a block):
139	//                        andIndentedBlockBelowMatches     some line of the
140	//                                                         matched line's block
141	//                                                         matches
142	//                        unlessIndentedBlockBelowMatches  no line of it does
143	//                        andWithinBlockOpenedBy           some enclosing line —
144	//                                                         any ancestor, walking
145	//                                                         out to column 0 —
146	//                                                         matches
147	//                        unlessWithinBlockOpenedBy        no enclosing line
148	//                                                         matches
149	//   countMatchingLines [{ linesMatching, atLeast, atMost, what, fix }]
150	//                      per file, the number of lines `linesMatching` hits must
151	//                      sit within the declared bounds (at least one bound;
152	//                      atMost: 0 forbids the pattern); too many anchors at the

154	//                      {count}/{atLeast}/{atMost} interpolate

158	//                      (`whenFileMatches` takes one RegExp or a list)
159	//   repoWide           [{ unlessSomeFileMatches, flagFilesMatching,

161	//                      unless some in-scope file matches `unlessSomeFileMatches`,
162	//                      flag every file (minus `neverFlagFiles`) satisfying a
163	//                      `flagFilesMatching` group — a list of all-must-match
164	//                      RegExp lists — anchored at the first group's first
165	//                      pattern's first matching line
166	//   requirePaths       [{ path, what, fix }] — each path must exist on disk
167	//   extractValueSets   [{ setName, fromParsedFile | fromParsedFilesMatching
168	//                         (+ whereFileContains), valuesOfArraysAtFields,
169	//                         whenSetEmpty }]
170	//                      each entry extracts one NAMED value set the rule's
171	//                      other assertions may quantify over: the string values
172	//                      of the arrays at every listed field path, across every
173	//                      selected parsed document. whenSetEmpty is declared,
174	//                      never defaulted — "assertNothing" (the sole mode until
175	//                      a flagging customer exists) makes every consumer of an
176	//                      empty set assert nothing, so an absent source is inert
177	//                      by declaration rather than silently vacuous
178	//   requireIndexCoverage [{ eachTrackedPathMatching | eachScannedPathMatching

181	//                         whose content matches — read comment-blind under
182	//                         scanIgnoringComments)
183	//                         | eachValueOfSet: the name of an extractValueSets
184	//                           entry — its values are the subjects

186	//                         indexFile,

# core — working with Claudinite itself

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration, adoption and
the self-refresh. The contract a scheduled task is written to is claudinite-growth's.

- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.

- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.

- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.

- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.

- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.

- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.

- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `engineVersion` and
  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` or `ref`: the versioned flows stamp versions and
  nothing else, so those two hold the provenance of the last full re-vendor rather than of this
  mount, and a member converging nightly reads as weeks stale.

- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.

content.content:
1	# core
2	
3	Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
4	pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.
5	
6	**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
7	declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
8	into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`
9	reports it.
10	
11	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
12	
13	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
14	|---|---|---|---|
15	| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
16	| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
17	| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`claudinite-lifecycle-declared`) |
18	| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
19	| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
20	| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
21	| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
22	| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |
23	
24	## Checks
25	
26	Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
27	converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
28	not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.
29	
30	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
31	|---|---|---|---|
32	| `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
33	| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
34	| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
35	| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
36	| `conformance-work-scope` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
37	| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
38	
39	What goes wrong when one fires:
40	
41	- `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-settings.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
42	- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
43	- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` barrier edge).
44	- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
45	- `conformance-work-scope` — CI gates the tree but not the change, so every commit-scoped rule is enforced only where a session's Stop hook happens to run.
46	- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.
47	
48	The **task contract** and its checks are deliberately NOT here. Those ask whether a task is
49	*written* correctly, which is authoring; every check above asks whether Claudinite is *working* in
50	this repo. They live with the rest of the authoring surface.
51	
52	The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
53	this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
54	`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
55	what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays with the other

# core

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `claudinite-lifecycle-declared`
reports it.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading a rule that arrived from Claudinite | high | correctness | prose: 43 words + check (`claudinite-isolation`) |
| Finding a mounted skill's real path | medium | complexity | prose: 81 words |
| Wanting a pack's rules to apply here | high | correctness | prose: 47 words + check (`claudinite-lifecycle-declared`) |
| Adding a pack | medium | complexity | prose: 27 words |
| Setting a project up on Claudinite | medium | complexity | prose: 15 words |
| Deciding which pack owns a lesson | medium | complexity | prose: 59 words |
| Judging whether Claudinite is current here | medium | correctness | prose: 51 words |
| Answering "why did the mount not update" | medium | correctness | prose: 39 words |

## Checks

Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `rules-index-current` | critical | correctness | check: blocking |
| `claudinite-isolation` | high | complexity | check: blocking |
| `conformance-workflow` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `conformance-work-scope` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |

What goes wrong when one fires:

- `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` — this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-settings.json`, so none of the rules above run and the session cannot tell.
- `rules-index-current` — the generated index is missing, stale or unimported: the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session.
- `claudinite-isolation` — the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` barrier edge).
- `conformance-workflow` — nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands.
- `conformance-work-scope` — CI gates the tree but not the change, so every commit-scoped rule is enforced only where a session's Stop hook happens to run.
- `scheduler-workflow-shape` — the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted: staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break.

The **task contract** and its checks are deliberately NOT here. Those ask whether a task is
*written* correctly, which is authoring; every check above asks whether Claudinite is *working* in
this repo. They live with the rest of the authoring surface.

The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays with the other
doc-integrity rules.

## Skills

| Skill | For |
|---|---|
| [`adopt-claudinite`](skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md) | setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time — mount, hooks, checks, skills — and re-baselining one to pick up updates |
| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |

The adoption skills bundle two more checks of the same kind, over the answers a member stores
against each declared pack's questions:

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `adoption-answers-pending` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `interview-answer-stale` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

## Tasks

| Task | frequency | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `update` | daily (02:00 anchor) | the mount is behind the canon, or a declared pack moved |
| `adopt-requested-packs` | daily | the repo carries an open pack-adoption request |

`update` is the per-repo self-refresh — the task that converges a member's mount and stamps it. It
is why `claudinite-lifecycle-declared` is blocking: a member runs `update` from its **vendored** copy, and
`discoverTasks` finds only a literally-declared pack's tasks, so a repo that loses this pack's entry
loses its self-refresh, and nothing is left that could deliver it one. That is also why the task
arrived here a change later than the rest of the pack — it moved only once every non-dormant member's
declaration had been read back and confirmed to carry `core`.
