1	# Making changes to Claudinite without hurting consumers
2	
3	> **Status: provisional — beliefs, not law.** Every entry here says what we're *currently* doing
4	> and *why we think* it helps. When an entry blocks a better change, challenge the entry rather
5	> than contorting the change; being cited in this guide is not, by itself, a reason something
6	> must stay. We'll solidify entries once they've earned it.
7	
8	Claudinite is vendored into every consuming repo, so a change here lands in many places, on the
9	fleet's schedule, usually with no human watching. This guide collects what we currently believe
10	about making such changes safely. It is a maintainer document for sessions working *in* this
11	repo; it is not part of the vendored corpus.
12	
13	## First, know which channel the change travels
14	
15	Since the fleet moved to the tracked vendored mount (vendoring/DESIGN.md, phases 1–3 complete),
16	the channel model is small — nothing reaches a consumer instantly, and nothing arrives outside
17	its git history:
18	
19	- **The vendored corpus** (`engine/`, `packs/` — checks, prose, bundled skills) — each member
20	  holds a tracked snapshot under `.claudinite/shared/`, converged **whole-set** to the canon
21	  head by the nightly refresh and stamped with its provenance. Propagation lags one nightly,
22	  lands as a reviewable commit on the member's `claudinite/maintenance` PR (auto-merged on
23	  `auto-merge` delivery once the repo's checks pass, held for the owner on `review`), and the
24	  rollback story is the same channel: fix the canon, the next nightly re-heals. A wrong
25	  *blocking* check still fails every member's Stop hook — visible and recoverable, but
26	  fleet-wide noise, so treat check changes as production changes.
27	- **Migration notes** (`engine/migrations/<date>-<slug>/`, or `packs/<pack>/migrations/<date>-<slug>/`) — the channel for anything convergence
28	  can't express: renames of consumer-held wiring, declaration rewrites, one-off agentic steps.
29	  Stamp-day-gated and idempotent; the note's `legacyPresent` telemetry says when the fleet has
30	  moved and (for `retire: 'auto'`) retires the record itself.
31	- **Copied artifacts** (pack `stubs/`, seeded configs) — these do **not** propagate at all. Each
32	  consumer holds its own copy, which drifts silently unless a check enforces its shape. Changing
33	  the source file alone only affects repos bootstrapped *after* the change.
34	- **Bootstrap wiring** (the committed artifacts [bootstrap.md](bootstrap.md) seeds:
35	  `settings.json` hook registrations, the two gitignore lines, the pack declaration) —
36	  propagates through the nightly update's idempotent backfills on the same delivery PR.
37	  The discipline: a change here is written as steps that **converge from every layout in the
38	  wild**, not just from the latest.
39	
40	Out-of-repo state remains the one channel git never reaches: a web environment's pasted Setup
41	script is snapshotted at environment build. A change that moves what the pasted script calls
42	needs the script's own probe to fail fast and a member issue asking for the one human action
43	(re-paste).
44	
45	## Migrating a copied artifact (stubs and the like)
46	
47	Because copies won't move on their own, we currently migrate them through the conformance
48	checks, in one Claudinite-only change:
49	
50	1. Change the source artifact in the pack (the stub under `packs/<pack>/stubs/`).
51	2. Make sure the pack's conformance check enforces the properties that changed, with a `fix`
52	   that says how to align (usually "re-copy the stub"). A consumer's own next session then
53	   raises a blocking finding and performs the migration in that repo — no per-repo PR from
54	   here.
55	3. Keep the pack's `detect` fingerprint **tolerant of the legacy shape** while copies migrate
56	   (e.g. a `LEGACY_*` list beside the current constant), so a fresh `--init` still recognizes a
57	   not-yet-migrated repo and seeds the pack.
58	
59	Fleet-wide "everyone has migrated" telemetry exists — declare the rename as a
60	[baseline migration](engine/migrations/README.md), **in the same change that introduces the tolerance**: a
61	tolerance that lands without its record has no signal that will ever retire it. Any legacy shape a
62	tolerance keeps readable (an old path, a stub's old form, a legacy key *inside* a consumer's config
63	file) is trackable the same way, `legacyPresent` reading whatever expresses the old shape. The
64	fleet census probes every repo for the legacy shape and **auto-retires** the migration once none
65	remain. While a migration's tolerance still lives inline (readers not yet consulting its
66	`resolvePath`), keep it `retire:'manual'` and drop it deliberately.
67	
68	## Relocating wiring that consumers reference by path
69	
70	What we learned moving the sync hook between homes (#211/#213), and again retiring it (#385):
71	the file is only half the change — every *reference* to its old path is itself a consumer-held
72	copy that won't move on its own, and each needs a channel.
73	
74	- **Enumerate the reference holders before touching the file** — `settings.json` hook commands,
75	  other canon scripts, the fleet routine's discovery probe, docs — then grep for the old path
76	  afterward (the text-sweep skill owns the mechanics). Include state that lives
77	  **outside the repo entirely**: a web environment's pasted Setup script is snapshotted at
78	  environment build, where no check or update run can ever reach it.
79	- **Never break the channel the migration itself travels through.** Fleet discovery finds
80	  members by the tracked `.claudinite-settings.json`; a probe that recognizes only a new shape
81	  doesn't make noise like a wrong check — it **silently and permanently orphans** every
82	  unmigrated repo, since discovery is what reaches them to migrate them. Same for the settings
83	  registration: a session already running when the canon change lands still runs the old wiring,
84	  so the old entry point must keep working until the member's refresh lands (that's what the
85	  stable `engine/hooks/*-command` addresses are for — relocate what they call, not the
86	  addresses).
87	- **References nothing can reach get tolerance in the artifact instead** — prefer a probe that
88	  *detects* staleness (and asks for the one human action) over hoping the stale copy keeps
89	  working.
90	
91	## A vendored file executes in the consumer's context
92	
93	Canon files that ship into consumers — the whole vendor set (`engine/` and the declared packs) —
94	run at their *landed* path inside the consumer's repo, not in the canon checkout they were
95	written and tested in. Before changing one, audit every environment assumption against each
96	context it ships to: **git discovers `.git` by walking upward**, so introspection from a vendored
97	copy answers with the *consumer's* repo unless constrained to the expected toplevel (the
98	`--show-toplevel` guard in `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs` — an unconstrained `rev-parse HEAD` nearly
99	stamped a consumer sha as canon provenance, #340); relative paths resolve against the vendored
100	location; network access and credentials present where the file was written may be absent where it
101	lands. The co-located header comment at the usage site carries each specific trap; this entry is
102	the class.
103	
104	## Normalize requirements to canonical form at the door
105	
106	When a requirement arrives expressed in someone's local context — a schedule in a local
107	timezone, a path from one repo's layout, a phrasing tied to one project's vocabulary — we
108	currently translate it to its canonical form **once, on the way in**, and record only the
109	result. A "nightly at 3:30 my time" request lands in the canon as a fixed UTC cron, stated in
110	UTC and nothing else. The reasoning: the person who asked can carry the original framing;
111	consumers shouldn't inherit it, and the canon shouldn't have to re-explain a conversion (or its
112	edge cases, like DST) forever. If the origin matters for revisiting the decision, it belongs in
113	the issue/PR that made the change, not in the shipped artifact.
114	
115	## How to prove a change is consumer-safe
116	
117	Canon CI is not evidence about consumers. The canon's own packs are always already migrated, so a
118	change that breaks every member passes it green — which is exactly what #555 did, on 2026-07-29,
119	while eleven consumer packs stopped validating and (because a pack that fails validation
120	contributes no rules) their checks stopped running with no other symptom.
121	
122	So there is a procedure, in three layers, cheapest first.
123	
124	**1. The fixture rehearsal — automatic, every PR.** `vendoring/rehearsal/` builds four fixture
125	consumers, one per shape the fleet has, and runs the REAL converge against your working tree:
126	`apply-vendor-set` → `converge-wiring` → `engine/migrations/apply`, then `engine/selftest.mjs` and
127	`check_the_world`. It runs in **two modes**, and the second is the half people forget:
128	
129	| mode | stamp | answers |
130	|---|---|---|
131	| `fresh` | now | does the ordinary nightly path still work? |
132	| `stale` | pinned in the past | **does it work WITH a migration?** — note selection only fires against an old stamp, so a record that is missing, misdated, or not idempotent shows up here and nowhere else |
133	
134	Adding a shape is the cheap way to cover a case the fixtures don't: a new entry in
135	`fixtures.mjs` is a few lines, and it is one of the two things that discharge the
136	`consumer-safe-change` check.
137	
138	**2. The `consumer-safe-change` check — automatic, work scope.** A change touching a contract
139	consumers hold a copy of (the manifest vocabulary, a blocking rule's severity, the scheduler stub)
140	must ship **either** a migration record **or** a rehearsal fixture. They answer different
141	questions — *members are moved across* versus *members are unharmed* — and both are legitimate.
142	A genuinely additive change needs only the fixture; anything that renames or requires something
143	needs the record, because only a record moves a member that is already out there.
144	
145	**3. The live canary — the required final step of any core change.** A fixture only tests what
146	someone remembered to model. `.github/workflows/canary-rehearsal.yml` converges a real disposable
147	repo against a canon ref and asks whether it still works: manually via `workflow_dispatch`, and
148	automatically on merge to `main`. Post-merge is still worth having — knowing within minutes beats
149	finding out from the fleet two days later, which is how long #585 went unnoticed.
150	
151	Run it by hand before merging anything structural:
152	`gh workflow run canary-rehearsal.yml -f ref=<your-branch>`. The worker's rehearsal mode converges,
153	reports, and **restores** — no commit, no branch, no stamp. That last one matters: stamping a branch
154	head leaves the member `ref-not-on-trunk`, which the #328 anti-rewind guard then refuses to converge
155	over, so a careless rehearsal wedges the repo it was rehearsing on. That is not hypothetical; it
156	happened by hand to all thirteen members at once on 2026-07-30.
157	
158	**What none of this covers.** A change whose damage is invisible to both the self-test and the
159	conformance sweep — a behaviour change inside a task, say — is still on you to reason about. The
160	layers narrow the class; they do not close it.
161

  moved and (for `retire: 'auto'`) retires the record itself.
- **Copied artifacts** (pack `stubs/`, seeded configs) — these do **not** propagate at all. Each
  consumer holds its own copy, which drifts silently unless a check enforces its shape. Changing
  the source file alone only affects repos bootstrapped *after* the change.
- **Bootstrap wiring** (the committed artifacts [bootstrap.md](bootstrap.md) seeds:
  `settings.json` hook registrations, the two gitignore lines, the pack declaration) —
  propagates through the nightly update's idempotent backfills on the same delivery PR.
  The discipline: a change here is written as steps that **converge from every layout in the
  wild**, not just from the latest.

Out-of-repo state remains the one channel git never reaches: a web environment's pasted Setup
script is snapshotted at environment build. A change that moves what the pasted script calls
needs the script's own probe to fail fast and a member issue asking for the one human action
(re-paste).

## Migrating a copied artifact (stubs and the like)

Because copies won't move on their own, we currently migrate them through the conformance
checks, in one Claudinite-only change:

1. Change the source artifact in the pack (the stub under `packs/<pack>/stubs/`).
2. Make sure the pack's conformance check enforces the properties that changed, with a `fix`
   that says how to align (usually "re-copy the stub"). A consumer's own next session then
   raises a blocking finding and performs the migration in that repo — no per-repo PR from
   here.
3. Keep the pack's `detect` fingerprint **tolerant of the legacy shape** while copies migrate
   (e.g. a `LEGACY_*` list beside the current constant), so a fresh `--init` still recognizes a
   not-yet-migrated repo and seeds the pack.

Fleet-wide "everyone has migrated" telemetry exists — declare the rename as a
[baseline migration](engine/migrations/README.md), **in the same change that introduces the tolerance**: a
tolerance that lands without its record has no signal that will ever retire it. Any legacy shape a
tolerance keeps readable (an old path, a stub's old form, a legacy key *inside* a consumer's config
file) is trackable the same way, `legacyPresent` reading whatever expresses the old shape. The
fleet census probes every repo for the legacy shape and **auto-retires** the migration once none
remain. While a migration's tolerance still lives inline (readers not yet consulting its
`resolvePath`), keep it `retire:'manual'` and drop it deliberately.

## Relocating wiring that consumers reference by path

What we learned moving the sync hook between homes (#211/#213), and again retiring it (#385):
the file is only half the change — every *reference* to its old path is itself a consumer-held
copy that won't move on its own, and each needs a channel.

- **Enumerate the reference holders before touching the file** — `settings.json` hook commands,
  other canon scripts, the fleet routine's discovery probe, docs — then grep for the old path
  afterward (the text-sweep skill owns the mechanics). Include state that lives
  **outside the repo entirely**: a web environment's pasted Setup script is snapshotted at
  environment build, where no check or update run can ever reach it.
- **Never break the channel the migration itself travels through.** Fleet discovery finds
  members by the tracked `.claudinite-settings.json`; a probe that recognizes only a new shape
  doesn't make noise like a wrong check — it **silently and permanently orphans** every
  unmigrated repo, since discovery is what reaches them to migrate them. Same for the settings
  registration: a session already running when the canon change lands still runs the old wiring,
  so the old entry point must keep working until the member's refresh lands (that's what the
  stable `engine/hooks/*-command` addresses are for — relocate what they call, not the
  addresses).
- **References nothing can reach get tolerance in the artifact instead** — prefer a probe that
  *detects* staleness (and asks for the one human action) over hoping the stale copy keeps
  working.

## A vendored file executes in the consumer's context

Canon files that ship into consumers — the whole vendor set (`engine/` and the declared packs) —
run at their *landed* path inside the consumer's repo, not in the canon checkout they were
written and tested in. Before changing one, audit every environment assumption against each
context it ships to: **git discovers `.git` by walking upward**, so introspection from a vendored
copy answers with the *consumer's* repo unless constrained to the expected toplevel (the
`--show-toplevel` guard in `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs` — an unconstrained `rev-parse HEAD` nearly
stamped a consumer sha as canon provenance, #340); relative paths resolve against the vendored
location; network access and credentials present where the file was written may be absent where it
lands. The co-located header comment at the usage site carries each specific trap; this entry is
the class.

## Normalize requirements to canonical form at the door

When a requirement arrives expressed in someone's local context — a schedule in a local
timezone, a path from one repo's layout, a phrasing tied to one project's vocabulary — we
currently translate it to its canonical form **once, on the way in**, and record only the
result. A "nightly at 3:30 my time" request lands in the canon as a fixed UTC cron, stated in
UTC and nothing else. The reasoning: the person who asked can carry the original framing;
consumers shouldn't inherit it, and the canon shouldn't have to re-explain a conversion (or its
edge cases, like DST) forever. If the origin matters for revisiting the decision, it belongs in
the issue/PR that made the change, not in the shipped artifact.

## How to prove a change is consumer-safe

Canon CI is not evidence about consumers. The canon's own packs are always already migrated, so a
change that breaks every member passes it green — which is exactly what #555 did, on 2026-07-29,
while eleven consumer packs stopped validating and (because a pack that fails validation
contributes no rules) their checks stopped running with no other symptom.

So there is a procedure, in three layers, cheapest first.

**1. The fixture rehearsal — automatic, every PR.** `vendoring/rehearsal/` builds four fixture
consumers, one per shape the fleet has, and runs the REAL converge against your working tree:
`apply-vendor-set` → `converge-wiring` → `engine/migrations/apply`, then `engine/selftest.mjs` and
`check_the_world`. It runs in **two modes**, and the second is the half people forget:

| mode | stamp | answers |
|---|---|---|
| `fresh` | now | does the ordinary nightly path still work? |
| `stale` | pinned in the past | **does it work WITH a migration?** — note selection only fires against an old stamp, so a record that is missing, misdated, or not idempotent shows up here and nowhere else |

Adding a shape is the cheap way to cover a case the fixtures don't: a new entry in
`fixtures.mjs` is a few lines, and it is one of the two things that discharge the
`consumer-safe-change` check.

**2. The `consumer-safe-change` check — automatic, work scope.** A change touching a contract
consumers hold a copy of (the manifest vocabulary, a blocking rule's severity, the scheduler stub)
must ship **either** a migration record **or** a rehearsal fixture. They answer different
questions — *members are moved across* versus *members are unharmed* — and both are legitimate.
A genuinely additive change needs only the fixture; anything that renames or requires something
needs the record, because only a record moves a member that is already out there.

**3. The live canary — the required final step of any core change.** A fixture only tests what
someone remembered to model. `.github/workflows/canary-rehearsal.yml` converges a real disposable
repo against a canon ref and asks whether it still works: manually via `workflow_dispatch`, and
automatically on merge to `main`. Post-merge is still worth having — knowing within minutes beats
finding out from the fleet two days later, which is how long #585 went unnoticed.

Run it by hand before merging anything structural:
`gh workflow run canary-rehearsal.yml -f ref=<your-branch>`. The worker's rehearsal mode converges,
reports, and **restores** — no commit, no branch, no stamp. That last one matters: stamping a branch
head leaves the member `ref-not-on-trunk`, which the #328 anti-rewind guard then refuses to converge
over, so a careless rehearsal wedges the repo it was rehearsing on. That is not hypothetical; it
happened by hand to all thirteen members at once on 2026-07-30.

**What none of this covers.** A change whose damage is invisible to both the self-test and the
conformance sweep — a behaviour change inside a task, say — is still on you to reason about. The
layers narrow the class; they do not close it.

input.head: claude/nifty-archimedes-j0lbib
input.body:
## Summary

Weekly prose-to-checks sweep over `.claudinite/local/packs` and `packs` (per the [prose-to-checks](packs/claudinite-growth/skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) skill). Surveyed all 34 canon packs plus this repo's two local packs for always-testable working rules that were never converted; converted the two strongest candidates and deleted the prose they now fully cover.

- **`doc-pointer-resolves`** (`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite`, world scope) — every rule module's `doc:` field must resolve to a real file, repo-root-relative or relative to the rule's own pack (the corpus spells it both ways, inconsistently, so the check accepts whichever interpretation resolves). Replaces the RULES.md line asking a session to "grep for and re-verify every `doc:` field by hand" after a move. Verified silent against all 49 real `doc:` fields currently in the corpus.
- **`shared-tree-immutable`** (`packs/claudinite-lifecycle`, work scope) — flags any branch commit touching `.claudinite/shared/` directly, except the update flow's own commit. Replaces the RULES.md line "Never edit anything there." Ships `blocking`, so per `consumer-safe-change` it needed either a migration record or a rehearsal-fixture discharge; since a work-scope rule is never exercised by the fixture rehearsal (which runs only `selftest` and `check_the_world`, never `check_the_work`), I discharged it with a comment in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` explaining why rather than fabricating a fixture that would prove nothing — documented in the second commit.

Both checks ship with a see-it-fail fixture (a violating case and a clean case) and were verified silent against the real tree. Full suite (2674 tests), `check_the_work`, and `check_the_world` are all green.

Candidates considered but not converted this run (judgment calls or false-positive risk that didn't clear the bar — logged here rather than a separate backlog issue, since none reached the point of being built and rejected): aws-sam CORS `AllowOrigins`, chrome-extension service-worker module type and `web_accessible_resources` graph, headless-browser hardcoded browser path, macos `command -v swift` and entitlement/runtime-flag pairing, node `--test` path resolution, jwt committed key material, flutter port/plugin boundary, firebase `.gitignore`/ruleset catch-all, static-website root-relative URLs, web-speech `isFinal` trap. Several of these are strong future candidates for the next sweep.

## Changed folders

- **`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/`** — new `worldRules/doc-pointer-resolves.mjs` check + fixture test; RULES.md loses the paragraph it now covers; VERSIONS.md row.
- **`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/`** — new `workRules/shared-tree-immutable.mjs` check + fixture test; RULES.md loses the paragraph it now covers; README.md rule/check index updated to match; `pack.mjs` version bump + VERSIONS.md row (required — this pack ships to every member).
- **`vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`** — a documentation-only comment explaining why work-scope rules need no new fixture shape, discharging `consumer-safe-change` for the new blocking rule.

## Test plan

- [x] `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2674 pass, 0 fail
- [x] `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` — clean
- [x] `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking
- [x] Both new checks verified silent against the real tree (not just synthetic fixtures)

Closes #1274

1	// APPLYING a status transition — the write half of the vocabulary whose read half
2	// is `work-item.mjs`'s decode (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §4, the migration of #1119).
3	//
4	// One rule, and it is why this is not a plain `swapLabel`: the item may wear ANY
5	// engine version's spelling of the status it is leaving. A member's items outlive
6	// its converges, so an item filed as `task:ready` is picked up by an engine that
7	// writes `task:status:waiting-for-executor`, and a swap that named one spelling
8	// would leave the other standing — an item wearing two live statuses, which is the
9	// torn state the janitor exists to repair.
10	//
11	// Writes stay granular (add and remove named labels, never a set-write): with
12	// several executors and a scheduler run moving labels at once, a set-write from a
13	// stale snapshot clobbers a concurrent transition (DESIGN §4).
14	// The removes are UNCONDITIONAL — every spelling of the status being left, not
15	// only the ones the caller's snapshot shows. A caller holds the labels it read
16	// before its own earlier transitions, so filtering on that snapshot would skip
17	// exactly the label this engine just wrote; removing a label an issue does not
18	// carry 404s, which is the end state asked for and therefore success.
19	import { spellingsOf } from './work-item.mjs';
20	
21	// Move `item` out of `fromStatus` (canonical — every spelling of it goes) and into
22	// the label `to`, which is whatever spelling this engine writes.
23	export async function swapStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus, to) {
24	  await clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus);
25	  return api.addLabel(gh, repo, item.number, to);
26	}
27	
28	// Leave a status without entering another — the close path, where the terminal
29	// label is applied separately.
30	export async function clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, status) {
31	  for (const label of spellingsOf(status)) {
32	    await api.removeLabel(gh, repo, item.number, label);
33	  }
34	}
35
